admission_rule: Reviewed 1791 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph of 30 July 1791: 'A correspondent informs, that the treaty, lately held under commission from the President of the United States, by Timothy Pickering, Esq. of Wilkesbarre, with those Indian tribes commonly called the Six Nations, at Newtown-Point, on the north-west branch of the Susquehanna, in the state of New-York, was concluded on the 18th inst. to the satisfaction of all parties, by a recapitulatory speech from the Commissioner. The principal object of this treaty was, to confirm the peace that has subsisted between us, ever since the treaty of Fort Stanwix, in 1784, and prevent the Five Nations from joining the Western Indians, now at war.' A correspondent's account.
label: 'A correspondent informs, that the treaty, lately held under commission from the President of the United States, by Timothy Pickering': the treaty with the Six Nations at Newtown Point, July 1791

admission_rule: Reviewed 1781 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the account dated 'Royal Oak, Lynhaven Bay, March 21, 1781. On Friday the 16th instant, at 6 A. M. the Iris made the signal for discovering five strange sail to the N. N. E.', which a New York paper introduces as 'an account of an action fought on the 16th, between the British and French squadrons, off the Chesapeake', brought by an officer of Vice-Admiral Arbuthnot's flagship. The British squadron's account.
label: Royal Oak, Lynnhaven Bay, 21 March 1781: the British account of the action of 16 March between the British and French squadrons off the Chesapeake

admission_rule: Reviewed 1810 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the act of Congress approved on 1 May 1810, 'An act concerning the commercial intercourse between the United States and Great Britain and France and their dependencies, and for other purposes': 'That from and after the passage of this act, no British or French armed vessel shall be permitted to enter the harbors or waters under the jurisdiction of the United States'; its fourth section provides that in case either Great Britain or France shall, before the third day of March next, so revoke or modify her edicts as that they shall cease to violate the neutral commerce of the United States, which fact the President shall declare by proclamation, and the other nation shall not within three months revoke hers, sections of the non-intercourse act of 1809 shall be revived against that other nation. Counted where the act is printed under its own title; the bill printed before it passed is not counted with it (X-1803-10). The act of Congress.
label: The act of 1 May 1810 concerning the commercial intercourse between the United States and Great Britain and France

admission_rule: Reviewed 1791 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the act: 'An Act declaring the consent of Congress, that a new State be formed within the jurisdiction of the Commonwealth of Virginia, and admitted into this Union, by the name of the State of Kentucky. Whereas the legislature of the Commonwealth of Virginia, by an act entitled, "An act concerning the erection of the district of Kentucky into an independent State," passed the eighteenth day of December, one thousand seven hundred and eighty-nine, have consented, that the district of Kentucky, within the jurisdiction of the said Commonwealth, and according to its actual boundaries at the time of passing the act aforesaid, should be formed into a new State'. The Kentucky Gazette prints it twice, the second time among the papers of the Kentucky convention (C-08); the New-Hampshire Gazette's list of the session's acts of 16 June, which names it, is not counted (C-07). The act itself, as the papers print it.
label: An Act declaring the consent of Congress that a new State be formed within the jurisdiction of the Commonwealth of Virginia, and admitted into the Union by the name of the State of Kentucky

admission_rule: Reviewed 1792 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of 'An Act establishing a Mint, and regulating the Coins of the United States', of the first session of the Second Congress (the New Hampshire Gazetteer's title reads 'to establish a Mint, and regulate the Coins'): 'Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled', the mint, its officers, and the gold, silver and copper coins. Congress's own act.
label: Congress, April 1792: an act establishing a mint, and regulating the coins of the United States

admission_rule: Reviewed 1789 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the act of Congress approved on 27 July 1789, as the papers print it from the laws of the first session ('Congress of the United States. Begun and held at the City of New-York, on Wednesday the Fourth of March, One Thousand Seven Hundred and Eighty-Nine'): 'An ACT for establishing an Executive Department, to be denominated the Department of Foreign Affairs. BE it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled, That there shall be an executive department, to be denominated the department of foreign affairs, and that there shall be a principal officer therein, to be called the Secretary for the department of foreign affairs ...'. Lists of the session's acts that give only its title, and the Senate's journal naming the bill, are not counted (C-07).
label: An Act for establishing an Executive Department, to be denominated the Department of Foreign Affairs, approved 27 July 1789

admission_rule: Reviewed 1802 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings, among the laws of the first session of the Seventh Congress, of 'An Act Fixing the military peace establishment of the United States': 'That the military peace establishment of the United States, from and after the first of June next, shall be composed of one regiment of artillerists and two regiments of infantry, with such officers, military agents, and engineers, as are hereinafter mentioned'. Among its sections, the President is empowered to organise a corps of engineers, which 'shall be stationed at West Point in the State of New-York, and shall constitute a military academy'. Congress's own act, printed 'By Authority'.
label: The act of 16 March 1802 fixing the military peace establishment of the United States

admission_rule: Reviewed 1791 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the act: 'An Act for raising and adding another Regiment to the Military Establishment of the United States, and for making farther Provision for the Protection of the Frontiers. Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled, That there shall be raised an additional regiment of infantry, which, exclusive of the commissioned officers, shall consist of nine hundred and twelve non-commissioned officers, privates and musicians.' The New-Hampshire Gazette's list of the session's acts of 16 June, which names it, is not counted (C-07). The act itself, as the papers print it.
label: An Act for raising and adding another regiment to the military establishment of the United States, and for making further provision for the protection of the frontiers

admission_rule: Reviewed 1791 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the act: 'An Act for the admission of the State of Vermont into this Union. The State of Vermont having petitioned the Congress to be admitted a Member of the United States—Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled, and it is hereby enacted and declared, That, on the Fourth day of March, one thousand seven hundred and ninety-one, the said State, by the name and style of "The State of Vermont," shall be received and admitted into the Union, as a new and entire Member of the United States of America.' The Patowmac Guardian prints only the House's proceedings on the bill, and the New-Hampshire Gazette's list of the session's acts of 16 June names it; neither is counted (C-07). The act itself, as the papers print it.
label: An Act for the admission of the State of Vermont into this Union

admission_rule: Reviewed 1792 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of 'An Act for making farther and more effectual Provision for the Protection of the Frontiers of the United States', of the first session of the Second Congress: 'Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled', the battalions to be raised and their officers. Congress's own act.
label: Congress, March 1792: an act for making farther and more effectual provision for the protection of the frontiers of the United States

admission_rule: Reviewed 1792 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of 'An Act more effectually to provide for the National Defence, by establishing an Uniform Militia throughout the United States', of the first session of the Second Congress: 'Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled', who shall be enrolled in the militia, and their arms and officers. Congress's own act.
label: Congress, May 1792: an act more effectually to provide for the national defence, by establishing an uniform militia throughout the United States

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the act of Congress approved on 28 February 1806 'To suspend the commercial intercourse between the United States, and certain parts of the island of St. Domingo': trade with any part of the island 'not in possession, and under the acknowledged government of France, shall be, and is hereby prohibited'. A law.
label: The act of 28 February 1806 suspending trade with parts of St. Domingo

admission_rule: Reviewed 1792 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of 'An Act to establish the Post-Office and Post-Roads within the United States', of the first session of the Second Congress: 'Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America, in Congress assembled', the post roads, the postmaster general, the rates of postage and the carriage of newspapers. Congress's own act.
label: Congress, February 1792: an act to establish the post-office and post-roads within the United States

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of John Quincy Adams's letter of 8 June 1808 to the Massachusetts legislature, resigning his seat in the Senate after the legislature had passed resolutions disapproving of measures he had supported.
label: John Quincy Adams resigns from the Senate

admission_rule: Reviewed 1797 printings of the address or the answer, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of Vice President Adams's farewell address to the Senate (15 February 1797), plus the Senate's answer where printed separately.
label: Adams's farewell to the Senate

admission_rule: Reviewed 1797 printings of the speech text, checked against the scan (opening only).
definition: Printings of President Adams's speech of 16 May 1797 opening the special session of Congress. Pages that only quote phrases from it are not included.
label: Adams's speech to Congress

admission_rule: Reviewed 1791 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the Senate's address in answer to the President's speech, which the Vice-President and the Senate presented to the President on 31 October 1791: 'The Senate of the United States have received with the highest satisfaction, the assurances of public prosperity contained in your speech to both houses: the multiplied blessings of Providence have not escaped our notice, or failed to excite our gratitude.' The Senate's own address.
label: The address of the Senate to the President in answer to his speech, October 1791: 'The Senate of the United States have received with the highest satisfaction, the assurances of public prosperity contained in your speech'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: The addresses that the Provincial Congress of New York presented to General Washington on his way to the army, and that the Provincial Congress of Massachusetts presented to him and to General Lee on their arrival at Cambridge, with Washington's answer to the Massachusetts Congress, as the papers printed them in July and August 1775. The Congresses' and the general's own words.
label: Addresses to General Washington and General Lee, June and July 1775, and Washington's answer

admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Boston paragraph of 12 November 1778: 'In the violent storm of last week, the wind being at N. E. though variable, the British fleet under the command of Admiral Byron, consisting of sixteen sail of the line, were cruising near Cape Cod'; it reports that the Somerset, of 64 guns, was cast ashore near the Race, at the head of the Cape, and entirely lost. A Boston paper's report, at second hand.
label: Boston, November 1778: the British fleet under Admiral Byron, cruising near Cape Cod, in the violent storm

admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a New York paragraph of early March 1775: 'We are informed by a Captain of a vessel who arrived here a few days ago from Antigua, that Admiral Parry with the royal squadron under his command, on that station, has received orders to sail for Boston, where this gentleman will be second in command'. A report at second hand, from a ship's captain; a single paragraph of the papers' news (some papers print it after a paragraph on orders from Virginia for arms, which is counted apart).
label: New York, March 1775: a captain from Antigua reports that Admiral Parry and his squadron are ordered to Boston

admission_rule: Reviewed 1792 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a report of the Albany Gazette of July 1792: 'a deputation from the Chiefs of the Five Nations, are on their way to the Miami Village, where a treaty is shortly to be held by the hostile Indians. This deputation is sent under the direction of the Superintendant of Indian Affairs, and charged with a message from the Executive of the United States to the said Indians, demanding a cessation of hostilities'. The papers introduce it in their own words ('The Albany Gazette says, that'; 'A gentleman of respectability from the Genesee country informs, that'); the excerpt starts at the words they share (C-02). A report at second hand.
label: The Albany Gazette, July 1792: a deputation from the chiefs of the Five Nations on its way to the Miami village, where the hostile Indians are to hold a treaty

admission_rule: Reviewed 1781 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from a gentleman in Albany dated 8 September 1781: 'We have just received the disagreeable news, that out of forty men colonel Willet sent out on a scout from fort Plain (his present station) only twelve returned; the rest either being killed or taken, by a superior force of the enemy'. A letter-writer's account.
label: Albany, 8 September 1781: a letter that of forty men Colonel Willett sent on a scout from Fort Plain, twelve returned

admission_rule: Reviewed 1792 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an Albany paragraph of 9 February 1792: 'The Indians settled at Brothertown in Herkemer county, we are told, have sent a petition to the Legislature, praying to be put on the footing of free white citizens, except that they do not wish the privilege of selling their lands'; the reasons they give follow. A news paragraph reporting a petition.
label: Albany, 9 February 1792: the Indians settled at Brothertown petition the Legislature to be put on the footing of free white citizens

admission_rule: Reviewed 1791 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an Alexandria paragraph of 21 April 1791: 'On Friday the 15th inst. the Hon. Daniel Carroll, and Dr. David Stewart, arrived in this town, to superintend the fixing of the first Corner-Stone of the Federal District.' The paragraph goes on to the procession of the Mayor and Commonality and the members of the town's lodges to Jones's Point. An Alexandria paper's report.
label: Alexandria, April 1791: the commissioners Daniel Carroll and David Stewart arrive to superintend the fixing of the first corner-stone of the Federal District

admission_rule: Reviewed 1797 printings of this report, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Civitavecchia report (30 June 1797) of a battle near Messina between an Algerine cruiser and a ship of the King of the Two Sicilies. The battle itself is not independently verified.
label: Algerine–Sicilian sea battle

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: A New Bedford report of February 1808 that Algiers had declared war on the United States, the American consul general's circular of the same weeks that the dispute was settled, and a June report of the Dey's new demands. Contains those three groups.
label: Algiers and the American ships, 1808

admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Two items from Algiers printed from September to November 1805: a Salem report, by way of Leghorn, of an insurrection at Algiers, and the letter of 9 September of the American charge d'affaires at Algiers that 'the soldiers rose in a body and murdered the Dey'. Contains those two groups.
label: Reports from Algiers, 1805

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a New Bedford handbill of 30 January 1808: the ship Honestus, 42 days from the Downs, had been told off Cape Trafalgar that Algiers had declared war against America and captured American vessels. It is a report; the consul general's circular, printed in the same weeks, says the dispute had been settled.
label: New Bedford: 'War with Algiers'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a letter from Alicante of 27 March 1808, received at Boston and introduced as 'interesting particulars of the affairs of Spain': a rumour that the royal family meant to leave for Cadiz and embark on the English squadron brought crowds to the palace at Aranjuez; the Prince of Peace fell, and the King resigned his crown to his son. One paper prints only its later part.
label: Alicante letter: 'a rumour being spread at Aranjuez'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of another letter from Alicante of 27 March 1808, which reached Boston by the brig Sally: on the evening of 18 March the Prince of Peace ordered the Spanish and Walloon guards to Aranjuez; a report that the royal family meant to flee to Gibraltar and America brought a crowd to the palace crying 'kill the traitor'.
label: Alicante letter: the guards ordered to Aranjuez

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Two letters from Alicante, both dated 27 March 1808, on the rising at Aranjuez and the fall of the Prince of Peace, as American papers printed them in May 1808, several of them side by side ('Extract of another Letter'). Contains those two groups. Each is one letter-writer's account.
label: Revolution in Spain: two letters from Alicante

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the first number of The American Crisis, 'by the author of Common Sense' (Thomas Paine), printed in January 1777: 'These are the times that try men's souls: The summer soldier and the sunshine patriot will, in this crisis, shrink from the service of his country; but he that stands it now, deserves the love and thanks of man and woman. Tyranny, like hell, is not easily conquered'. Only printings dated 1777 are counted (C-11); Dunlap's Packet of 4 January prints its later part, whose opening stood in an issue of 1776 (C-06). The writer's own argument.
label: The American Crisis, Number I, by the author of Common Sense: 'These are the times that try men's souls'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1773 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter of 20 August 1773, headed from Amsterdam in three papers, from the Hague and from Paris in the others: 'By a Scheveling boat I have an opportunity of sending you this important information, that by a courier arrived last night at the Hague, from Paris, Madame Barre is disgraced. The Choiseul party are triumphant; and war will be declared against England in less than ten days ...'. A letter at second hand, as the London papers gave it and the papers reprinted it.
label: Amsterdam (the Hague, or Paris), 20 August 1773: a letter: 'By a Scheveling boat I have an opportunity of sending you this important information, that by a courier arrived last night at the Hague, from Paris, Madame Barre is disgraced'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from Daniel Crommelin and Sons, Amsterdam, 30 December 1807, received at New York on 13 February 1808: official news of a decree of the French Emperor at Milan under which vessels that had submitted to British search or paid duties in Britain were to be treated as denationalised. It is a merchant house's summary, not the decree.
label: An Amsterdam letter on the Milan decree

admission_rule: Reviewed 1781 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from a gentleman at Amsterdam dated 10 May 1781: 'His Excellency Mr. Adams, who has been well received at the Hague, presented last week a Memorial to their High Mightinesses, which will bring on the great question of your Independence'. A letter-writer's account.
label: Amsterdam, 10 May 1781: a letter that Mr. Adams has presented a memorial to the States General

admission_rule: Reviewed 1790 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an anecdote, headed 'Anecdote' in the New-Hampshire Gazetteer: 'The following incident lately occurred in one of the eastern States. A French Gentleman, totally unacquainted with our language, being introduced to a circle of young ladies and gentlemen in a country town, after the usual compliments had passed, he seated himself beside a beautiful young lady ...'. No one is named. A story told for amusement, as the papers print it (C-10).
label: Autumn 1790: 'The following incident lately occurred in one of the eastern States. A French Gentleman, totally unacquainted with our language ...'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1773 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from Annapolis of 2 July 1773 (5 July in the New-Hampshire Gazette) in two wordings: 'Our Assembly is passing an act, to sell out 40,000l. bank stock, and lend it to the people in Maryland, to keep up their credit, which will be of great service at this time ...' (the others: 'Our assembly are passing an act for selling forty thousand pounds sterling bank stock ...'). A letter at second hand, as the papers reprinted it.
label: Annapolis, July 1773: a letter: 'Our Assembly is passing an act, to sell out 40,000l. bank stock, and lend it to the people in Maryland, to keep up their credit'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of President Jefferson's annual message to Congress of 2 December 1806: 'It would have given me, fellow citizens, great satisfaction to announce, in the moment of your meeting, that the difficulties in our foreign relations, existing at the time of your last separation, had been amicably and justly terminated'. The executive's own account of the year.
label: The President's annual message of 2 December 1806

admission_rule: Reviewed 1791 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the address of the House of Representatives in answer to the President's speech, which the Speaker delivered to the President at his house on 28 October 1791: 'In receiving your address at the opening of the present session, the House of Representatives have taken an ample share in the feelings inspired by the actual prosperity, and flattering prospects of our country: And whilst, with becoming gratitude to heaven, we ascribe this happiness to the true source from which it flows, we behold with an animating pleasure'. The House's own address.
label: The answer of the House of Representatives to the President's speech, October 1791: 'In receiving your address at the opening of the present session, the House of Representatives have taken an ample share in the feelings inspired by the actual prosperity, and flattering prospects of our country'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from the master of an American vessel, dated Antigua, 28 December 1805, first printed in the Norfolk Gazette, which had it from 'a mercantile friend': 'Every American vessel coming from a French Island, with cargo, is certain to be carried in'. One writer's account; it alleges that 'a junto consisting of the Judge, the Lawyers, the owners of privateers' shares the costs charged to Americans.
label: A shipmaster's letter from Antigua: American vessels carried in

admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from a house in Antwerp to one in Bordeaux (28 September 1807), brought by the Sally-Barker-Windsor: 'We understand' that the Emperor had ordered every vessel bound to or from England to be captured, 'a mortal blow to the American commerce'. It reports a rumoured order.
label: An Antwerp letter: ships to or from England to be taken

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Boston Gazette report of 5 September 1808: the ship Arcturus, 48 days from St. Sebastian, had arrived with P. R. Livingston, bearer of dispatches from the French government, and with passengers' accounts that General Dupont had been defeated at Cordova and Andujar. A report from passengers ('is said').
label: News from Spain by the Arcturus

admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the armistice between the French and Russian armies agreed at Tilsit on 21 June 1807 (signed by Berthier and Prince Labanoff), the preliminary to the peace.
label: Armistice between France and Russia

admission_rule: Reviewed 1810 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the extract of General Armstrong's letter to the Secretary of State of 10 March 1810: 'I have at length received a verbal message in answer to my note of the 21st ult. It was from the minister of foreign relations, and is in the following words:—"His Majesty has decided to sell the American property seized in Spain, but the money arising therefrom shall remain in depot"', followed by his letter of that day to the Duke of Cadore, which asks whether the seizures are reprisals for the non-intercourse law and argues that the law, operating only within the United States, gave France no ground for reprisal. The American minister's own letters.
label: General Armstrong to the Secretary of State, 10 March 1810: 'His Majesty has decided to sell the American property seized in Spain', with his letter of that day to the Duke of Cadore

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a copy of a letter of General Armstrong, the American minister at Paris, 23 February 1809: 'His Majesty has been pleased to raise the Embargo on American vessels within the ports of France and her dependencies and (the better to assure their direct return to the United States) to place them altogether at my disposition.' The American minister's report.
label: General Armstrong's letter of 23 February 1809: the French embargo raised

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of General Armstrong's letter to the Secretary of State from Bourbon l'Archambault, 28 August 1808, sent to Congress with the President's message: he would not return to Paris to renew his discussions with Champagny, being convinced that a new attempt would be useless and probably injurious.
label: Armstrong to Madison, 28 August

admission_rule: Reviewed 1810 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the extract of General Armstrong's letter to the Secretary of State dated Paris, 7 April 1810: 'The Emperor left Paris two days ago for St. Cloud, whence he goes to Compiegne, where he will remain till Easter. It is not probable that I shall have an answer to my propositions till he returns to Paris'; it reports what the minister told him the day before the Emperor set out. The American minister's own letter.
label: General Armstrong to the Secretary of State, 7 April 1810: 'The Emperor left Paris two days ago for St. Cloud'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1780 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of General Arnold's letter to General Washington, on board the Vulture, 25 September 1780: 'The heart which is conscious of its own rectitude, cannot attempt to palliate a step which the world may censure as wrong ...'; he asks protection for Mrs. Arnold. The papers' headings ('Arnold's infamous letter') are their own. The writer's own letter.
label: General Arnold to General Washington, on board the Vulture, 25 September 1780

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: The papers of April 1809 on the arrangement between the Secretary of State, Robert Smith, and the British minister, David Montague Erskine, as the papers printed them: the National Intelligencer's paragraph of 19 April, the notes exchanged on 17, 18 and 19 April, the President's proclamation of 19 April renewing trade with Great Britain from 10 June, and the Secretary of State's answer to the Philadelphia Chamber of Commerce. Contains those four groups. Official documents and the government paper's account.
label: The arrangement with the British minister, April 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the articles of convention of October 1777: 'I. The troops under Lieut. Gen. Burgoyne are to march out of their camp, with the honors of war, and the artillery of the intrenchments, to the verge of the river ... where the arms and artillery are to be left'; 'II. A free passage to be granted to the army, under Lieutenant Gen. Burgoyne, to Great-Britain, upon condition of not serving again in North-America, during the present contest'. Published by order of Congress. The two generals' own convention.
label: The articles of convention between Lieutenant General Burgoyne and Major General Gates, Saratoga, October 1777

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: The two armies' own accounts of the battle fought on 21 and 22 May 1809 near Vienna, on the left bank of the Danube, as American papers printed them in July and August from London papers: a London summary of the French tenth bulletin, and the Austrian official bulletin published by order of the Archduke Charles. Contains those two groups. Each is one side's account.
label: The battle on the Danube, 21 and 22 May 1809: the French and the Austrian bulletins

admission_rule: Reviewed 1801 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the note that the French general Augereau sent to the commander of the Austrian troops in Germany in November 1800, on orders from his government: 'GENERAL, According to the orders I have received from my government, I hereby notify to you the termination of the armistice. Hostilities will therefore recommence in fourteen days from this day, that is on the 22d of November.' Five papers print it within a report from Frankfort of 10 November ('While we were flattering ourselves with hopes of peace, appearances here have suddenly become very warlike. Yesterday General Augereau received a courier from Paris, with orders to give notice immediately of the termination of the armistice'); the National Intelligencer and the Republican Ledger print it in other runs of European news. The note, which all of them print, is counted as the item (C-02). Every paper prints the general's name 'Angereau'. A French general's own note, as the European papers reported it.
label: Frankfort, November 1800: General Augereau's note to the Austrian commander that the armistice is at an end

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Four accounts of the battle of 2 December 1805 near Austerlitz, between the French army and the armies of Russia and Austria, as American papers printed them in February and March 1806: a notice of the British government, a letter of Marshal Berthier, the French army's thirtieth bulletin, and the Emperor's proclamation to his army. Each is one side's account. Contains those four groups.
label: The battle of Austerlitz in the papers, 1806

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Two Austrian state papers of April 1809 that American papers printed in June from London papers: the Emperor Francis's declaration on leaving Vienna, and the Archduke Charles's address to the German nation. Contains those two groups. Each is the Austrian government's own statement.
label: Austria goes to war, April 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an address to the German nation that, as the papers print it, 'The Archduke Charles has issued': 'His Majesty the Emperor of Austria is forced to take up arms, because the French Emperor will not tolerate the existence of a State which does not acknowledge his supremacy of power'. The Austrian side's own statement.
label: The Archduke Charles's address to the German nation, April 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the Austrian army's bulletin 'Published by order of his Imperial Highness, the Archduke Charles': 'the following preliminary report of the brilliant victory obtained the 21st and 22nd of May, is issued on the 23rd from the head quarters at Breitenlee'. Most papers head it 'AUSTRIAN OFFICIAL BULLETIN OF THE DEFEAT OF THE FRENCH'. The Austrian army's own account.
label: The Austrian official bulletin of the battle, 23 May 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the President's message delivered to both Houses on 20 March 1804 by Mr. Harvie: 'I communicate to Congress a letter received from captain Bainbridge, commander of the Philadelphia frigate, informing us of the wreck of that vessel on the coast of Tripoli, and that himself, his officers and men, have fallen into the hands of the Tripolitans'; it asks for an addition to the naval appropriation. Most papers print with it the captain's letter, dated Tripoli, 1 November 1803: 'Misfortune necessitates me to make a communication the most distressing of my life'. The Kentucky Gazette printed the letter in its next issue. The President's message, and the captain's own account.
label: The President's message of 20 March 1804 with Captain Bainbridge's letter on the loss of the frigate Philadelphia

admission_rule: Reviewed 1792 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Baltimore paragraph of early June 1792: 'By the brigantine Greyhound, Captain Elias Porter, who arrived here in thirteen days from Cape-Francois, we are informed, that the situation of affairs, respecting the disturbances in Hispaniola, wore every day a more melancholy aspect—that all hopes of peace being restored, were relinquished'. The Potowmac Guardian prints it under Boston, 16 June, as 'The last accounts from Cape Francois state' (C-02). A report of a ship's news.
label: Baltimore, June 1792: by the brigantine Greyhound from Cape-Francois, affairs in Hispaniola wore every day a more melancholy aspect

admission_rule: Reviewed 1802 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a report from Baltimore, dated 3 March 1802 in some papers and 4 March in others, headed 'Conflagration of the Cape' in most: 'Arrived last evening, capt. Rogers of the Schooner Nelly, from Cape-Francois, which he left on the 14th February. The news by capt. R. is most distressing; both on account of the American property which has been destroyed at the Cape, and the scenes of horror and bloodshed which have and will take place.' It goes on, in the Baltimore paper's words, with the arrival of the French fleet off the Cape on 3 February, the negotiations, the firing of the town on the night of the 4th and the killings that followed. A ship captain's report at second hand, in the Baltimore paper's words.
label: Baltimore, March 1802: 'Conflagration of the Cape', from the captain of the schooner Nelly

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.

label: Baltimore, 17 March 1777: a report from North Carolina of a large French fleet seen at Charleston

admission_rule: Reviewed 1802 printings, checked against the scan.

He has been caught by the blacks and burnt alive."' The Baltimore paper adds that the same report was current at Norfolk, 'tho' not generally credited', and gives its own guesses at how it happened. label: Baltimore, January 1802: a letter from Alexandria reports that Toussaint 'is no more'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1780 printings, checked against the scan.

label: Bridgetown, Barbados, 28 October 1780 (from the Antigua Gazette): the account of 'the late terrible storm' of 10 October

admission_rule: Reviewed 1779 printings, checked against the scan.

label: Basseterre, St. Christopher's, 17 July 1779: 'Admiral Byron engaged Mons. d'Estaing's fleet off Grenada'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1783 printings, checked against the scan.

label: Basseterre, St. Christopher, 15 January 1783: 'The important and agreeable intelligence of a PEACE being concluded between the belligerent powers ... seems now to be confirmed'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1801 printings, checked against the scan.

label: The bill for the impartial administration of justice in the cases of persons questioned for acts done in the execution of the law in Massachusetts Bay, as printed in June 1774

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.

label: Bishop Moore's letter to the Evening Post, 12 July 1804, on General Hamilton's last hours

admission_rule: Reviewed 1797 printings, checked against the scan.

admission_rule: Reviewed 1800 printings, checked against the scan.

admission_rule: Reviewed 1780 printings, checked against the scan.

label: Boston, April 1782: 'The authentic account we have lately received of the conclusion of a new treaty between France and the States of Holland, is very important'

definition: Printings of the speech with which Mr. Breckenridge, senator from Kentucky, opened the Senate's debate of 8 January 1802 on his resolution to repeal the act of the last session 'for a new organization of the Judiciary System' (the act of 13 February 1801, which had created sixteen circuit judges): 'It will be expected of me, I presume, Sir, as I introduced the resolution now under consideration, to assign my reasons for wishing a repeal of this law. This I shall do; and shall endeavour to shew, 1. That the law is unnecessary and improper, and was so at its passage'. Most papers print it under the heading 'Judiciary Establishment', from the National Intelligencer's report of the Senate's debates. A senator's own argument, as the papers reported the debate.
label: Mr. Breckenridge's speech in the Senate, 8 January 1802, on his motion to repeal the judiciary act of 1801

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph from London papers of February 1806: 'A private letter from Bremen of the 11th inst. contains the following article, relative to the sentences passed on the officers whose conduct produced the recent misfortunes to the House of Austria'. A report at second hand, from a private letter.
label: A Bremen letter on the sentences of the Austrian officers

admission_rule: Reviewed 1782 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Massachusetts paragraph of September 1782: 'Yesterday arrived at Beverly a brig of 16 guns, late in the service of his Britannic Majesty. The crew of the Hope (a small privateer lately captured by her) being prisoners on board her, to the number of 21, rose upon the brig's people, in number 62, while laying in a small harbour on the Labrador shore; overcame them, and took the command of the vessel...' Printed by all four newspapers that survive for its weeks; admitted by the rule's first part. A report at second hand.
label: September 1782: 'arrived at Beverly a brig of 16 guns, late in the service of his Britannic Majesty. The crew of the Hope ... being prisoners on board her ... rose upon the brig's people'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan (round three: stories once held back for framing, at the 6-paper threshold for 1793).
definition: Printings of a New York report of late July 1793 on the brig Mary, Captain Langdon, from Cap Français, which she left on 9 July: her forty passengers said that from six to nine hundred people lost their lives 'in the affair of the 20th' (most papers add 'instead of 10 thousand as we heard'; the Patowmac Guardian prints 'two thousand'), that not more than two thirds of the town was burnt, that 'upwards of 20,000 mulattoes and blacks are now under arms there', that 'the negroes never came in from the country on the late occasion', and that the Spaniards had taken a town and were on the march. The passengers' account, at second hand.
label: The brig Mary's passengers on Cap Français

admission_rule: Reviewed 1783 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a New York paragraph of 12 February 1783: 'By the brig Ranger, captain Roger Boyce, who left France the 23d of December, 1782, and was captured on the 6th instant, by the Eagle privateer, captain George Benneison, which arrived here last night, the following letter was received', with the extract of Mr. Townshend's letter to the Lord Mayor of London of 3 December 1782: 'I take the earliest opportunity to inform your lordship, that an express has just arrived from Paris, who brings the preliminary articles for a peace, signed on the 30th of November, by the ambassadors on the part of England, and those on the part of the united states of America'. A New York paper's report, with the secretary of state's own letter.
label: New York, 12 February 1783: by the brig Ranger, taken by the Eagle privateer, Mr. Townshend's letter to the Lord Mayor of London of 3 December 1782

admission_rule: Reviewed 1810 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Boston report: 'Last evening capt. Vinal, in the brig Enterprise, arrived here from Algeziras. He furnishes a detailed account of the seizure by a military force, and sale, without form or trial, but in the name of the French Imperial government, at Malaga, of the brig Two Marias' and other American vessels. The report names the masters of the seized vessels; the excerpts end before their names (C-12). A report at second hand, from the master of a vessel.
label: Boston, July 1810: the brig Enterprise from Algeziras brings an account of the seizure and sale of American vessels at Malaga in the name of the French government

admission_rule: Reviewed 1780 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: The Hague paragraph on Sir Joseph Yorke's memorial of 21 March 1780 to the States General and the King's Order in Council of 17 April suspending the treaties with the United Provinces, as the papers printed them. Each counted by its own words. Contains those two groups.
label: Britain and the States General, 1780: Sir Joseph Yorke's memorial and the Order in Council of 17 April

admission_rule: Reviewed 1781 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: The King's manifesto against the States General of the United Provinces and the order of the King in Council of 20 December 1780 for general reprisals against their ships, goods and subjects, as the papers printed them from London papers in March, April and May 1781. The British government's own words.
label: Britain and the United Provinces, December 1780: the King's manifesto and the order for general reprisals, as the papers printed them in 1781

admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a London paragraph of October 1807: the British ministers had delivered to Monroe and Pinkney their final answer on the leading points in dispute, so that 'the question of peace or war with America' was decided as far as it could be in England, and Monroe was preparing to leave. It is a London paper's report and forecast.
label: London: 'the question of peace or war'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1794 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the King's instructions: 'Additional instructions to the commanders of all ships of war and privateers that have, or may have letters of marque against France ... That they shall stop and detain all ships laden with goods, the produce of any colony belonging to France, or carrying provisions or other supplies for the use of any such colony'. An act of the British government, as the papers printed it from a Kingston (Jamaica) paper.
label: Britain's additional instructions of November 1793 to the commanders of ships of war and privateers: ships with the produce of French colonies to be stopped

admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Philadelphia paragraph of 20 June 1778: 'The British army, early last Thursday morning, completed their evacuation of this city, having before transported their stores and most of their artillery into Jersey, where they had thrown up some works, and several of their regiments were encamped'. A Philadelphia report.
label: Philadelphia, 20 June 1778: the British army completes its evacuation of the city

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a New York report of May 1809, by the ship Projector from Canton: 'an expedition fitted out at Bengal and Penang, under the direction of admiral Drury, for the purpose of taking possession of Macao', had arrived in September 1808, and the Portuguese governor refused to surrender the place. A report at second hand.
label: News from Canton: Admiral Drury's expedition to Macao

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: The House of Representatives and the President on stopping imports from Great Britain in 1806, as the papers printed it: Mr. Gregg's resolution, Mr. J. Randolph's speech against it, the National Intelligencer's paragraph on the vote for Mr. Nicholson's resolution, the act of 18 April prohibiting certain British goods, and the President's message of 3 December asking that the act be suspended. Contains those five groups.
label: Congress and British goods, 1806

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the King's instructions to the commanders of British ships of war and privateers (Windsor, 11 April 1808): they were not to interrupt neutral vessels laden with lumber and provisions bound to the British colonies, under the conditions the instructions set.
label: British instructions of 11 April on provisions for the colonies

admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a report of September 1778 from New England: 'Last Saturday about 40 sail of British men of war and transports appeared off Bedford, at six o'clock they landed about 4000 British troops, Tories, &c. under the command of General Gray'; the papers' versions go on in different words to the rope-walks, houses, stores and shipping burned, and one adds a comment of its own ('Oh Clinton! can you expect that after such savage and cowardly conduct, that Americans will treat with Britons upon terms of reconciliation'). Printed by every paper that survives for its weeks, the New-York Gazette among them. A report at second hand.
label: September 1778: about forty sail of British ships appear off Bedford and land some 4,000 men

admission_rule: Reviewed 1794 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a state paper: 'The following is the copy of a note which has been transmitted by the English Ministers to the Imperial Court. Because it is not equitable that the states of Austria alone should bear the expenses of the war ... it is the intention of the King of Great Britain, I. That, during the present and the succeeding campaigns, subsidies will be granted'. A note of the British government, as the papers printed it.
label: A state paper: the British ministers' note to the Imperial court on subsidies for the war

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the British order in council of 26 April 1809, from the London Gazette of 29 April: 'At the Court at the Queen's Palace, the 26th of April, 1809 ... Whereas his Majesty, by his order in council of the 11th November, 1807, was pleased ... to order' the restrictions of a blockade; the order revokes those orders and in their place puts the ports of France, Holland and Italy, and their colonies, under blockade. The British government's order.
label: The British order in council of 26 April 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Two items on British orders concerning American vessels that carried the produce of the enemy's colonies, as the papers printed them from September 1805: a London paragraph of 7 and 8 August reporting an order to detain such vessels, and the Privy Council's minute of 3 August as the British consuls published it in November. Contains those two groups.
label: British orders on American vessels carrying colonial produce, 1805

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Documents the President sent to Congress in January 1806 on the capture of American vessels and the impressment of American seamen by Britain: his message of 17 January, the letter of the American minister in London to Lord Mulgrave that was sent with it, and the Secretary of State's report on 'new principles interpolated into the law of nations'. Contains those three groups.
label: British seizures and impressment: papers sent to Congress, January 1806

admission_rule: Reviewed 1797 printings of this report, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of Captain Kennard's report that the brig Brothers was boarded by a privateer on the way from Grenada to Portsmouth, N.H. (September 1797). Not independently verified.
label: Brothers boarded by privateer

admission_rule: Reviewed 1797 reports of the fire or of Brown's death, checked against the scan.
definition: Reports of the fire at the Philadelphia house of the printer Andrew Brown (27 January 1797) and notices of his death a week later. Several different texts.
label: Andrew Brown house fire

admission_rule: Reviewed 1794 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Brussels paragraph: 'All the motions and preparations which the combined armies have made on the frontiers are only on the defensive ... it has been agreed upon, that the combined armies shall not begin to act until the great reinforcements which are expected from Germany and England shall have arrived'. A report from Brussels, as the papers printed it.
label: Brussels, 15 March 1794: the allied armies on the defensive until their reinforcements arrive

admission_rule: Reviewed 1794 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Brussels paragraph: 'The French, it is positively asserted, have agreed to give a large sum of money to the King of P——, part of which has already passed their frontier, in consideration whereof, his P——n Majesty ... signs with them a treaty of peace and alliance'. A report, in the papers' words.
label: Brussels, 16 March 1794: a report that the French will pay the King of Prussia for a treaty of peace

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a London paragraph of September 1806: 'The official news of the capture of Buenos Ayres is received. It capitulated on the 27th of June. There fell into the hands of the English 1,291,338 dollars'. A report from the British side.
label: London, September 1806: Buenos Ayres captured

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Two reports from Buenos Ayres printed by American papers in 1809, grouped by subject: a London paragraph of 12 June 'announcing the total defeat and submission of Liniers', and an extract of a letter from Rio de Janeiro of 3 August that a new Spanish viceroy had arrived and that Liniers 'gave up the government quietly'. Contains those two groups. Reports at second hand.
label: Buenos Ayres, 1809: reports of Liniers giving up the government

admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the 66th bulletin of the French Grand Army (Osterode, 14 March 1807): the army rests in cantonments, with skirmishes between the outposts. New York papers had it by the brig Alonzo from Bordeaux, with the 65th.
label: The French army's 66th bulletin

admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an abstract of the 78th bulletin of the French Grand Army (Heilsberg, 12 June 1807), received at Boston from Nantes: the overtures of peace made in the winter, broken off by the Russian attacks, and the action of Spanden on 5 June.
label: The 78th bulletin: the action of Spanden

admission_rule: Reviewed 1810 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the letter of Sir Francis Burdett, member of Parliament for Westminster, to his constituents, 'the People of England': 'The House of Commons having passed a vote, which amounts to a declaration, that an order of theirs is to be of more weight than Magna Charta and the Laws of the Land, I think it my duty to lay my sentiments before you'; it argues that the House has no power to imprison the people of England. The House of Commons committed him to the Tower for it in April 1810, which the papers reported in the same weeks. Sir Francis Burdett's own argument.
label: Sir Francis Burdett's address to the people of England on the power of the House of Commons to imprison, as the London papers printed it in March 1810

admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: The letters exchanged by two former comrades on opposite sides, as the papers printed them in July and August 1775: General Burgoyne's answer from Boston to a letter of General Lee, proposing an interview, and Lee's answer from Cambridge declining it. The generals' own letters.
label: General Burgoyne and General Lee, July 1775: Burgoyne's letter proposing an interview, and Lee's answer declining it

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of General Burgoyne's letter to Sir William Howe, brought by Lieutenant Valancy of the 62d regiment: 'In conformity to my orders, "to proceed by the most vigorous exertions to Albany," I passed the Hudson's river at Saratoga, on the 13th of September. No exertions have been left untried. The army under my command has fought twice against great superiority of numbers'. The British commander's own account.
label: General Burgoyne to Sir William Howe, October 1777: his account of the campaign and the convention

admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the letter that General Burgoyne wrote from Boston in July 1775 in answer to one from General Lee: 'Dear Sir, When we were last together in service, I should not have thought it within the vicissitude of human affairs, that we should meet at any time, or in any sense, as foes'; he defends the authority of Parliament and proposes an interview on Boston Neck. General Burgoyne's own letter.
label: General Burgoyne's letter to General Lee from Boston, July 1775: 'When we were last together in service'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the proclamation of Lieutenant General John Burgoyne, commanding the expedition from Canada, 1777: 'The forces intrusted to my command are designed to act in concert, and upon a common principle, with the numerous armies and fleets which already display, in every quarter of America, the power, the justice, and, when properly sought, the mercy of the King'. The Connecticut Courant calls it 'Burgoyne's pompous proclamation'. The British commander's own proclamation.
label: General Burgoyne's proclamation, 1777: 'The forces intrusted to my command are designed to act in concert ... with the numerous armies and fleets'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a report of Mr. Burke's words in the House of Commons on the American contest and the proclamation for a fast: 'Mr. Burke, in the House of Commons, speaking on the American contest, in which he was very severe against the Ministry, said—That, after having been massacred, first by the Hessians and then by the Lawyers, they now talked of a revisal of the acts that had been complained of seven years ago'; 'he complained bitterly of some expressions in the proclamation for the general fast'. Printed after the proclamation. A report of a member's speech, his own argument as the papers gave it.
label: Mr. Burke's remarks in the House of Commons on the proclamation for a general fast

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan (round two: stories once held back for framing, at the year's 7-paper rule).
definition: Printings of a Burlington (Vermont) paragraph of 5 August 1808, headed 'Melancholy Event': a revenue cutter with a lieutenant, a sergeant and twelve privates, sent by the collector of the customs after a large boat 'well known to have been some time employed in smuggling', took her on Onion river; men on the bank then fired on the cutter's crew, and two of the crew and a man of the town were killed. The report says that eight persons were taken and put in gaol, that a jury of inquest found 'wilful murder', and that 'all opinion' should be suspended until the facts were known. A local report.
label: 'Melancholy Event': Burlington, Vermont, August 1808

admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Documents and reports of Aaron Burr's alleged conspiracy and his trial, as the 1807 papers printed them: the President's message to Congress of 22 January, a New York report of news from New Orleans (February), Chief Justice Marshall's opinion on committing Burr (April), the jury's verdict in the treason trial (September), and Marshall's opinion of 20 October after the trial. Contains those five groups; the wider coverage is not included. The message and the reports carry allegations; the jury found the charge of treason not proved.
label: Burr's conspiracy and trial

admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of President Jefferson's message to Congress of 22 January 1807, sent at the request of the House, on 'an illegal combination of private individuals' against the peace of the Union and a military expedition planned against Spanish territory, with the measures taken to suppress it. It names Aaron Burr as the principal actor. Its enclosures (General Wilkinson's affidavit and letters) are not counted separately.
label: The President's message on the conspiracy

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: The first widely printed items on Aaron Burr's enterprise in the West, November 1806: a Chillicothe report of an affidavit against him in Kentucky, and the President's proclamation of 27 November against a military expedition against the dominions of Spain. Contains those two groups.
label: Colonel Burr's enterprise in the papers, November 1806

admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a New York report (3 February 1807) of news from New Orleans brought by the brig Neptune: General Wilkinson had refused Burr passage, the city was under arms, and Burr was said to be at Natchez with 600 men and an advanced guard of 200 cavalry. The numbers are a report, not an observed fact.
label: News from New Orleans: 'Burr in arms'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the jury's written verdict in Aaron Burr's trial for treason at Richmond on 1 September 1807, 'We of the jury find that Aaron Burr is not proved to be guilty under this indictment by any evidence submitted to us. We therefore find him not guilty', quoted in accounts of that day's proceedings, with Burr's objection to its form. Three different accounts carry it; most papers printed the same one.
label: The verdict: 'not proved to be guilty'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1791 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph of early October 1791, in a Philadelphia form ('arrived here on Saturday last') and a New York form of 5 October ('arrived at Philadelphia on Saturday morning'): 'By the Schooner Hardy, Capt. Green, which sailed from Cape-Francois the 12th ult. and arrived here on Saturday last, we have received intelligence, that the mulattoes and free blacks have got fire-arms, &c. out of the King's store at the Cape, and done more execution against the black insurgents than the white inhabitants had been able to effect: above 3000 of the insurgents have been killed.' A report of the intelligence a ship brought.
label: By the schooner Hardy from Cape-Francois, October 1791: intelligence of the insurrection in Saint-Domingue

admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan (round two, 6-paper threshold for 1793).
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from a gentleman at Cadiz to his brother in New York, dated 24 June 1793 (New York, 12 August): 'a hot war with the Spaniards and French', a battle near Malaga reported won by the French, and news of the fleets. One writer's account, partly hearsay ('We had accounts').
label: A letter from Cadiz, 24 June: 'a hot war with the Spaniards and French'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a New York report of 25 March 1809 on the arrival of the ship Bordeaux, 51 days from Cadiz: her master's account, given 'verbally', that the English army had been 'attacked near Valladolid' and was retreating towards Corunna and that the American vessels at Algeciras were to be released, followed by an abstract furnished by the supercargo. Two papers printed a shorter New York paragraph ('We learn by a gentleman who arrived here yesterday from Cadiz'). Reports at second hand.
label: News from Cadiz by the ship Bordeaux: a battle near Valladolid

admission_rule: Reviewed 1810 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the letter of the French minister of foreign relations to General Armstrong, dated Paris, 5 August 1810: 'I have laid before his Majesty the Emperor and King, the Act of Congress of the 1st of May, extracted from the paper of the United States, which you had transmitted to me'; it declares that 'the decrees of Berlin and Milan are revoked, and that after the first of November they will cease to have effect; it being understood that, in consequence of this declaration, the English shall revoke their orders in council, and renounce the new principles of blockade, which they have wished to establish; or that the United States, conformably to the act you have just communicated, shall cause their rights to be respected by the English', and says 'His Majesty loves the Americans'. The Enquirer and the Norfolk Gazette print it again in December, in another translation, with the documents sent to Congress with the President's message. The French minister's own letter, in the translation of the New York papers.
label: The Duke of Cadore's letter to General Armstrong of 5 August 1810: 'the decrees of Berlin and Milan are revoked, and after the first of November they will cease to have effect'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1810 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the note of the Duke of Cadore, the French minister of foreign relations, to General Armstrong, the American minister at Paris, in three translations: 'The undersigned has informed his Majesty, the Emperor and King, of the conversation, which he had with Mr. Armstrong, Minister Plenipotentiary of the United States of America. His Majesty authorises him to make the following reply: His Majesty would regard his Decrees of Berlin and Milan as violations of the principles of eternal justice, had they not been the necessary consequences of the British Orders in Council' (a second translation opens 'The undersigned having rendered an account to the Emperor and King, of the conversation'; the government's translation, printed late in May as an 'official copy', 'The undersigned has rendered an account to his majesty the emperor and king'). It offers that if the American minister will engage that American vessels shall not submit to the British Orders in Council of November 1807, the undersigned is authorized to conclude a convention tending to renew the treaty of commerce. Counted together (C-02). The French minister's own note.
label: The French minister of foreign relations' note to General Armstrong of 14 February 1810, as the papers printed it in April and May

admission_rule: Reviewed 1803 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an account of a storm and flood at Funchal, Madeira, headed 'Calamity at Madeira' in several papers: 'This extraordinary event, which we briefly noticed in our paper of yesterday, happened on Sunday the 9th of October, at eight in the evening. The day had been previously very cloudy and a continual rain had fallen'; it tells of torrents from the mountains carrying 'churches, convents, streets, trees, bridges, battlements and eight hundred human beings into the bottom of the deep'. A report at second hand, from a daily paper.
label: 'Calamity at Madeira': an account of the storm and flood of 9 October 1803

admission_rule: Reviewed 1791 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Boston paragraph of 15 January 1791, headed 'Tippo Saib' in three of the papers: 'By an arrival at Salem, from India, a Calcutta paper has been received, which gives accounts of the operations of that inveterate enemy of the English, Tipoo Saib, the successor of the famous Hyder Ali, against the Rajah of Travencore. In one battle with the Rajah, Tippo is said to have been defeated, with the loss of 1300 men—and in a second, he is said to have assaulted the Rajah lines with incredible ferocity and bravery, and after a long contest, obtained a victory.' A Boston paper's report from a Calcutta paper.
label: Boston, January 1791: 'By an arrival at Salem, from India, a Calcutta paper has been received', with accounts of Tippoo Saib's operations against the Rajah of Travancore

admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the dispatch of Vice-Admiral Sir Robert Calder to Admiral Cornwallis, 'Prince of Wales, July 23, 1805', from the London Gazette: 'Yesterday at noon ... I was favored with a view of the combined squadrons of France and Spain, consisting of 20 sail of the line'; he 'brought on an action which lasted upwards of four hours' and took two ships. The British commander's own account.
label: Admiral Calder's dispatch on the action of 22 July

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of Lieutenant Colonel Campbell's letter to General Howe (Boston, 19 June 1776), reporting that he and two companies of Highlanders had been taken in Boston harbour.
label: Campbell's letter after his capture

admission_rule: Reviewed 1797 printings of the dispatches, checked against the scan (opening only).
definition: Printings of Admiral Duncan's official dispatches on the defeat of the Dutch fleet off Camperdown (11 October 1797), from the London Gazette Extraordinary. Earlier first-news reports are not included.
label: Duncan's Camperdown dispatches

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a London newspaper report of 24 May 1809, headed 'AMERICAN AFFAIRS' and brought by way of Halifax: in the House of Commons 'lord Henry Petty put a question to Mr. Canning', who replied that the agreement made by Mr. Erskine 'was not made in conformity with the wishes of his majesty nor such as his majesty could approve of', and that American merchants who had acted on it would be protected. A newspaper's report of debate.
label: London, 24 May 1809: Canning tells the Commons the agreement was not authorised

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of Mr. Canning's dispatch to Mr. Erskine, Foreign Office, 23 January 1809, as laid before Parliament and printed from London papers ('Copy of a dispatch from Mr. Secretary Canning to the hon. D. M. Erskine'): it names three conditions on which the orders in council could be withdrawn. The British government's instructions to its minister.
label: Canning's instructions to Erskine, 23 January 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the correspondence between George Canning and James Monroe on the attack on the Chesapeake, with Monroe's letters to the Secretary of State (No. II of the papers laid before Congress), counted by its first document, Canning's note of 25 July 1807 on the first news of the attack.
label: Canning and Monroe on the Chesapeake

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a report of George Canning's remarks in the House of Commons on 24 June 1808, answering Mr. Whitbread: no communication had come from the American government since Mr. Rose's return; he could only conjecture that America was negotiating with France; reparation for the Chesapeake had been offered without giving up the right of search. The papers' heading calls him the Prime Minister; he was Foreign Secretary.
label: Canning in the Commons on America, 24 June

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of George Canning's note to William Pinkney (Foreign Office, 23 September 1808), sent to Congress with the President's message: Britain declined the American offer to suspend the embargo as to Britain if the Orders in Council were withdrawn. The British side's own statement.
label: Canning's answer to Pinkney, 23 September

admission_rule: Reviewed 1787 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from an American house in Cape Francois, Hispaniola, of 4 September 1787, to a gentleman in Boston: 'We are informed by an Ordinance of this day, that NO American vessel (except in distress) will be permitted to enter any French ports in the West-Indies, unless the Captain is provided with a Pass from the Consul resident at the place of his departure'. A merchants' letter reporting a French ordinance.
label: Cape Francois, September 1787: by an ordinance, no American vessel may enter a French port in the West Indies without a pass from the consul

admission_rule: Reviewed 1783 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Philadelphia paragraph of 12 August 1783: 'Captain Dalton, superintendant of Indian affairs for the United States, arrived here last week from Canada, which he left about a month since, in company with 200 Americans, who are at length happily liberated from a cruel captivity'; it says that a number of others 'are still retained as prisoners by the Indians'. A Philadelphia paper's report; the excerpts end before it turns to Captain Dalton's family.
label: Philadelphia, 12 August 1783: Captain Dalton, superintendent of Indian affairs for the United States, arrives from Canada with 200 Americans

admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a report of the burning of Falmouth in Casco Bay by the ships under Captain Mowat on 18 October 1775, with the letter he sent the town: 'Canceaux, Falmouth, October 16th, 1775. After so many premeditated attacks on the legal prerogative of the best of sovereigns', he gives the inhabitants two hours to remove; the report gives the number of houses and stores burnt. A report from the town, with Captain Mowat's own letter.
label: Falmouth, Casco Bay, October 1775: an account of the town's burning by Captain Mowat, with his letter to the people of Falmouth of 16 October

admission_rule: Reviewed 1810 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a state paper of the supreme junta of Caracas, Venezuela, received at New York by the brig Thomas from Cumana and headed in several papers 'Spanish America—Declared Independent' or 'Declaration of Independence': 'It has pleased Almighty God to grant to every country alike the natural right of its own sovereignty. These provinces, planted by Spain, fostered and protected by her power, have, and of right ought to have, submitted to her guidance and direction during the period of infancy'; it declares that, the King being taken from Spain and the lawful government there destroyed, the provinces will not submit to the domination of any European or foreign power. The junta's own words, as the New York papers translated them.
label: The address of the supreme government of Caracas, 1810, as the papers printed it from New York in June: 'It has pleased Almighty God to grant to every country alike the natural right of its own sovereignty'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1782 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Two texts printed in August 1782: the letter of the British commanders at New York to General Washington, published there 'at the request of the inhabitants', that negotiations for a general peace had begun at Paris; and the resolutions of Congress that called it 'mere matter of information'.
label: Sir Guy Carleton and Admiral Digby to General Washington, 2 August 1782, and Congress's resolutions of 12 August on it

admission_rule: Reviewed 1782 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the letter of the British commander in chief and the admiral at New York to General Washington, as the Royal American Gazette of New York published it 'at the request of the inhabitants of New York': 'Sir, The pacific disposition of the parliament and people of England towards the thirteen provinces, has already been communicated to you... We are acquainted, Sir, by authority, that negotiations for a general peace have already commenced at Paris...' The Pennsylvania Packet printed it twice, the second time with the resolutions of Congress. The British commanders' own letter.
label: Sir Guy Carleton and Rear Admiral Digby to General Washington, New-York, 2 August 1782: 'We are acquainted, Sir, by authority, that negotiations for a general peace have already commenced at Paris'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the 'official note' sent to the Lord Mayor of London, Downing Street, 14 August 1809, as a New York paper of 30 September printed it from London papers brought by the ship Triton: the enemy 'attacked the combined armies posted at Talavera, on the 27th and 28th ult.' and 'on both days he was defeated with the most distinguished gallantry'. The British government's announcement.
label: Lord Castlereagh's note to the Lord Mayor on the battle of Talavera, 14 August 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1801 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the second circular of the American consul at Tripoli to the agents and consuls of the United States, dated at Tripoli on 15 May 1801: 'GENTLEMEN, IN addition to my circular of the 11th instant, I am sorry to inform you that our flag staff was chopped down upon Thursday the 14th instant, and War was declared in form by the Basha of Tripoli against the United States of America. You will please to give every possible publicity to this circular, and transmit a copy thereof to the Department of State. I shall depart from Tripoli to Tunis in a few days, where I mean to wait the President's orders.' Several papers print 'cut down' for 'chopped down'. The consul's own circular.
label: The American consul at Tripoli's circular of 15 May 1801: 'War was declared in form by the Basha of Tripoli against the United States'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1801 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the circular of James L. Cathcart, consul of the United States at Tripoli, dated at the 'Chancery of the United States of America at Tripoli in Barbary, this 3d day of January 1801', 'To the Agents and Consuls of the United States of America residing in the different Ports of France, Spain, Portugal, Italy, the Barbary States and the British Garrisons in the Mediterranean': 'GENTLEMEN, I had the honor to inform you in my Circular of the 12th of November 1800, that certain unjust demands having been made by the Basha of Tripoli upon the United States of America, which I found it my duty to repel; that said Basha had publicly announced in an official manner that he would declare War against the United States of America in six months, to commence from the 22d day of October 1800'; as a treaty of peace had been concluded between Sweden and Tripoli on 3 January, 'it is now no longer safe for the merchant vessels of said United States of America to remain in these seas'. The consul's circular of 21 February ('all hopes of accommodation have subsided'), in 4 papers, is not counted with it. The consul's own circular.
label: The American consul at Tripoli's circular of 3 January 1801 to the agents and consuls of the United States in the Mediterranean

admission_rule: Existing inspected selections only; additional candidates require an explicit documented admission.
definition: Printed translated decree and attached allegation; original decree and itemized allegations remain unresolved.
label: Cayenne decree and commentary

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the report adopted by Congress on 10 July 1776 on the cartel General Arnold agreed with Captain Foster after the surrender at the Cedars, with its resolutions.
label: Congress on the Cedars cartel

admission_rule: Reviewed 1801 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the National Intelligencer's paragraph of 16 September 1801 on the returns of the second census: 'The total population of the United States, as taken in 1790, amounted to 3,929,326.
