The present census amounts to 5,064,801. In this statement Tennessee is wanting, the numbers of which state, with those deficient in N. York and Maryland, may be estimated at 150,000'; it goes on to the increase in ten years and to the numbers of slaves in 1790 and in the new returns, with the paper's own calculation. The Oracle prints the increase as 1,185,475 (the others 1,285,475), and the Republican Gazette gives the paragraph in shorter words ('more than 5,166,877'). The government paper's statement of the census returns and its own reckoning.
label: Washington, September 1801: 'The total population of the United States, as taken in 1790, amounted to 3,929,326. The present census amounts to 5,064,801'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the letter of the French foreign minister, Champagny, to General Armstrong, the American minister (Paris, 15 January 1808), made public by Congress on 2 April: the Emperor considered war as existing between England and the United States from the day England published her decrees, and had 'no doubt of a declaration of war against her by the United States'. It is France's own document.
label: Champagny to Armstrong, 15 January 1808

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a letter of the French minister of foreign affairs, Champagny, to General Armstrong, Altenburg, 22 August 1809, in a translation from European papers: 'His Majesty, understanding that you are about to despatch a ship to the United States, commands me to make known to you the unalterable principles which have and will regulate his conduct in the great question respecting neutrals'. The French government's statement.
label: Champagny's letter to Armstrong, Altenburg, 22 August 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of Charles IV's letter to Murat, 'Brother, my absence and infirmities…', enclosing the royal decree (Bayonne, 4 May 1808) that made him lieutenant-general of the kingdom, to govern in the King's name. A document issued under French control.
label: Charles IV names Murat lieutenant-general of Spain

admission_rule: Reviewed 1794 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from a gentleman in Georgia to his friend in Charleston: 'The people here have got recruiting-mad, for the French service to go against West-Florida, Augustine, and New-Orleans'. A letter-writer's report, as the papers printed it.
label: Charleston, 3 January 1794: a letter from Georgia on men enlisting for the French service against West Florida, St. Augustine and New Orleans

admission_rule: Reviewed 1792 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Charleston paragraph of 18 April 1792: 'By a letter received in town from the Rock Landing, we are informed that on information of Mr. Bowles's having taken possession of the store of Messrs. Panton, Leslie, and Co. the Indians had dispatched a party to put him to death, but were prevented by the Spaniards'; the Spaniards drew him on board a vessel, 'seized him and immediately made sail for St. Augustine'. Some papers print it as 'A Charleston paper mentions, that' (C-02). A report from a letter.
label: Charleston, April 1792: a letter from the Rock Landing reports that the Spaniards seized Mr. Bowles and carried him to St. Augustine

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Charleston paragraph of 20 February 1777: 'Last night Capt. Cockran, in the armed Brigantine Notre Dame, arrived here from France, with a valuable cargo, after a passage of 7 weeks'; it reports news brought from France, among it Dr. Franklin's arrival and the burning of the dockyard at Portsmouth. A report at second hand.
label: Charleston, 20 February 1777: the armed brigantine Notre Dame arrives from France with a valuable cargo

admission_rule: Reviewed 1779 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph of Charlestown (South Carolina) news dated 3 March 1779: 'Col. Campbell's expedition from Savannah to Augusta, with the Highlanders and Col. Brown's rangers, has proved as unfortunate as Major Gardiner's to Port Royal; to escape a Burgoyne he has made a very sudden and precipitate retreat down the country, leaving us in possession of all the back counties of Georgia, and his friends the Tories to fall a sacrifice, a whole regiment whereof... have already been defeated, and upwards of 150 of them made prisoners.' A Charlestown paper's report. The film of the Pennsylvania Packet of 10 April holds the sheet of 6 April a second time; that second scan is not counted as a printing.
label: Charlestown, 3 March 1779: 'Col. Campbell's expedition from Savannah to Augusta ... has proved as unfortunate as Major Gardiner's to Port Royal'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1779 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph of the Gazette of the State of South-Carolina of 15 September 1779: 'We are assured, that exclusive of draughts, the militia turn out volunteers, in all parts of the State, with such spirit and alacrity, that the ferry men at the several rivers cannot carry the men across fast enough. By the last accounts from Count d'Estaing's fleet, seven British vessels had fallen into their hands...' The Charlestown paper's own report, reprinted in the north in October and November.
label: Charlestown, 15 September 1779: 'the militia turn out volunteers, in all parts of the State', and news of the Count d'Estaing's fleet

admission_rule: Reviewed 1782 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Charlestown paragraph first printed by the Royal Gazette of Charleston (held by the British) on 24 July 1782, and dated 'Charlestown, July 30' by the other papers in September: 'The town of Savannah was evacuated by the British troops, on the 11th of this month; the public stores and the effects of the inhabitants who have come away, being previously removed down to the island of Tybee. On the 20th of the same month, a fleet sailed from Tybee for Jamaica, with about 1800 negroes, and other property...' A report printed in the town the British held.
label: Charlestown, July 1782: 'The town of Savannah was evacuated by the British troops, on the 11th of this month'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the declaration made on 1 March 1805 by the President of the Senate, after the votes on the eight articles, as the papers' accounts of the court quote it: 'there not being a constitutional majority on any one article, it becomes my duty to pronounce that Samuel Chase, Esq. is acquitted', or, in the National Intelligencer's account, 'Hence it appears that there is not a constitutional majority of votes finding Samuel Chase, Esquire, guilty, on any one article'. The declaration as each account quotes it.
label: The declaration that Judge Chase is acquitted, 1 March

admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the speech of Samuel Chase before the Senate sitting as a court of impeachment, 2 January 1805: 'I appear, in obedience to a summons from this honorable court, to answer articles of impeachment exhibited against me'; he asks for time until the next session to prepare his answer. The accused judge's own words.
label: Judge Chase's speech to the Senate, 2 January

admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of 'The answer, and pleas of Samuel Chase, one of the associate justices of the supreme court of the United States, to the articles of impeachment exhibited against him', given in the Senate on 4 February 1805: 'This respondent, in his proper person, comes into the said court, and protesting that there is no high crime or misdemeanor particularly alleged'. A long document printed in parts; the accused judge's own defence.
label: The answer and pleas of Samuel Chase, 4 February

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the report of the committee appointed to prepare articles of impeachment against Samuel Chase, laid on the table of the House on 26 March 1804: 'Articles exhibited by the House of Representatives of the United States, in the name of themselves and of all the people of the United States, against Samuel Chase, one of the associate justices of the Supreme Court of the United States, in maintenance and support of their impeachment against him, for high crimes and misdemeanors', the first article on his conduct at the trial of John Fries. The House's charges as its committee drafted them (allegations). The articles reported again on 30 November are a group of their own.
label: The articles of impeachment against Judge Chase reported to the House, 26 March 1804

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the report of the committee to which the House referred, on 6 November 1804, the report of March: 'The committee to whom was referred, on the sixth instant, the report of a select committee appointed on the thirteenth of March last, "to prepare and report articles of impeachment against Samuel Chase ..." submit to the House the following REPORT. Articles exhibited by the House of Representatives ...'. These are the articles the House adopted in December and carried to the Senate, which tried the judge in 1805. The House's charges (allegations).
label: The articles of impeachment against Judge Chase reported to the House again, 30 November 1804

admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Four printed pieces of the trial of Samuel Chase, an associate justice of the Supreme Court, before the Senate on the articles of impeachment exhibited by the House of Representatives, as the 1805 papers printed them: his speech of 2 January, his answer and pleas of 4 February, the House's replication, and the declaration of 1 March that he was acquitted. Contains those four groups. Each side's words are its own: the speech and the answer are the accused judge's, the replication the House's.
label: The impeachment trial of Judge Chase, 1805

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a letter from Samuel Chase to the editors of the (Baltimore) Federal Gazette that opens 'As soon as there appeared reason for believing, that the house of representatives intended to adjourn, without preferring articles before the senate, in support of the impeachment voted against me, the inclosed memorial was prepared, and transmitted (on Saturday last) to a member', with the memorial itself, addressed to the House. The accused judge's own argument.
label: Judge Chase's memorial on the impeachment, with his letter to the Federal Gazette, April 1804

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the London Gazette's notice of 2 September 1809 of a dispatch from the Earl of Chatham, dated headquarters, Batz, 29 August: the enemy's force near Antwerp is too strong, and 'however mortifying to me to see the progress arrested of an army, from whose good conduct and valor I had every thing to hope, I feel that my duty left me no other course than to close my operations here'. The British commander's own account.
label: Lord Chatham's dispatch of 29 August 1809: the operations closed

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the London Gazette's notice, Downing Street, 19 August 1809, of a dispatch from Lieutenant General the Earl of Chatham, dated headquarters, Middleburg, 15 or 16 August: 'the batteries before Flushing being completed', a fire was opened on the 13th, and the town surrendered. The British commander's own account.
label: Lord Chatham's dispatch of 15 August 1809: the surrender of Flushing

admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Documents and reports of the attack of the British ship Leopard on the American frigate Chesapeake off the Virginia capes on 22 June 1807, and its aftermath, as the 1807 papers printed them: the National Intelligencer's account, the President's proclamation of 2 July, Admiral Berkeley's order, the opinion of the court of inquiry on Commodore Barron, and the House committee's report. Contains those five groups; the wider coverage is not included.
label: The Chesapeake affair

admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the National Intelligencer's account of 26 June 1807, headed 'British Outrage': the Leopard, one of the British squadron at the capes, followed the Chesapeake out to sea, demanded three men said to be deserters, and fired on her until she struck.
label: The National Intelligencer's account of the attack

admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the opinion of the naval court of inquiry held on board the Chesapeake at Norfolk (5 October to 4 November 1807) on the conduct of Commodore James Barron: among other findings, that the Chesapeake was prematurely surrendered when she was nearly prepared for battle. Includes one printing of its conclusion only.
label: The court of inquiry on the Chesapeake

admission_rule: Reviewed 1773 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from Chester of 10 November 1772, under Liverpool and London datelines: 'On Thursday night last, the 5th instant, the inhabitants of this city were thrown into the utmost consternation by an instantaneous shock, supposed at first to have been occasioned by the violence of an earthquake ...' (gunpowder deposited in a warehouse in Water-Gate-Street). A letter at second hand, as the papers reprinted it.
label: Chester, 10 November 1772: a letter: 'On Thursday night last, the 5th instant, the inhabitants of this city were thrown into the utmost consternation by an instantaneous shock, supposed at first to have been occasioned by the violence of an earthquake'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1772 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Christiansted (St. Croix) paragraph of 4 September 1772: 'On Monday night last blew the most violent hurricane that has ever been known here, or perhaps on any island, in the memory of man. Words are wanting to describe the horrors of the night ...'. A report from the island, as the papers reprinted it. Accounts of the same storm from other islands are other texts.
label: Christiansted (St. Croix), 4 September 1772: 'On Monday night last blew the most violent hurricane that has ever been known here, or perhaps on any island, in the memory of man'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the definitive convention of 30 August 1808 (the Convention of Cintra) between the British and French commanders in Portugal: the French army was to leave Portugal and be carried to France in British ships.
label: The convention for the evacuation of Portugal

admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: The address and petition that the Lord Mayor, Aldermen and Commons of London in Common Council resolved on in July 1775, praying the King to suspend hostilities in America, and the King's answer, as the papers printed them in September and October 1775. The City's and the King's own words.
label: The City of London's address and petition of July 1775 for ending the hostilities in America, and the King's answer

admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Boston paragraph of 1 January 1778: 'The owners of the privateer Civil Usage, of Newbury Port, have made a present to the honourable John Hancock, Esq; of an elegant coach, which was lately taken in one of their prizes; as a token of their respect for that gentleman, who has so nobly distinguished himself in the present contest with Great-Britain'. The New-York Gazette, printed under British occupation, gives it twice in February among other Boston paragraphs. A Boston paper's report.
label: Boston, 1 January 1778: the owners of the privateer Civil Usage present John Hancock with a coach taken in one of their prizes

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the proclamation 'By his Excellency William C. C. Claiborne, Governor of the Mississippi Territory, exercising the powers of Governor-General and Intendant of the province of Louisiana', issued at New Orleans on taking possession in December 1803: it recites the cession of Louisiana from Spain to France and from France to the United States, and declares that 'the government heretofore exercised over the said Province of Louisiana, as well under the authority of Spain as of the French republic' has ceased and that of the United States is established. The governor's own words; Jenks' Portland Gazette prints only its beginning ('It begins:').
label: Governor Claiborne's proclamation at New Orleans, December 1803: the government of Louisiana under Spain and France has ceased

admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a letter of the Austrian general Clairfayt to Count Starhemberg, the Imperial minister at The Hague (dated Tournay, 31 March 1793; some papers date it 3 April): Dumouriez had written to him that he had sent to the Austrian camp, as prisoners, General Bournonville and the commissioners whom the Convention had sent to arrest him. One side's account of what Dumouriez wrote.
label: Clairfayt's letter from Tournay: the commissioners sent as prisoners

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of Captain Clark's letter to his brother, dated St. Louis, 23 September 1806: 'We arrived at this place at 12 o'clock to-day, from the Pacific Ocean, where we remained during the last winter, near the entrance of the Columbia river'. One of the party's own account of the journey.
label: Captain Clark's letter to his brother, St. Louis, 23 September

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the statement of Daniel Clark, delegate from the Territory of Orleans, laid before the House on 11 January 1808 and sworn before Judge Cranch: that General Wilkinson had dealings with the Spanish government and received money from it. It is an allegation.
label: Daniel Clark's statement to the House

admission_rule: Existing inspected selections only; additional candidates require an explicit documented admission.
definition: Two observed versions of the same clearance provisions; content verification does not establish implementation.
label: 1794 clearance resolution

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: The Speaker of the House of Commons' address to the King and the King's speech at the close of the session of Parliament on 6 June 1777, as the papers printed them from September to November. Contains those two groups.
label: The close of the session of Parliament, 6 June 1777: the Speaker's address and the King's speech

admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the proclamation 'to the French' of the Austrian commander, the Prince of Saxe-Cobourg (Mons, 5 April 1793): he supported Dumouriez's declaration to the French nation, would act only as an auxiliary, and would hold any fortress handed to him only as a sacred trust. He withdrew these pledges in a proclamation of 9 April, which the same papers printed beside it.
label: The Prince of Saxe-Cobourg's proclamation to the French, 5 April 1793

admission_rule: Reviewed 1779 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the address of the commanders of a British expedition to the Connecticut coast in July 1779: 'By Commodore Sir George Collier, Commander in Chief of His Majesty's Ships and Vessels in North-America; and Major-General William Tryon, Commanding His Majesty's Land Forces on a Separate Expedition. Address to the Inhabitants of Connecticut. The ungenerous and wanton Insurrection against the Sovereignty of Great-Britain, into which this Colony has been deluded by the Artifices of desperate and designing Men for private Purposes...' It is dated on board the Camilla in the Sound, 4 July 1779. The Newport Gazette, printed in the town the British held, prints it on 8 July (a separate sheet of that paper, which the collection files under 2 July although it prints the address and a Newport paragraph of 5 July, is left out until its date is settled); the Connecticut Courant prints it as one of 'the following insolent Addresses' left in New Haven by the British troops, and the Pennsylvania Packet and the New-Jersey Gazette after General Parsons's letter on the expedition. Satirical verses printed under the same title by three papers are not counted. The British commanders' own address.
label: Commodore Sir George Collier and Major General Tryon, July 1779: their address to the inhabitants of Connecticut

admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the London Gazette Extraordinary of 6 November 1805: 'Dispatches, of which the following are copies, were received at the Admiralty this day at one o'clock A. M. from vice-admiral Collingwood', with his dispatch 'Euryalus, off Cape Trafalgar, Oct. 22': 'The ever to be lamented death of vice-admiral lord viscount Nelson, who, in the late conflict with the enemy, fell in the hour of victory'. The British commander's own account.
label: Admiral Collingwood's dispatch on the action off Cape Trafalgar

admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Williamsburg paragraph of 9 October 1778, 'Intelligence from the south-western frontiers of this state': 'Col. Clark, with a body of militia, has taken possession of Fort Charters and the other western posts between the river Ohio and Mississippi. The Commandant is on his way to this city'. A Williamsburg paper's report.
label: Williamsburg, October 1778: intelligence that Colonel Clark has taken Fort Chartres and the other western posts between the Ohio and the Mississippi

admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the letter that the agents of the colonies in London sent to the speakers of the assemblies on 24 December 1774: 'having received the Petition of the General Congress to the King, we immediately communicated the same to Lord Dartmouth, Secretary of State for the American Department', who told them that the King had received it very graciously and would lay it before his two Houses of Parliament when they met. The agents' own letter.
label: The colony agents' letter from London, 24 December 1774: the Congress's petition delivered to Lord Dartmouth, and 'his Majesty had been pleased to receive it very graciously'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the declaration of three of the British commissioners, the Earl of Carlisle, Sir Henry Clinton and William Eden, dated New York, 26 August 1778: they 'have received a declaration of the American Congress, dated the 11th instant, which relates to a gentleman with whom they have the honour to be joined in commission'; 'they hereby think proper on their part solemnly to declare, that they had not any knowledge, either directly or indirectly, of the letter and conversation alluded to in the said Declaration until they saw them made public in the news-papers', and they go on to the treaty with France. Printed in the New York and Newport papers with the papers sent to Congress, and in the American papers after Congress's resolution of 31 August. The commissioners' own declaration.
label: The declaration of the Earl of Carlisle, Sir Henry Clinton and William Eden, 26 August 1778, on Congress's declaration about their colleague

admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the manifesto and proclamation of the Earl of Carlisle, Sir Henry Clinton and William Eden, dated New York, 3 October 1778: 'To the Members of the Congress, the Members of the General Assemblies or Conventions of the several colonies, plantations and provinces' and all the free inhabitants; the commissioners say they will return to England, renew the offers made to the Congress and the assemblies, proclaim a pardon to those who return to their allegiance, and declare the manifesto in force for forty days, from 3 October to 11 November. The New-York Gazette prints it in three issues and the Newport Gazette in two; American papers print it with comments of their own. The commissioners' own manifesto.
label: The British commissioners' manifesto and proclamation of 3 October 1778, to the members of Congress, the assemblies and all the inhabitants

admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the requisition of the British commissioners, the Earl of Carlisle, Sir Henry Clinton and William Eden, dated New York, 26 August 1778: 'Upon a representation from the Commander in Chief of his Majesty's forces, that the troops lately serving under Lieutenant-General Burgoyne'; it requires that passports be given for transports to the harbour of Boston 'for the immediate embarkation of the said troops; and that they be allowed to depart for Great-Britain in term of the said Convention', offers 'to renew, on the part of Great-Britain, all the stipulations of the said Convention', and is sent 'to the American Congress for their direct and explicit answer'. Printed with the commissioners' other papers of 26 August. The commissioners' own requisition.
label: The commissioners' requisition of 26 August 1778: the troops of the convention of Saratoga to be allowed to embark for Great Britain

admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of 'The humble Address and Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons of the City of London, in Common Council assembled' to the King, of July 1775: the City's loyal subjects lament the hostilities in America and pray the King to suspend them and to adopt measures that will restore union and confidence. The Common Council's own address.
label: The address and petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen and Commons of London in Common Council to the King, July 1775

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Philadelphia report (September 1776) that Franklin, John Adams and Edward Rutledge had set off for New York to confer with Lord Howe.
label: Committee sets off to meet Lord Howe

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the committee's report to Congress on its meeting with Lord Howe on Staten Island, published by order of Congress in September 1776.
label: Committee's report on the conference

admission_rule: Reviewed 1787 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of Congress's resolution of 12 July 1787: 'That all officers in the line of the late army who may be entitled to pensions, in pursuance of the acts of Congress in that behalf made, shall previous to the receipt of such pension, deposit with the proper officers appointed to discharge the same in the States in which they reside, a certificate from the Commissioner of Army Accounts, purporting that no balance is due from the claimant to the United States'. Congress's own resolution.
label: Congress, 12 July 1787: officers of the late army entitled to pensions to deposit a certificate that no balance is due from them

admission_rule: Reviewed 1780 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of Congress's resolutions of 4 October 1780, 'That the board of war be and hereby are directed to erase from the register of the names of the officers of the army of the United States the name of Benedict Arnold', and of 3 November, giving thanks, a silver medal and a pension to each of the three young militiamen of New York who intercepted Major Andre (X-1780-03: the excerpts end before their names). Congress's own resolutions.
label: Congress, 4 October 1780: Benedict Arnold's name erased from the register of officers; 3 November: thanks to the three militiamen who intercepted Major Andre

admission_rule: Reviewed 1779 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of Congress's address headed 'In Congress, January 13, 1779': 'We cannot review the progress of the revolution which has given freedom to America, without admiring the goodness and gratefully acknowledging the interposition of Divine Providence...' It says that taxation was impracticable at the start of the war, that Congress 'from necessity, embraced the expedient of emitting paper money on the faith of the United States', and that the enemy had counterfeited the bills, and it recommends the resolutions of 2 January to the legislatures. Congress's own words.
label: Congress, 13 January 1779: 'We cannot review the progress of the revolution which has given freedom to America': Congress's address on its paper money

admission_rule: Reviewed 1779 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the address of Congress 'To the inhabitants of the United States of America', done in Congress by unanimous consent on 26 May 1779 and signed by John Jay, President: 'Friends and Countrymen, The present situation of public affairs demands your most serious attention, and particularly the great and encreasing depreciation of your currency requires the immediate, strenuous, and united efforts of all true friends to their country...' It reviews the war and the alliance and asks the states to fill their battalions, pay their quotas, lend money and sink their own emissions. Congress's own words.
label: Congress to the inhabitants of the United States, 26 May 1779: 'The present situation of public affairs demands your most serious attention'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1800 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Two documents of February 1800 on a seaman held at Charleston in 1799 whom the British minister claimed under the 27th article of the treaty of 1794 with Great Britain (the article on delivering up persons charged with murder or forgery). In the words of Mr. Livingston's later resolutions (20 February, not admitted), he was a person 'claiming to be a citizen of the United States, impressed on board a British ship of war', committed for trial for 'piracy and murder' alleged to have been committed on board the British frigate Hermione, and delivered up to the British consul on the President's advice. The papers name him; the excerpts and these descriptions do not. Contains those two groups.
label: Congress asks for the papers on a seaman delivered to the British under the 27th article of the treaty, February 1800

admission_rule: Reviewed 1780 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Congress's resolutions of 18 March 1780 on the currency and its recommendation of 20 March that the States revise their tender laws, as the papers printed them. Each counted by its own words. Contains those two groups.
label: Congress and the currency, March 1780: the resolutions of 18 March and the recommendation of 20 March on the tender laws

admission_rule: Reviewed 1779 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Two acts of the Continental Congress on its bills of credit, printed in January and February 1779, often together: the resolutions of 2 January calling on the states for their quotas and taking two emissions out of circulation, and Congress's address of 13 January explaining why it had issued paper money and why it now called for taxes.
label: Congress and its paper money, January 1779: the resolutions of 2 January and Congress's address of 13 January

admission_rule: Reviewed 1779 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of the journals of Congress: 'In Congress, Sept. 28, 1779. Congress having appointed the Hon. John Jay, Esq; their Minister Plenipotentiary, to negotiate a treaty of amity and commerce and of alliance between the United States of America and his Catholic Majesty, and he having signified his acceptance of that office, and thereupon resigned the chair, Resolved, That Congress proceed to the choice of a President...'; Samuel Huntington was elected, and on 1 October Congress thanked Mr. Jay for his conduct in the chair. Congress's own journal.
label: Congress, 28 September 1779: John Jay appointed minister plenipotentiary to Spain, Samuel Huntington chosen President, and the thanks of 1 October to Mr. Jay

admission_rule: Reviewed 1787 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph of October 1787: 'Congress yesterday appointed the Hon. Samuel Holden Parsons, John Armstrong, jun. and James M. Varnum, Esqrs. to be Judges in the Western Territory of the United States' (the time words change with each paper's date). A news paragraph reporting Congress's appointments.
label: New York, October 1787: Congress appoints Samuel Holden Parsons, John Armstrong and James M. Varnum judges in the western territory

admission_rule: Reviewed 1779 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Philadelphia report of Congress's entertainment and public audience for the new French minister: 'Last Wednesday an entertainment was given by Congress to the Minister Plenipotentiary of France, at which were present by invitation several Foreigners of distinction, and gentlemen of public character. In Congress, November 17, 1779. According to order the Hon. the Chevalier De la Luzerne, Minister Plenipotentiary of his Most Christian Majesty, was introduced to an audience...', with the minister's address ('Since treaties dictated by moderation have fixed upon a permanent base the Union of France with the American Republic...') and the President's answer. The minister's and Congress's own words, in a Philadelphia report.
label: Congress, 17 November 1779: the public audience of the Chevalier de la Luzerne, minister plenipotentiary of France, with his address and the President's answer

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of Congress's resolution of 11 January 1776 that anyone who refused the Continental bills of credit, or discouraged their circulation, should be treated as an enemy of his country.
label: Congress on refusing Continental bills

admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the declaration of Congress of 11 August 1778: 'Whereas George Johnstone, Esq. one of the British Commissioners for restoring peace in America, on the eleventh of April last, did write and send a letter to Joseph Reed, Esq. a Member of Congress'; it recites the passages of his letters and the account Mr. Reed gave of an offer made to him, and declares it incompatible with the honour of Congress to hold any manner of correspondence or intercourse with Mr. Johnstone. The New-York Gazette and the Newport Gazette print it with the commissioners' answers. Congress's own declaration; the allegations are those of Congress and of Mr. Reed's account.
label: Congress's declaration of 11 August 1778 on George Johnstone, one of the British commissioners

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of Congress's resolution of 16 March 1776 recommending that Friday 17 May be kept throughout the colonies as a day of humiliation, fasting and prayer. Includes a one-sentence notice of it and a New York committee's notice that quotes it.
label: Congress's fast day of 17 May

admission_rule: Reviewed 1800 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Two documents on the honours paid to George Washington, who died on 14 December 1799, as the 1800 papers printed them: the joint resolutions of Congress of 23 December 1799, and the President's message of 8 January 1800 sending Congress Mrs. Washington's answer. Contains those two groups.
label: Congress and the President honour Washington, December 1799 to January 1800

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of resolutions of Congress of 29 July to 1 August 1777: 'Resolved, That an inquiry be made into the reasons of the evacuation of Ticonderoga and Mount Independence, and into the conduct of the general officers who were in the Northern department at the time of the evacuation'; General St. Clair and General Schuyler are directed to repair to headquarters, and General Washington to send a general officer to relieve General Schuyler. Congress's own resolutions.
label: Congress, 29 July 1777: an inquiry into the evacuation of Ticonderoga and Mount Independence; Generals St. Clair and Schuyler to repair to headquarters

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the 'Intelligence received in Congress, October 21st, from the Middle and Northern Departments': General Mercer's raid on Staten Island and Arnold's fleet engaging the British on Lake Champlain on 11 October.
label: Intelligence received in Congress, October 1776

admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the manifesto of Congress done on 30 October 1778: 'These United States, having been driven to hostilities by the oppressive and tyrannous measures of Great Britain; having been compelled to commit the essential rights of man to the decision of arms'; it declares 'That if our enemies presume to execute their threats, or persist in their present career of barbarity, we will take such exemplary vengeance as shall deter others from a like conduct'. Printed by every paper that survives for its weeks; the New-York Gazette prints it twice, the second time 'with the remarks subjoined to it'. Congress's own manifesto.
label: The manifesto of Congress, 30 October 1778

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of Congress's resolution of 15 May 1776, with its preamble, recommending that the colonies adopt governments under the authority of the people. Includes printings that quote it in full in reports of other bodies' proceedings.
label: Congress's resolution of 15 May

admission_rule: Reviewed 1800 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: The President's speech at the opening of the second session of the Sixth Congress, the first held in the new city of Washington, on 22 November 1800, the addresses of the Senate and the House of Representatives in answer, and his replies, as the papers printed them. Contains those five groups.
label: Congress meets in Washington, November 1800: the President's speech, the answers of the two houses and his replies

admission_rule: Reviewed 1781 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the resolutions of Congress of 23 July 1781: 'Resolved, That five suitable persons be appointed and authorized to open a subscription for a loan of thirty thousand dollars, for the support of such of the citizens of the States of South-Carolina and Georgia, as have been driven from their country'. The resolutions of Congress.
label: Congress, 23 July 1781: a loan and donations for citizens of South Carolina and Georgia driven from their country

admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the proceedings of Congress of 6 June 1778: 'Letter of the 27th of May from Lord Howe, and one of the 3d of June from General Clinton, at Philadelphia, accompanied with three acts of Parliament, were read'; Congress ordered an answer, which the President sent: 'they have already expressed their sentiments upon bills, not essentially different from those acts, in a publication of the 22d of April last', and 'when the King of Great-Britain shall be seriously disposed to put an end to the unprovoked and cruel war waged against these United States, Congress will readily attend to such terms of peace as may consist with the honour of independent nations'. The proceedings of Congress and the President's letter, as published.
label: Congress, 6 June 1778: Lord Howe's and General Clinton's letters with three acts of Parliament, and the President's answer

admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the resolutions of Congress of 19 December 1777: 'Whereas Sir William Howe, Commander in Chief of his Britannic Majesty's forces, has required, that provisions should be sent in for the subsistence of the American prisoners in his possession, ... and has prohibited the circulation of the money struck by the authority of these States'; it resolves that the accounts of all provisions and other necessaries supplied by the public to prisoners in the power of these States shall be discharged in provisions of equal quality and kind, or in gold and silver at four shillings and six pence sterling for every dollar, before the release of any prisoners. The resolutions of Congress, as the papers printed them.
label: Congress, 19 December 1777: accounts for provisions supplied to prisoners to be discharged in kind or in gold and silver before any release

admission_rule: Reviewed 1788 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the resolution of Congress of 13 September 1788: 'Whereas the Convention assembled in Philadelphia, pursuant to the Resolution of Congress of the 21st February, 1787, did, on the 17th of September in the same year, report to the United States in Congress assembled a Constitution'; it resolves the days for appointing electors and for their votes, and the time and place for commencing proceedings under the Constitution. The resolution of Congress; the drafts read in Congress in August are not counted.
label: Congress, 13 September 1788: the days for appointing electors, for choosing the President and for beginning proceedings under the Constitution

admission_rule: Reviewed 1788 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the Journal of Congress of 2 and 3 June 1788: 'According to order the House was resolved into a Committee of the whole ... and Mr. Otis reported ... That in their opinion it is expedient that the district of Kentucky be erected into an Independent State'; on 3 June Congress agreed to the report and chose a committee of a member from each State to prepare an act. The Journal of Congress.
label: Congress, 2 and 3 June 1788: the report that the district of Kentucky be erected into an independent State, and its committee to prepare an act

admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the resolutions of Congress of 26 February 1778: 'Whereas it appears to Congress by the copy of a letter from General Washington to General Howe of the 10th of this month, that he has consented to the propositions of General Howe to the following effect, "That an exchange of all prisoners now in our possession, officer for officer, soldier for soldier, and citizen for citizen, so far as number and rank will apply"'; since its resolution of 19 December requires the accounts for prisoners' provisions to be settled before any release, it asks the states for their accounts of what they have supplied to prisoners. The resolutions of Congress, as the papers printed them from York-Town.
label: Congress, 26 February 1778: the propositions on an exchange of prisoners that General Washington accepted from General Howe

admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the resolution of Congress of 4 September 1778: 'Whereas Congress did, on the eighth day of January, 1778, Resolve, "That the embarkation of Lieutenant General Burgoyne, and the troops under his command, be suspended till a distinct and explicit ratification of the Convention of Saratoga shall be properly notified by the Court of Great Britain to Congress"'; it resolves 'That no ratification of the Convention of Saratoga, which may be tendered in consequence of powers which may reach that case by construction and implication, or which may subject whatever is transacted relative to it to the future approbation or disapprobation of the Parliament of Great Britain, can be accepted by Congress'. Congress's answer, in effect, to the commissioners' requisition of 26 August on those troops. Printed by every paper that survives for its weeks. The resolution of Congress.
label: Congress, 4 September 1778: no ratification of the convention of Saratoga resting on powers 'by construction and implication', or subject to the approval of Parliament, can be accepted

admission_rule: Reviewed 1797 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of Adams's speech opening the second session of the Fifth Congress (23 November 1797), the Senate's and House's answers, and his reply to the House.
label: Opening of Congress, November 1797

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of Congress's resolutions of 6 April 1776 opening American ports to trade with all countries not under the British crown.
label: Congress opens the ports

admission_rule: Reviewed 1782 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the resolution of Congress of 7 November 1782, which several papers head 'Copy of an order of Congress, releasing Capt. Asgill': 'By the United States in Congress assembled, November 7, 1782. On the report of a Committee to whom was referred a letter of the 19th of August, from the Commander in Chief, a report of a Committee thereon, and motion of Mr. Williamson and Mr. Rutledge relative thereto, and also another letter of the 25th of October from the Commander in Chief, with a copy of a letter from the Count de Vergennes...' Printed by all five newspapers that survive for its weeks; admitted by the rule's first part. Congress's own resolution.
label: Congress, 7 November 1782: the order releasing Captain Asgill

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph of April 1777: 'The Honourable the Congress have ordered a monument to be erected in Boston, in honour of Major General Warren; and in Virginia, in honour of Brigadier General Mercer, as a testimony of their illustrious virtues, and of the gratitude of their country. They have likewise ordered the eldest son of the former of those Gentlemen, and the youngest son of the latter, to be educated at the expence of the United States.' A report of Congress's resolutions.
label: 'The Honourable the Congress have ordered a monument to be erected in Boston, in honour of Major General Warren; and in Virginia, in honour of Brigadier General Mercer'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1782 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the proclamation of Congress of October 1782 appointing a day of public thanksgiving: 'It being the indispensable duty of all nations, not only to offer up their supplications to Almighty God, the giver of all good, for his gracious assistance in a time of distress, but also in a solemn and public manner to give him praise for his goodness in general, and especially for great and signal interpositions of his providence in their behalf...' Printed by all four newspapers that survive for its weeks; admitted by the rule's first part. Pages that recite it inside a state's proclamation are not counted (C-07). Congress's own proclamation.
label: Congress's proclamation of a day of thanksgiving, October 1782: 'It being the indispensable duty of all nations, not only to offer up their supplications to Almighty God'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1783 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the proclamation of Congress of 11 April 1783: 'By the United States of America in Congress assembled. A Proclamation, Declaring the Cessation of Arms, as well by Sea as by Land, agreed upon between the United-States of America and His Britannic Majesty; and enjoining the Observance thereof. Whereas Provisional Articles were signed at Paris on the Thirtieth Day of November last, between the Ministers Plenipotentiary of the United-States of America for treating of Peace'. The New-Jersey Gazette prints it whole within a New Jersey proclamation, which recites it 'in the words following, to wit' (counted, C-02; X-1783-05). Congress's own proclamation.
label: The proclamation of the United States in Congress assembled, 11 April 1783, declaring the cessation of arms agreed upon between the United States and the King

admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the proceedings of Congress of 6 August 1778: 'According to order the Honourable the Sieur Gerard being introduced to an audience by the two Members for that purpose appointed, and being seated in his chair, his Secretary delivered to the President a letter from his most Christian Majesty, which was read in the words following'; with the King's letter, the minister's address and the President's answer. The proceedings of Congress, as published.
label: Congress, 6 August 1778: the audience of the Sieur Gerard, Minister Plenipotentiary of the King of France

admission_rule: Reviewed 1787 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a New York paragraph of April 1787: 'On Friday last the United States in Congress assembled passed a resolution recommending it to the different states, to repeal all their laws, now in force, which are inconsistent with the treaty of peace between the United States of America, and the King of Great Britain' (one paper dates it 'April 14' and reads 'Yesterday'). A news paragraph reporting Congress's resolution.
label: New York, April 1787: Congress recommends that the States repeal their laws inconsistent with the treaty of peace

admission_rule: Reviewed 1780 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of Congress's resolution of 20 March 1780: 'Resolved, That it be recommended to the States to revise their laws enacted pursuant to a former resolution of Congress, making the Continental bills of credit a tender in discharge of debts and contracts, and to amend the same in such manner as they shall judge most conducive to justice in the present state of the paper currency'. Congress's own resolution.
label: Congress, 20 March 1780: the States to revise their laws making the Continental bills a tender in discharge of debts

admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the report agreed to by Congress on 22 April 1778: 'The Committee to whom was referred the General's letter of the 18th, containing a certain printed paper sent from Philadelphia, purporting to be the draught of a bill for declaring the intentions of the Parliament of Great-Britain'; it gives, point by point, the committee's reasons for believing the bills will be brought into Parliament ('1st. Because their General hath made divers feeble efforts to set on foot some kind of treaty during the last winter'), and ends with resolutions of Congress, among them that the Congress is 'invested with an exclusive authority to treat with the King of Great Britain', and on 'any man, or body of men, who shall presume to make any separate or partial convention or agreement with the King of Great-Britain'. The Newport Gazette heads it 'Extract from a Rebel Paper'. Congress's own report.
label: Congress, 22 April 1778: the report on the printed draught bills, agreed to by Congress

admission_rule: Reviewed 1787 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of Congress's resolutions of 11 October 1787 on a report of the Board of Treasury and a motion of Mr. Kean 'respecting the requisition for 1787': the sums wanting for the year's interest on the foreign and domestic debt, the quotas of the states, and the indents of interest to be received in payment. Congress's own resolutions.
label: Congress, 11 October 1787: the requisition for 1787

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a resolution of Congress of 10 September 1777: 'Resolved, That the interest which shall arise, after the date of this resolution, on loan office certificates already issued, or which shall be issued before the first day of March next, be annually paid at the respective loan offices in bills of exchange on the Commissioners of the United States in Paris, at the rate of five livres of France, for every Spanish milled dollar'. Congress's own resolution.
label: Congress, 10 September 1777: the interest on loan office certificates to be paid in bills of exchange on the commissioners in Paris

admission_rule: Reviewed 1782 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the resolutions of Congress of 12 August 1782: 'Whereas from the late publications, the people throughout the United States may be induced to believe that Congress have received authentic communications upon the subject of an approaching peace. Resolved, That the letter of August 2d, 1782, from Sir Guy Carleton and Admiral Digby to the Commander in Chief be made public. Resolved, That Congress consider the above letter as mere matter of information, inexplicit as to the nature and extent of the independence directed to be proposed by the British Plenipotentiary...' Congress's own resolutions.
label: Congress, 12 August 1782: 'Resolved, That Congress consider the above letter as mere matter of information'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1779 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the resolutions of the Continental Congress of 2 January 1779, headed 'In Congress, January 2, 1779': 'Whereas these United States, unprovided with revenues, and not heretofore in a condition to raise them, have, in the course of the present war, repeatedly been under the necessity of emitting bills of credit, for the redemption of which the faith of these United States has been solemnly pledged...' The resolutions call on the states to raise by taxes their quotas of fifteen millions of dollars for 1779, and, 'whereas many counterfeits have appeared in circulation' of the emissions of 20 May 1777 and 11 April 1778, take those two emissions out of circulation. The Pennsylvania Packet printed them in five issues; four papers print them again after Congress's address of 13 January, which recommends 'the annexed resolutions'. Congress's own resolutions.
label: Congress, 2 January 1779: 'Whereas these United States, unprovided with revenues ... have ... been under the necessity of emitting bills of credit': the states' quotas, and two emissions taken out of circulation

admission_rule: Reviewed 1782 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the resolutions of Congress of 4 October 1782: 'Whereas by the articles of confederation and perpetual union, the sole and exclusive right of making peace is vested in the United States in Congress assembled; and by the treaty of alliance between His Most Christian Majesty and these United States, it is declared that neither of the contracting parties shall conclude peace or truce with Great Britain without the consent of the other... Resolved unanimously, That congress are sincerely desirous of an honourable and permanent peace: that as the only means of obtaining it, they will inviolably adhere to the treaty of alliance...' The Pennsylvania Packet printed them twice; a page of the Connecticut Courant (29 October) that repeats their preamble prints a state assembly's resolutions, not counted (C-07). Printed by all four newspapers that survive for their weeks; admitted by the rule's first part. Congress's own resolutions.
label: Congress, 4 October 1782: 'Resolved unanimously, That congress are sincerely desirous of an honourable and permanent peace' and will conclude neither a separate peace nor a truce

admission_rule: Reviewed 1779 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the resolutions of Congress of 19 November 1779: 'Whereas the fluctuating state of prices not only causes inequality and injustice in private dealings, and in furnishing the public supplies from the several States, but renders it impracticable to make the proper estimates for future expences, and to fix equitable salaries...' They recommend that the states pass laws limiting the prices of labour and of articles of domestic produce, 'not to exceed twenty fold of the prices current through the various seasons of the year 1774', from 1 February 1780. Two papers print them with the President's letter sending them to the states; the Pennsylvania Packet printed them twice. Congress's own resolutions.
label: Congress, 19 November 1779: 'Whereas the fluctuating state of prices not only causes inequality and injustice in private dealings': laws to limit prices recommended to the states

admission_rule: Reviewed 1780 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of Congress's resolutions of 18 March 1780: 'These United States having been driven into this just and necessary war at a time when no regular civil governments were established ...'; the States to bring in their quotas of fifteen million dollars monthly, silver and gold to be received at one Spanish milled dollar for forty dollars of the bills, and new bills to be emitted on the funds of the States. Pennsylvania's and New Jersey's acts that recite the resolutions are not counted (C-07). Congress's own resolutions.
label: Congress, 18 March 1780: resolutions on the currency (the States' monthly quotas; silver and gold at one for forty; new bills to be emitted)

admission_rule: Reviewed 1780 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of Congress's resolutions of 10 and 24 August 1780 on the memorial of the general officers: 'Congress took into consideration the report of the Committee on the memorial of the general officers; whereupon, Resolved, That the said general officers be informed, that Congress have at no time been unmindful of the military virtues ...'; grants of land extended to general officers, two months' pay, rations. Congress's own resolutions.
label: Congress, 10 and 24 August 1780: resolutions on the memorial of the general officers (lands, pay and rations)

admission_rule: Reviewed 1779 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the resolutions of Congress of 26 July 1779: 'Resolved unanimously, that the thanks of Congress be given to his Excellency General Washington, for the vigilance, wisdom and magnanimity, with which he hath conducted the military operations of these States...'; the thanks to Brigadier General Wayne 'for his brave, prudent and soldierly conduct', and the sense of Congress of the good conduct of the officers and soldiers in the assault. Congress's own resolutions.
label: Congress, 26 July 1779: the thanks of Congress to General Washington, General Wayne and the officers and soldiers at Stony Point

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of resolutions of Congress of 25 July 1777: 'Resolved, That Congress have a just sense of the merit of Lieutenant-Colonel Meigs, and the officers and men under his command, who distinguished their prudence, activity, enterprise, and valour in the late expedition to Long-Island; and that an elegant sword be provided ... and presented to Lieut. Colonel Meigs'; a second resolution does the same for Lieutenant Colonel Barton, who made prisoner of Major General Prescott. Congress's own resolutions.
label: Congress, 25 July 1777: thanks and swords to Lieutenant Colonel Meigs for the expedition to Long Island and to Lieutenant Colonel Barton for taking General Prescott

admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the resolutions of Congress of 7 July 1778: 'Resolved unanimously, That the thanks of Congress be given to General Washington for the activity with which he marched from the camp at Valley Forge in pursuit of the enemy; for his distinguished exertions in forming the order of battle; and for his great good conduct in leading on the attack and gaining the important victory of Monmouth over the British grand army'. The resolutions of Congress.
label: Congress, 7 July 1778: the thanks of Congress to General Washington and the officers and men who distinguished themselves at Monmouth

admission_rule: Reviewed 1800 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph of London news quoting a letter from Constantinople dated 28 July 1800: 'A few days ago fresh intelligence reached us from Egypt. General Kleber has been murdered, and General Menou has succeeded him in command'; it adds what was reported of the killer and of reprisals at Cairo, and the writer's view that suspicions fell on Menou. A report at second and third hand.
label: A letter from Constantinople, 28 July 1800: 'General Kleber has been murdered'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1773 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from Constantinople of 29 May 1773 (19 May in the New-Hampshire Gazette): 'A Ragusan sloop of war, in the service of the Porte, is just arrived here from the Palus Maeotis, or the sea of Asoph, and brings the following account of the success which the Turkish fleet met with ...'. A letter at second hand, as the papers reprinted it.
label: Constantinople, 29 May 1773: a letter: 'A Ragusan sloop of war, in the service of the Porte, is just arrived here from the Palus Maeotis, or the sea of Asoph, and brings the following account of the success which the Turkish fleet met with'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1802 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the proclamation of the Consuls of the Republic dated Paris, 17 Brumaire, year 10 (8 November 1801), which General Leclerc published at St. Domingo in February 1802: 'Inhabitants of St. Domingo, Whatever may be your origin and your colour, you are all Frenchmen, you are all free and all equal before God and the Republic. France, like St. Domingo, has been a prey to factions'; it announces the Captain General sent with the army and warns those who would not rally to him. The papers print it in two translations: four that begin 'Inhabitants of St. Domingo, Whatever may be your origin, and your colour, you are all Frenchmen' and go on 'But an entire change has taken place', and three that read 'ye are all Frenchmen, ye are all free' and 'But all is changed'; counted together as one item in two printed forms. Several papers print it after Leclerc's own short proclamation, which is not counted here (5 papers). The French government's own proclamation, as the papers translated it.
label: The Consuls of the French Republic to the inhabitants of St. Domingo, 8 November 1801: 'Whatever may be your origin and your colour, you are all Frenchmen'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1774 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the Association that the delegates signed at Philadelphia: 'We his Majesty's most loyal subjects, the Delegates of the several Colonies of New-Hampshire, Massachusetts-Bay, Rhode-Island, Connecticut, New-York, New-Jersey, Pennsylvania, the three Lower Counties of New-Castle, Kent, and Sussex, on Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, North-Carolina, and South-Carolina ... avowing our allegiance to his Majesty, our affection and regard for our fellow subjects in Great-Britain and elsewhere'; its articles bind them, from 1 December 1774, not to import goods from Great Britain or Ireland and the other goods it names, nor to 'import nor purchase any slave imported after the first day of December next', and its eleventh article directs that a committee be chosen in every county, city and town to see it observed. The papers that print its eleventh article again by itself are not counted again (C-07). The delegates' own Association.
label: The Association of the Continental Congress, October 1774: no importation from Great Britain or Ireland after 1 December 1774

admission_rule: Reviewed 1774 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Four papers of the Congress of delegates of the colonies that met at Philadelphia from 5 September 1774, as the papers printed them: its resolution of 22 September asking the merchants to send no more orders to Great Britain, its resolves of 8 October approving the opposition of Massachusetts Bay to the late acts, its declaration and resolves of 14 October, and its Association. Contains those four groups.
label: The Continental Congress at Philadelphia, September and October 1774: its resolutions, its association and its declaration of 14 October

admission_rule: Reviewed 1774 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the declaration and resolves that the Congress adopted on 14 October 1774, at the head of the printed extracts of its proceedings: 'Whereas, since the close of the last war, the British Parliament claiming a power, of right to bind the people of America, by statute in all cases whatsoever, hath in some acts expressly imposed taxes on them'; it lists the acts of Parliament the colonies complain of, and resolves that the inhabitants of the English colonies in North America 'are entitled to life, liberty, and property: and they have never ceded to any sovereign power whatever, a right to dispose of either without their consent', and to the rights, liberties and immunities of free and natural-born subjects within the realm of England. The Congress's own declaration.
label: The Congress's declaration and resolves of 14 October 1774: 'Whereas, since the close of the last war, the British Parliament claiming a power of right to bind the people of America, by statute in all cases whatsoever'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Three papers of the second Continental Congress, as the papers printed them from July 1775: its resolve of 4 July on the two acts restraining the trade of the colonies, its declaration of 6 July setting forth the causes and necessity of taking up arms, and its petition to the King of 8 July. The Congress's own words.
label: The Continental Congress at Philadelphia, July 1775: its resolve on the restraining acts, its declaration of the causes of taking up arms, and its second petition to the King

admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the petition to the King adopted by the Continental Congress in October 1774 and printed by the papers from January 1775: 'To the King's Most Excellent Majesty. Most Gracious Sovereign, We your Majesty's faithful subjects of the colonies of New-Hampshire, Massachusetts-Bay, Rhode-Island and Providence Plantations, Connecticut, New-York, New-Jersey, Pennsylvania, the counties of Newcastle, Kent and Sussex on Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, North-Carolina and South-Carolina, in behalf of ourselves and the inhabitants of those colonies who have deputed us to represent them in General Congress, by this our humble petition, beg leave to lay our grievances before the throne'; it lists the standing army, the new duties and courts and the acts of 1774, and asks the King's interposition. The Congress's own petition (its second petition of July 1775 opens with the same words and is a separate story).
label: The Continental Congress's petition to the King, October 1774: 'we beg leave to lay our grievances before the throne'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: The petition to the King that the Congress at Philadelphia adopted in October 1774, which the papers printed in January and February 1775, and the letter of the colony agents in London, dated 24 December 1774, saying they had delivered it to Lord Dartmouth and that the King had received it graciously. The Congress's and the agents' own words.
label: The Continental Congress's petition to the King of October 1774, as printed in 1775, and the colony agents' letter on its delivery

admission_rule: Reviewed 1774 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the resolution of the Congress of 22 September 1774: 'Resolved unanimously, That the Congress request the merchants and others, in the several colonies, not to send to Great-Britain any orders for goods, and to direct the execution of all orders already sent to be delayed or suspended, until the sense of the Congress, on the means to be taken for the preservation of the liberties of America, is made public', with the secretary's attestation. The Massachusetts Spy prints it again in December with the Congress's proceedings. The Congress's own resolution.
label: The Congress's resolution of 22 September 1774: the merchants not to send any orders for goods to Great Britain

admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the resolve of the Continental Congress of 4 July 1775: 'Resolved, that the two acts passed in the first session of the present parliament, the one entitled "an act to restrain the trade and commerce of the provinces of Massachusetts Bay and New Hampshire, and colonies of Connecticut and Rhode Island and Providence plantations"', and the act restraining the trade of the other colonies; the Congress resolves against them. The Congress's own resolve.
label: The Continental Congress's resolve of 4 July 1775 on the two acts restraining the trade of the colonies

admission_rule: Reviewed 1774 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the Congress's resolution of 8 October 1774: 'Resolved, That the Congress approve of the opposition, by the inhabitants of the Massachusetts-Bay, to the execution of the late Acts of Parliament, and if the same shall be attempted to be carried into execution by force, that in such case all America ought to support them in their opposition', printed with its resolves of 10 and 11 October. The papers print it in two forms: from Philadelphia, under the date of the session, in October, and in the printed extracts of the Congress's proceedings ('Resolved, That this Congress do approve of the opposition made by the inhabitants of the Massachusetts-Bay'), from late October; counted together (C-02), and printed again counts again (C-08). Rind's Virginia Gazette prints the extracts too, but its transcriptions lack the resolution's opening, so that printing is not counted (C-06). The Congress's own resolves.
label: The Congress's resolves of 8 October 1774: it approves the opposition of the inhabitants of Massachusetts Bay to the late acts of Parliament

admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the petition to the King adopted by the Continental Congress on 8 July 1775: 'To the King's Most Excellent Majesty. Most Gracious Sovereign, We your Majesty's faithful subjects of the colonies of New-Hampshire, Massachusetts-Bay', and the others, ask the King to procure a happy and permanent reconciliation, and that in the meantime measures be taken to prevent the further destruction of lives and to repeal the statutes that most distress the colonies. The Congress's own petition (its petition of October 1774 opens with the same words and is a separate story).
label: The Continental Congress's second petition to the King, 8 July 1775: 'the union between our Mother Country and these colonies'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1779 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Boston paragraph of August 1779: 'Saturday last arrived here the Continental Frigates Providence, Queen of France & Ranger; during their cruise they fell in with a Jamaica Fleet of upwards of 100 sail, under convoy of several Frigates.—This favourable opportunity they improved as well as circumstances would admit.—They picked out nine ships and one brig deeply laden with rum, sugar, &c. seven of which have arrived here, and one at Cape Ann.' Some papers print 'Sunday last', and the Connecticut Courant 'Saturday se'nnight' (a week before); the papers differ on how many of the prizes had arrived and where. A Boston paper's report.
label: Boston, August 1779: 'arrived here the Continental frigates Providence, Queen of France and Ranger', with ships of a Jamaica fleet

admission_rule: Reviewed 1783 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph of the southern news, printed from early June 1783: 'The continental troops who were at Savanna, are on their march to Charlestown, where vessels are providing to transport them to their respective states. General Wayne is gone to settle a treaty of peace with some tribes of Indians on the frontiers of Georgia. They are to negotiate the business at Augusta.' A paper's report of news from the south.
label: June 1783: 'The continental troops who were at Savanna, are on their march to Charlestown, where vessels are providing to transport them to their respective states'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1800 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the text of the convention signed at Paris on 30 September 1800 by the French plenipotentiaries and the American envoys, before the Senate had acted on it, in two translations. Six papers print the one that begins 'The First Consul of the French Republic, in the name of the French people, and the President of the United States of America, equally animated with a desire to put an end to the differences which have arisen between the two States' and whose first article reads 'There shall be a firm, inviolable and universal peace' (the National Intelligencer gives its opening in somewhat different words: 'The Premier Consul of the French Republic in the name of the people of France, and the President of the United States of America, equally desirous to terminate the differences'); the Alexandria Advertiser and the Virginia Argus print another, from the Paris papers, whose first article reads 'There shall be a sincere and universal Peace, and inviolable Friendship between the two countries'. Counted together as one item in two printed forms. The two governments' agreement, as printed before ratification.
label: The convention between France and the United States, signed 30 September 1800

admission_rule: Reviewed 1803 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the convention signed the same day: 'The President of the United States of America, and the First Consul of the French Republic, in the name of the French people, in consequence of the treaty of cession of Louisiana, which has been signed this day, wishing to regulate definitively every thing which has relation to the said cession'; by it the United States are to create a stock of eleven millions two hundred and fifty thousand dollars bearing an interest of six per cent. The two governments' convention.
label: The convention of 30 April 1803 for the payment of sixty million francs

admission_rule: Reviewed 1800 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the articles 'agreed upon between Major General Knox, duly authorised by his Royal Highness the Duke of York, Commander in Chief of the combined English and Russian Army, and Citizen Rostollant ... duly authorised by Citizen Brune, General and Commander in Chief of the French and Batavian Armies' (the names vary from paper to paper): 'From the date of this convention, all hostilities shall cease between the two armies'; the combined army 'shall evacuate the territory, coasts, islands, and internal navigation of the Dutch Republic, by the 30th of November, 1799', and 'Eight thousand prisoners of war, French and Batavians ... now detained in England, shall be restored'. The London Gazette of 26 October 1799 published it with the Duke of York's dispatch of 20 October, and most papers printed the two together; the Portland Gazette printed the articles alone. The two commanders' agreement, as the British government published it.
label: The convention of October 1799 between the Duke of York and General Brune for the British and Russian army to leave Holland

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: The articles of convention between Lieutenant General Burgoyne and Major General Gates (October 1777), under which General Burgoyne's troops were to march out and leave their arms, printed by all seven papers that survive for its weeks, and General Burgoyne's letter to Sir William Howe on the campaign and the convention, as the papers printed them from October to December. Contains those two groups.
label: The convention of Saratoga, October 1777: the articles of convention and General Burgoyne's letter to Sir William Howe

admission_rule: Reviewed 1803 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the convention between the civil and military deputies of the Regency of Hanover and Lieutenant-General Mortier, commander in chief of the French army, signed at Suhlingen on 14 Prairial, year 11 (3 June 1803): 'Art. 1. Hanover shall be occupied by the French army, as well as the forts dependent on it. 2. The Hanoverian troops shall retire behind the Elbe; they shall engage on their parole of honor not to commit any hostilities'. The papers print it in two translations, after General Mortier's letter to the minister of war (8 papers, not admitted on its own; see the README). The parties' agreement, in translation.
label: The convention of June 1803 for the occupation of Hanover by the French army

admission_rule: Reviewed 1803 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the second convention signed the same day: 'The President of the United States of America, and the First Consul of the French Republic, in the name of the French people, having by a treaty of this date terminated all difficulties relative to Louisiana, and established on a solid foundation the friendship which unites the two nations, and being desirous, in compliance with the second and fifth articles of the convention of the 8th Vendemiaire, ninth year of the French Republic (30th September, 1800) to secure the payment of the sums due by France to the citizens of the United States'. The two governments' convention.
label: The convention of 30 April 1803 for the payment of debts due by France to citizens of the United States

admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan (round two, 6-paper threshold for 1793).
definition: Printings of the 'Declaration made by the President of the National Convention to the French Nation' (Paris, May 1793): after a scandalous scene in the galleries, he declared his conviction of a conspiracy, revealed to him by good citizens, to destroy the Convention, and his resolve to wait the event at his post. One man's declaration of an alleged plot.
label: The President of the National Convention's declaration of a plot

admission_rule: Reviewed 1800 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the convention 'For the prolongation of the suspension of arms between the French army of the Rhine and the army of his Imperial Majesty in Germany', agreed by the Count de Lehrbach and the Baron de Lauer for the Emperor and a general of brigade for the French army of the Rhine in September 1800: the Emperor 'consents that the places of Philippsburg, Ulm, and the fortresses which depend upon it, with the place of Ingolstadt ... shall be given up to the disposition of the French army, as a pledge of his intentions'.
