Most papers print it after General Moreau's letter announcing it. The two sides' agreement, as the papers printed it.
label: The convention of September 1800 prolonging the armistice in Germany

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: The two conventions of late August and early September 1808 that ended the French occupation of Portugal, as American papers printed them from London papers in October and November: the surrender of the Russian fleet in the Tagus, and the evacuation of Portugal by the French army. Contains those two groups.
label: The conventions in Portugal, 1808

admission_rule: Reviewed 1782 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of Lord Cornwallis's letter to the British commander in chief, as the London Gazette published it ('White-Hall, Nov. 27. Copy of a letter from Earl Cornwallis, to his Excellency Sir Henry Clinton, dated York-Town, Virginia, October 13, 1781'): 'Last evening the enemy carried my two advanced redoubts on the left by storm, and during the night have included them in their second parallel, which they are at present busy in perfecting...' The Pennsylvania Packet prints it twice and dates it 'Octo. 15', as the New-Jersey Gazette does. A British commander's own letter, published by his government. Sir Henry Clinton's letter to Lord George Germain, published with it, is listed as not chosen.
label: Earl Cornwallis to Sir Henry Clinton, York-Town, Virginia, 13 October 1781: 'Last evening the enemy carried my two advanced redoubts on the left by storm'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of Lord Cornwallis's letter to General Washington, dated Brunswick, 3 April 1777: 'I enclose to you a paper which Lieutenant Colonel Walcott delivered yesterday to Lieutenant Colonel Harrison, and which Lieut. Col. Harrison did not then think proper to receive', with the paper itself: Lieutenant Colonel Walcott's 'Demand ... of return of prisoners' of 2 April, that General Washington return prisoners for those sent back to him. A letter and the paper it encloses are one item (X-1810-01). The British commanders' own letter and demand.
label: Lord Cornwallis to General Washington, Brunswick, 3 April 1777, with Lieutenant Colonel Walcott's demand for the return of prisoners

admission_rule: Reviewed 1781 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of Lord Cornwallis's proclamation: 'By Charles Earl Cornwallis, Lieutenant General of his Majesty's Forces, &c. Proclamation. Whereas, by the blessing of Almighty God, his Majesty's arms have been crowned with signal success, by the complete victory obtained over the rebel forces on the 15th instant, I have thought proper to issue this proclamation, to call upon all loyal subjects to stand forth'. Lord Cornwallis's own words; some papers print it with comments of their own.
label: Lord Cornwallis's proclamation after the action of 15 March 1781, calling on loyal subjects to take an active part

admission_rule: Reviewed 1781 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of Lord Cornwallis's letter to the Commander in Chief: 'York Town, in Virginia, October 20th, 1781. Sir, I have the mortification to inform your Excellency, that I have been forced to give up the posts of York and Gloucester, and to surrender the troops under my command, by capitulation'. Lord Cornwallis's own account.
label: Lord Cornwallis to Sir Henry Clinton, York Town, Virginia, 20 October 1781

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the New York reports, dated 3, 4 and 13 August 1804, of the verdict of the jury of inquest that the coroner summoned on General Hamilton's death: most quote it, 'That Aaron Burr, Esq. Vice President of the United States, was guilty of the murder of Alexander Hamilton' (three papers print 'is guilty'), and name the two seconds as accessaries; a shorter New York paragraph says the inquest 'brought in a verdict of MURDER by AARON BURR', and the Norfolk Gazette gives it in its own words. The accounts are counted together, as 1805 counted the accounts of Judge Chase's acquittal and 1807 the Burr verdict; the Berkeley and Jefferson Intelligencer printed two accounts and the Enquirer three. An inquest's verdict, which accuses a named public man; the excerpts end before the seconds' names.
label: The coroner's jury on General Hamilton's death, August 1804: a verdict of murder against Aaron Burr, as the papers reported it

admission_rule: Reviewed 1810 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Two letters of the correspondence between the American minister in London, William Pinkney, and the British Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, the Marquis Wellesley, on the conduct and recall of the British minister to the United States, Francis James Jackson, as the papers printed them from the National Intelligencer of 21 May 1810 with an extract of Mr. Pinkney's letter of 21 March to the Secretary of State. Contains those two groups.
label: Mr. Pinkney and Lord Wellesley on the British minister Jackson, as the papers published their correspondence in May 1810

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the minutes of the council of general officers held at Ticonderoga on 5 July 1777, published by order of Congress: 'At a Council of General Officers held at Ticonderoga, July 5, 1777. Present, Major General St. Clair, Brig. General de Roche Fermoy, Brig. General Poor, Brig. General Paterson, Col. Commandant Long'; General St. Clair put to them whether the posts could be held or should be evacuated. The council's own minutes.
label: The council of general officers held at Ticonderoga, 5 July 1777

admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the French minister's message to Congress, published by order of Congress: 'His Excellency the Count D'Estaing, Vice-Admiral of France, commanding the King's squadron, is desirous of enabling all the armaments either public or private in the United States of North-America, to derive every possible advantage from the operations of this squadron in order to make prizes of the common enemy'; such armaments shall enjoy the protection of the squadron, and their prizes shall belong to them only. Signed Gerard. The French minister's message, as Congress published it.
label: Monsieur Gerard's message to Congress, July 1778: Count d'Estaing offers American armaments the protection of the French squadron, and the prizes they take

admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from General Count Pulaski to the President of Congress dated 16 October 1778: 'For fear that my first letter concerning my engagement should miscarry or be delayed, and having other particulars to mention, I thought proper to send you this letter'; it gives his account of the enemy's attack on his men on the 15th, at three o'clock in the morning, with 400 men, and of the pursuit. The commander's own report.
label: Count Pulaski to the President of Congress, 16 October 1778: his account of the enemy's attack on his men on the 15th

admission_rule: Reviewed 1801 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the sentence of the court martial held on board the frigate Constitution on Captain George Little, of the frigate Boston, on charges brought by officers of the French corvette Le Berceau, which the Boston had taken in 1800: 'The Court, having heard all the evidence, and prisoner's defence, and maturely and seriously considered the whole, are unanimously of opinion, that the charges are malicious and ill-founded. The Court do, therefore, unanimously and honorably acquit the said Capt. George Little', dated on board the Constitution, 7 September 1801, and signed by the president of the court and its members; with the letter of the Navy Department of 25 September 1801, which approves the sentence and states that 'The evidence adduced in this trial clearly proves, that the prisoners on board the prize have been pillaged' by some persons belonging to the Boston. Several papers print them after a Boston paper's comment on the trial ('The trial of Captain Little ... has excited much sensibility in the breasts of every real friend to the American navy'). The court martial's own sentence and the Navy Department's own letter.
label: The sentence of the court martial on Captain George Little, 7 September 1801, with the Secretary of the Navy's letter of 25 September

admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of 'A letter from Jonathan Cowdery, Esq. Surgeon of the late frigate Philadelphia, now a captive in Tripoli, to Dr. Mitchell, dated 24th November, 1804': the Bashaw 'has taken me from the prison where my fellow-officers are confined, and ordered me to attend his sick slaves, who are principally Neapolitans, negroes, and our unfortunate crew'. A captive officer's own account, in a letter to a member of Congress.
label: Surgeon Cowdery's letter from captivity in Tripoli

admission_rule: Reviewed 1797 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a letter dated at the headquarters of the Archduke Charles of Austria, 27 October 1796, which the London Gazette of 13 November published with others from Captain Anstruther and R. Crauford: 'My Lord, I have the honour to inform your Lordship, that in the course of the last night Gen. Moreau's army retreated across the Rhine at Huningen' (the Patowmac Guardian's words); it is signed Robert Crauford. Three papers print it after a London paragraph of 14 November that introduces it as 'the last of the letters alluded to'; the New Hampshire Gazette prints the letter alone, from New York. The writer's report from the Austrian headquarters, as the London Gazette published it.
label: From the Archduke Charles's headquarters, 27 October 1796: Moreau's army retreats across the Rhine

admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph of the National Intelligencer of 18 November 1805: 'A very advantageous TREATY has been made, we understand, at this place, with the chiefs of the Creek Nation; by which a large cession of land is made to the United States, and the right given to open a direct road to New Orleans'. The government paper's report ('we understand'); 'very advantageous' is its own judgement.
label: Washington paragraph on a treaty with the chiefs of the Creek Nation

admission_rule: Reviewed 1801 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the passage of a letter from Commodore Dale, commanding the squadron of frigates the United States sent to the Mediterranean in 1801, to Mr. Gavino, the American consul at Gibraltar, dated Malta, 19 August 1801: 'I am happy to inform you that Mr. Sterrett, in the Schooner Enterprise, of 12 guns, and 90 men, fell in with one of the Tripolitan cruisers off this island ... He took her after an action of three hours ... Not a man hurt on board the Schooner.' Six papers print it as the commodore's letter, in runs of news from Gibraltar; the Republican Ledger and the Rhode-Island Republican print the same passage as a Boston paragraph, 'Lieutenant Sterett, in the Schooner Enterprise ... off the island of Malta', counted with them (C-02). The commodore's own report, as the papers printed it.
label: Commodore Dale's letter from Malta, 19 August 1801: the schooner Enterprize takes a Tripoline cruiser

admission_rule: Reviewed 1791 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from Danville, Kentucky, dated 22 August 1791, sent by way of Richmond: 'An express from Gen. Wilkinson has this moment reached this place, informing of his success. He has destroyed a large Indian town situated on the Wabash; also a Kickapoo town, containing about 30 houses, and killed and taken 42 of the enemy. His loss, 2 men killed and one wounded.' A letter writer's report of General Wilkinson's express.
label: Danville, Kentucky, 22 August 1791: an extract of a letter, 'An express from Gen. Wilkinson has this moment reached this place, informing of his success'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1781 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Boston paragraph of 10 May 1781: 'Last Sunday arrived in this harbour, after a passage of about 6 weeks from Brest, M. M. de Barras, Rear Admiral appointed to the chief command of the squadron of his most Christian Majesty at Newport, in the frigate la Concorde'. A Boston paper's report.
label: Boston, 10 May 1781: Rear-Admiral de Barras arrives from Brest in the frigate la Concorde

admission_rule: Reviewed 1781 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from the Count de Grasse to the Chevalier de la Luzerne, minister plenipotentiary of France, dated Cape Henry, 13 September 1781: 'Nothing gave me greater pleasure than the approach of the armies under general Washington and count de Rochambeau'. The admiral's own account, as a Philadelphia paper printed it.
label: The Count de Grasse to the Chevalier de la Luzerne, Cape Henry, 13 September 1781

admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan (round two, 6-paper threshold for 1793).
definition: Printings of a letter from the commissioners of the National Convention with the army of the North, Valenciennes, 9 May 1793, read in the Convention: General Dampierre, whose thigh was carried away by a ball the day before, died that morning, regretted by the whole army. The French government's commissioners' own account.
label: The commissioners' letter on General Dampierre's death

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Documents printed after Alexander Hamilton died on 12 July 1804 of a wound received in a duel with Aaron Burr, the Vice President, on the morning of the 11th, as the papers date them: Bishop Moore's letter on his last hours, Gouverneur Morris's funeral oration, the correspondence between Hamilton and Burr, Hamilton's will, Hamilton's own statement written before the meeting, and the coroner's jury's verdict as the papers reported it. Contains those six groups.
label: The death of General Hamilton after the duel with Colonel Burr, July and August 1804

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of Lieutenant Decatur's report to Commodore Preble, dated 'On board the ketch Intrepid, at sea, February 17th, 1804': 'I have the honor to inform you, that in pursuance of your orders of the 1st inst. to proceed with this ketch off the harbour of Tripoli, there to endeavour to effect the destruction of the late frigate Philadelphia', he went in with the brig Syren in company, boarded the frigate and set her on fire. Published by the government in Washington on 23 May with other letters of the squadron. The officer's own account.
label: Lieutenant Decatur's letter to Commodore Preble, 17 February 1804: the frigate Philadelphia destroyed in the harbour of Tripoli

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph headed 'OFFICIAL' in the National Intelligencer of 25 May 1804: 'As a testimonial of the President's high opinion of the gallant conduct of Lieutenant Decatur, in taking and destroying the frigate the Philadelphia, a commission to him as Captain in the Navy has been duly issued, and will without delay be transmitted to Commodore Preble.' The government paper's notice.
label: 'As a testimonial of the President's high opinion': the official notice of 25 May 1804 that Lieutenant Decatur is made a captain

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the Declaration of Independence (4 July 1776), plus one printing of its conclusion with a summary a week before that paper printed the full text.
label: Declaration of Independence

admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of 'A Declaration by the Representatives of the United Colonies of North-America, now met in General Congress at Philadelphia, setting forth the Causes and Necessity of their taking up Arms': 'If it was possible for men, who exercise their reason, to believe, that the divine Author of our existence intended a part of the human race to hold an absolute property in, and an unbounded power over others'; it recites the colonies' grievances and declares that they have taken up arms in defence of their liberty and will lay them down when hostilities cease. The New-Hampshire Gazette prints only a report that it was read to the army, with its title (not counted). The Congress's own declaration.
label: A declaration by the representatives of the United Colonies, 6 July 1775, setting forth the causes and necessity of their taking up arms

admission_rule: Reviewed 1780 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the declaration of the Empress of Russia to the Courts of London, Versailles and Madrid (1780): 'The Empress of all the Russias has so fully manifested her sentiments of equity and moderation ... of the regard she has for the rights of neutrality and the liberty of universal commerce ...'; the principles of neutral navigation. The Empress's own declaration.
label: The declaration of the Empress of Russia to the Courts of London, Versailles and Madrid on the rights of neutral commerce

admission_rule: Reviewed 1792 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the National Assembly's decree of August 1792 against M. La Fayette, which the papers print after an account of soldiers of his army at the bar of the Assembly: '1. It appears to this Assembly that there is just ground for accusation against M. de la Fayette, heretofore Commander of the army of the North. 2. The Executive Power shall in the most expeditious manner possible, put the present decree into execution'; all authorities, citizens and soldiers are enjoined to secure his person, and the army of the north is forbidden to obey him. The National Gazette gives the account before the decree in its own words (C-02). The Assembly's own decree, in translation.
label: The National Assembly of France, August 1792: decree of accusation against M. La Fayette, heretofore commander of the army of the north

admission_rule: Reviewed 1792 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the decree of the National Assembly of France of Friday 20 April 1792, 'declaring war against the King of Hungary and Bohemia': 'The National Assembly deliberating on the formal proposition of the King, considering that the Court of Vienna, in contempt of treaties, has continued to grant an open protection to French rebels'; the considerations and the decree follow. The Assembly's own decree, in translation.
label: The National Assembly of France, 20 April 1792: decree declaring war against the King of Hungary and Bohemia

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Three measures of the warring powers against neutral commerce, as American papers printed them in the first half of 1808: the British Order in Council of 11 November 1807, a merchant house's account of Napoleon's Milan decree, and the British instructions of 11 April 1808 on provisions for the West Indies. Contains those three groups; the grouping is by subject.
label: Orders and decrees against neutral trade

admission_rule: Reviewed 1802 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the text of the 'Definitive Treaty of Peace, between the French Republic, the King of Spain, and the Batavian Republic, on the one part, and His Majesty the King of the United Kingdom of Great-Britain and Ireland on the other', signed at Amiens on 27 March 1802 and brought to America in May from London and Havre papers: 'The First Consul of the French Republic, in the name of the French Nation, and His Majesty the King of the United Kingdom of Great-Britain and Ireland, being equally animated with a desire to put an end to the calamities of war'. Among its articles, Spain cedes the island of Trinidad and the Batavian Republic its possessions in Ceylon to Great Britain, and Malta is to be restored to the Knights of St. John. The powers' own treaty, as the papers printed it.
label: The definitive treaty of peace signed at Amiens, 27 March 1802

admission_rule: Reviewed 1797 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the report made in the French Council of Five Hundred (sitting of 4 August 1797; 3 August in the Mirror) by Delarue ('Delarne' in the Mirror and the Kentucky Gazette) for its committee of inspectors, 'on the march of the troops': 'It results from the information we have procured, 1. That from 26 to 27,000 men have been detached from the army of the Sambre and Meuse, instead of 9000, as was stated by Gen. Hoche. 2. That this force directed its march towards Paris' (the Gazette of the United States prints 6000, 'as was said'). It goes on to say that the soldiers had been 'misled and seduced' against the Legislative Body and that troops kept marching on Paris 'by order of Gen. Hoche'. A committee's report and charges in the legislature, as the Paris papers gave them.
label: Delarue's report to the Council of Five Hundred on the march of the troops, August 1797

admission_rule: Reviewed 1803 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Three documents of Congress on the suspension of the right of deposit at New Orleans by the Spanish Intendant there in October 1802, as the papers of 1803 printed them: the President's message of 22 December 1802 sending the Secretary of State's report, the House of Representatives' resolution of 7 January 1803, and the resolutions the Senate adopted in February 1803 on Mr. Breckenridge's motion. Contains those three groups.
label: The right of deposit at New Orleans withdrawn, before Congress: the President's message of 22 December 1802 and the resolutions of the two houses, January and February 1803

admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the deposition that Edward Thoroton Gould, an officer of the King's Own regiment of foot taken prisoner, made before the Massachusetts authorities and that the Provincial Congress published: 'I Edward Thoroton Gould, of his Majesty's own regiment of foot, being of lawful age, do testify and declare, that on the evening of the 18th instant, under the orders of General Gage, I embarked with the light infantry and grenadiers of the line'; he describes the march to Concord and the firing at the bridge. The officer's own sworn account, as the Provincial Congress published it.
label: The deposition of Lieutenant Edward Thoroton Gould, of the King's Own regiment, wounded and taken prisoner, on the march to Concord on 19 April 1775

admission_rule: Reviewed 1803 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the speech that Colonel Edward Marcus Despard, convicted with six others of high treason for a conspiracy against the King and the government, made to the crowd before his execution in London on 21 February 1803: 'Fellow citizens, I come here, as you see, after having served my country faithfully, honorably and usefully for thirty years and upwards, to suffer death upon a scaffold for a crime of which I protest I am not guilty'. The papers print it within three different London accounts of the execution; the speech, printed in nearly the same words, is counted as the item, and accounts that do not print it (the Alexandria Advertiser, the Kentucky Gazette) are not counted. The National Intelligencer printed it on 8 and 13 April, in two of the accounts. A condemned man's own words, as the London papers reported them.
label: Colonel Despard's speech on the scaffold, London, 21 February 1803, as the papers reported his execution for high treason

admission_rule: Reviewed 1810 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Two of the despatches that the frigate John Adams brought from France in June 1810 and the National Intelligencer published, as the papers reprinted them: General Armstrong's letter of 10 March 1810 to the Secretary of State, with his letter of that day to the Duke of Cadore, and his letter of 7 April. The publication holds about twenty letters of General Armstrong and Mr. Pinkney; the others are in 7 or 8 papers each (see the README). Contains those two groups.
label: Despatches received by the frigate John Adams from Paris and London, published in June 1810: General Armstrong on the seizures of American property

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from a gentleman at Detroit, dated 1 June 1806: traders had reported to the acting governor 'the frequent secret councils held by the Indians', and the writer says 'We are now no longer in doubt, that the Indians are preparing to commence war against the United States'. One American writer's account of traders' reports, with his forecast.
label: A letter from Detroit of 1 June on councils of the Indian nations

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a National Intelligencer paragraph of 24 June 1808 ('We understand'): after the settlement of December, the Dey had demanded in March two thousand dollars a man for Algerine seamen lost in the rescue of a captured American vessel, threatening to put Consul Lear in chains. It is a report from the government's paper.
label: Washington: the Dey of Algiers makes new demands

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the fourth part of the documents sent with the message of 29 November 1809, counted by its first document: 'Gen. Armstrong to Mr. Smith, Secretary of State. Paris, 4th September, 1809. Sir, The letter of which I send you a copy, was received during my absence', with the letter of Champagny it encloses and further extracts. Each letter is its writer's own account.
label: The documents, part four: General Armstrong's letters from Paris, with Champagny's

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the first part of the documents sent to Congress with the President's message of 29 November 1809, counted by its first document, Mr. Erskine's letter to the Secretary of State of 31 July 1809 ('I have the honor to inclose to you a copy of an order, which was passed by His Majesty in Council'); the letters of July and August between Mr. Erskine, the Secretary of State and the Secretary of the Treasury follow it. Each letter is its writer's own account.
label: The documents, part one: Mr. Erskine's letters of July and August 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the documents that accompanied a message from the President to Congress in November 1804, published in the National Intelligencer of 14 November as 'DOCUMENT No. I' and onward, counted by the first: an extract of a letter from Don Pedro Cevallos, minister of state of his Catholic Majesty, to Charles Pinckney, dated at the Pardo, 10 February 1804, in translation: 'his majesty has thought fit to renounce his opposition to the alienation of Louisiana made by France'. The documents that follow include the correspondence on the act of Congress that allowed the President to erect the shores and waters of the bay and river of Mobile into a collection district. The Spanish government's and the two governments' ministers' own words.
label: The documents sent to Congress with the President's message, November 1804: Spain's minister of state on the cession of Louisiana

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the second part of the documents sent with the message of 29 November 1809, counted by its first document: 'THE SECRETARY OF STATE TO MR. JACKSON … Department of State, October 9th, 1809. Sir—An arrangement, as to the revocation of the British Orders in Council, as well as to the satisfaction required in the case of the attack on the Chesapeake frigate, has been made in due form'. Eight letters follow to the Secretary's of 8 November, which ends the correspondence, with two notes delivered for Mr. Jackson by his secretary. Each letter is its writer's own account.
label: The documents, part two: the Secretary of State and Mr. Jackson, October and November 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the third part of the documents sent with the message of 29 November 1809, counted by its first document: the Secretary of State's letter to Mr. Pinkney in London, 23 November 1809, giving the government's account of the correspondence with Mr. Jackson and asking that he be recalled. Mr. Canning's note to Mr. Pinkney of 27 May 1809, with Mr. Pinkney's answer, follows it in several papers. The government's own account.
label: The documents, part three: the Secretary of State to Mr. Pinkney, 23 November 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: The diplomatic papers that President Madison sent to Congress with his message of 29 November 1809, as the papers printed them over one to four issues, in the publication's order: Mr. Erskine's letters of July and August with the Secretary of State and the Secretary of the Treasury; the correspondence of the Secretary of State and Mr. Jackson from 9 October to 13 November; the Secretary of State's letter to Mr. Pinkney of 23 November; and General Armstrong's letters from Paris with Champagny's. Contains those four groups, each counted by its first document. Each letter is its writer's own account.
label: The documents sent to Congress with the message of 29 November 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a New York paragraph of 9 June 1806 headed 'MASSACRE AT CAPE FRANCOIS': Captain Dodge of the schooner Mary Ann, arrived from Cape François, reported 'that on the 14th and 15th of May, a general massacre of all the remaining white inhabitants of Cape Francois took place, and it was said, generally, throughout that part of this ill-fated island under the dominion of Dessalines'. A shipmaster's report, partly hearsay, in the paper's words.
label: Captain Dodge's report from Cape François, June 1806

admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: The letters exchanged in July 1807 between Commodore John E. Douglas, commanding the British squadron in Hampton Roads, and Richard E. Lee, Mayor of Norfolk, over the Norfolk committee's ban on communication with the British ships, with the report of Littleton W. Tazewell, who carried the Mayor's answer. Contains those four groups.
label: Commodore Douglas and the Mayor of Norfolk

admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of Commodore Douglas's letter to the Mayor of Norfolk (Bellona, Hampton Roads, 3 July 1807): unless the committee's resolution forbidding communication with the British consul and ships was annulled, he would stop every vessel bound in or out of Norfolk; it rested with the inhabitants 'either to engage in a war or remain on terms of peace'.
label: Commodore Douglas's letter of 3 July

admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of Commodore Douglas's second letter to the Mayor of Norfolk (Bellona, Hampton Roads, 6 July 1807): every circumstance had been discussed with the gentlemen who carried the Mayor's answer, and he would use every exertion, consistent with the honour of the British flag, toward an amicable end.
label: Commodore Douglas's letter of 6 July

admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the draught of the first of Lord North's two bills: 'A Bill for declaring the intentions of the Parliament of Great-Britain, concerning the exercise of the right of imposing taxes within his Majesty's colonies, provinces and plantations in North-America'; it declares that Parliament will impose no duty, tax or assessment payable in the colonies, except duties for the regulation of commerce, whose net produce is to be paid and applied for the use of the colony where it is levied. The New-York Gazette prints it in three issues; American papers print it with Congress's report on it. The British government's draught bill, as printed in America.
label: The draught of a bill for declaring the intentions of the Parliament of Great Britain concerning the exercise of the right of imposing taxes in the colonies

admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the draught of the second of Lord North's two bills: 'A Bill to enable his Majesty to appoint Commissioners, with sufficient powers to treat, consult, and agree upon the means of quieting the disorders now subsisting in certain of the colonies, plantations, and provinces of North-America'; the commissioners may treat, consult and agree 'with such body or bodies political and corporate, or with such assembly or assemblies of men, or with such person or persons, as in their wisdom and discretion they shall think meet', suspend the act prohibiting trade with the colonies, and appoint governors. The New-York Gazette prints it in three issues; American papers print it with Congress's report on it. The British government's draught bill, as printed in America.
label: The draught of a bill to enable the King to appoint commissioners to treat, consult and agree upon the means of quieting the disorders in the colonies

admission_rule: Reviewed 1773 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Dresden paragraph of 2 June 1773: 'We have received a very disagreeable account of great damage having been done by a storm of thunder and lightning in the circle of Voigtland in this electorate: The whole town of Reichenbach is entirely ...'. A report from Dresden, as the London papers gave it and the papers reprinted it.
label: Dresden, 2 June 1773: 'We have received a very disagreeable account of great damage having been done by a storm of thunder and lightning in the circle of Voigtland in this electorate'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the answer of Captain William Love, commanding the British sloop of war Driver (Rebellion Roads, Charleston, 3 May 1807), to Captain Kalteisen: he doubted the authority by which the demand was written, knew nothing of a proclamation of May 1807, and would not leave until ready.
label: The Driver's commander answers

admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Reports of the British sloop of war Driver, which the President had barred from American ports, anchoring in Charleston harbour in April and May 1807: the commandant of Fort Johnson's demand that she leave, and her commander's answer. Contains those two groups.
label: The Driver at Charleston

admission_rule: Reviewed 1803 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a copy of a letter from Dublin, dated Sunday 11 o'clock, 24 July 1803, to a merchant in Liverpool, published at Liverpool on 28 July and headed 'Rebellion in Ireland' in several papers: 'You will be shocked to hear that we are at this moment in a more alarming situation than at any period during the unfortunate rebellion: At an early hour yesterday evening, a variety of inflammatory proclamations were distributed in every part of the town, calling on people to unite, as before, in opposition to English oppression'; it reports a general engagement in the streets and the officers, soldiers and yeomen killed. The New Hampshire Gazette prints the letter without its first sentence. A letter-writer's account at second hand.
label: A letter from Dublin of 24 July 1803 on the rising of the 23rd: 'You will be shocked to hear that we are at this moment in a more alarming situation than at any period during the unfortunate rebellion'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1792 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from Dublin, 13 September 1792: 'It is said that in the course of last week a subscription, amounting to three millions sterling'. Two papers print it under Dublin, 13 September, without the words 'Extract of a letter' (C-02). A report of what is said, from a letter.
label: Dublin, 13 September 1792: it is said that a subscription amounting to three millions sterling was made in the course of the last week

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of news brought to Philadelphia in May 1776 by a passenger from Europe with a Dublin paper of 2 March: that a large naval force was coming to America and was ordered to sail on 10 April, followed by London paragraphs from that paper. The forecast is a report, not an observed event.
label: A Dublin paper: British force coming

admission_rule: Reviewed 1794 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the letter, as the London Gazette gave it: 'A letter, dated Tournay, May 13, 1794, of which the following is an extract, was yesterday received from his Royal Highness the Duke of York ... Since my last letter no attempt has been made by the enemy to harass or molest any of my posts. On Sunday morning, however, they attacked in great force General Clairfayt's corps'. The British commander's own words.
label: Whitehall, May 1794: the Duke of York's letter from Tournay of 13 May (General Clairfayt's action at Courtrai)

admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of General Dumouriez's address 'to the French Nation', dated the Baths of St. Amand, 2 April 1793, printed from London papers: his services since the Revolution, his charges against the Convention and the Jacobins, his plan to restore the constitution with his army, and his oath to give up every public function afterwards. One side's account and a policy argument.
label: Dumouriez's address to the French nation, 2 April 1793

admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: News of General Dumouriez's break with the National Convention in April 1793, as American papers printed it from late May: Clairfayt's letter that Dumouriez had sent the Convention's commissioners to the Austrian camp as prisoners, a London rumour that he had left his army, his own address to the French nation, and the Prince of Saxe-Cobourg's proclamation in support of it. Contains those four groups.
label: Dumouriez's defection, April 1793

admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of General Dumouriez's letter to the President of the National Convention, dated Brussels, 14 November 1792, and read in the Convention on 22 November: the Austrians had disputed the heights of Anderlecht with his advanced guard, and he had entered Brussels. One army's own account.
label: Dumouriez's letter on entering Brussels, 14 November 1792

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the convention of 1805 'between the United States of America and his highness Hamet Caramalli, bashaw of Tripoli', made by William Eaton, one of the documents sent with the President's message of 13 January 1806: 'GOD IS INFINITE. ARTICLE I. There shall be a firm and perpetual peace and free intercourse' between the two. An agreement, as the message printed it.
label: The convention between William Eaton and Hamet Caramalli

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of Congress's resolutions of 16 September 1776 to raise eighty-eight battalions to serve during the war, with each state's quota and the bounties, plus one condensed report.
label: Congress orders 88 battalions

admission_rule: Reviewed 1782 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a letter of the British governor of Gibraltar as the papers took it from 'a Gazette extraordinary, printed at Cork' ('Admiralty-Office, Sept. 19, 1782. Extract of a letter from Governor Elliot, to Secretary Stevens, dated Sept. 12, 1782'): 'I have taken an opportunity of sending this by [the master of] the Speedwell cutter, who is to sail to-morrow for England, with the subsequent account of our success against the Spaniards, in their so much boasted attack with their floating batteries... As it was always my opinion that we should be attacked by their whole force on St. Louis's day...' Printed by all five newspapers that survive for its weeks; admitted by the rule's first part. The letter as a Cork paper printed it.
label: Governor Elliot to Secretary Stevens, Gibraltar, 12 September 1782, from 'a Gazette extraordinary, printed at Cork': 'our success against the Spaniards, in their so much boasted attack with their floating batteries'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the act of 22 December 1807 laying an embargo on all ships and vessels in the ports and harbors of the United States: no clearance for a foreign port, and bonds for coasting vessels. This group holds the act's 1808 printings; it was first printed in late December 1807, and those printings are not included.
label: The Embargo Act of 22 December 1807

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the act of 25 April 1808 in addition to the embargo acts: vessels whose trade is confined to bays, sounds, rivers and lakes must give bond, and collectors may detain vessels and unusual deposits of goods suspected of evading the embargo.
label: The act of 25 April enforcing the embargo

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the act of 12 March 1808 in addition to the supplementary act: no boat that is neither registered nor licensed, and no foreign vessel, may depart, and goods may not be exported from the United States by land or by water.
label: The additional act of 12 March

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Two acts of the second session of the Tenth Congress, the act of 9 January 1809 to enforce the embargo and the act of 1 March 1809 to interdict commercial intercourse with Great Britain and France, the Treasury's circular of 3 March to the collectors on the second, and the act of 28 June 1809 of the first session of the Eleventh Congress that amended and continued it, as the 1809 papers printed them, most of them 'by authority'. Contains those four groups.
label: The embargo enforcing act and the non-intercourse laws, 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Reports and executive documents on the embargo's working in April and May 1808: a Georgia letter on its effect at Mobile and Pensacola, the President's proclamation on Lake Champlain, and his letter to five governors on supplies of flour. Contains those three groups; the grouping is by subject.
label: The embargo at home, spring 1808

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: The Embargo Act of 22 December 1807 and the acts of the first session of the Tenth Congress that extended it, enforced it and allowed the President to suspend it, as the 1808 papers printed them, most of them 'by authority': the supplementary act of 9 January, the additional act of 12 March, the act of 22 April authorising a suspension and the act of 25 April. Contains those five groups. Only 1808 printings are included; the Embargo Act was first printed in December 1807.
label: The embargo laws

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the act of 9 January 1808 supplementary to the Embargo Act: vessels licensed for the coasting trade, and fishing and whaling vessels, may not depart without bond that they will not go to a foreign port, with penalties for evading the embargo.
label: The supplementary act of 9 January

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the act of 22 April 1808 authorising the President, during the recess of Congress, to suspend the embargo in whole or in part if peace, a suspension of hostilities or changes in the belligerents' measures made American commerce sufficiently safe.
label: The act allowing the President to suspend the embargo

admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Brussels paragraph of 17 October 1792, printed in American papers in January and February 1793: word from the provinces of Namur and Luxembourg that the army of the French princes, Monsieur and the Count (or Duke) d'Artois, and that under the Duke de Bourbon were disbanded, and that their men wandered in great distress. A report ('We hear').
label: Brussels, 17 October 1792: the emigrant princes' armies disbanded

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the Emperor Francis's declaration on leaving Vienna, April 1809, headed 'DECLARATION OF WAR By Francis I. Emperor of Austria': 'Before his Imperial Majesty left this capital, he was pleased to issue the following proclamation ... People of Austria!—I leave my capital to join the brave defenders of the country'. The Austrian government's own statement.
label: The Emperor Francis's declaration of war, Vienna, April 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the act of 9 January 1809 'to enforce and make more effectual an act, entitled, An act laying an embargo on all ships and vessels in the ports and harbors of the United States, and the several acts supplementary thereto': goods may not be put on board any vessel or carriage with intent to export them without a permit, and the collectors are given powers to seize, detain and require bonds.
label: The act of 9 January 1809 to enforce the embargo

admission_rule: Reviewed 1792 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an article of an English paper of 24 October 1791: 'It is said that one of the first acts of Colonel Simcoe's Government in Canada will be, to deliver up the British Posts situated on the east of the River St. Lawrance, and to the south of Nova-Scotia, according to certain articles in the peace with America.' (two papers print 'administration' for 'Government' and 'the treaty of peace'). A report of what is said, from a London paper.
label: An English paper of 24 October 1791: it is said that one of the first acts of Colonel Simcoe's government in Canada will be to deliver up the British posts

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: The papers of July and August 1809 on Britain's refusal to stand by the arrangement Mr. Erskine had made in April, as the papers printed them: a London report of 24 May that Mr. Canning told the Commons the agreement was not authorised, the order in council of 24 May, Mr. Canning's instructions to Mr. Erskine of 23 January as laid before Parliament, and the National Intelligencer's paragraph of 16 August on Mr. Erskine's letter of explanation. Contains those four groups. Each is one government's statement or its paper's account.
label: Britain disavows the April arrangement, July and August 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the British minister's note to the Secretary of State, Washington, 15 June 1809: 'I have the honor to inclose a copy of an order of his majesty in council issued on the 26th of April last ... I am enabled to assure you that it has no connexion whatever with the overtures which I have been authorised to make', with the Secretary of State's answer of the same day. Each note is its writer's own account.
label: Mr. Erskine's note of 15 June 1809 on the order of 26 April, and the Secretary of State's answer

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the six notes exchanged at Washington between the British minister, D. M. Erskine, and the Secretary of State, Robert Smith, on 17, 18 and 19 April 1809, printed in one run (Nos. I to VI) and counted by the first: 'I have the honor to inform you, that I have received his Majesty's commands, to represent to the government of the United States, that his Majesty is animated by the most sincere desire for an adjustment of the differences'. Diplomatic notes, each in its writer's words.
label: The notes of Mr. Erskine and the Secretary of State, 17 to 19 April 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1790 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph of comment: 'There is a strange idea that prevails in the world, that wars are necessary at the return of different periods in the age of a nation; and on this principle there are those who justify a pleasing anticipation of this most capital of all misfortunes: It will however be generally found on examination, that this insensibility to the misery of our species, arises from an unprincipled love of gain ...'. A writer's opinion, as the papers print it.
label: Autumn 1790: 'There is a strange idea that prevails in the world, that wars are necessary at the return of different periods in the age of a nation'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from Cork (January 1776) on the gifts collected for Colonel Ethan Allen and his fellow prisoners in the Solebay, with Allen's note of thanks.
label: Ethan Allen at Cork

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Documents printed in July, August and September 1777 on the American army's evacuation of Ticonderoga and Mount Independence before General Burgoyne's army: the council of general officers of 5 July, General St. Clair's letter to Congress of 14 July and Congress's resolutions of 29 July for an inquiry (6 papers each). Of the same affair, General Schuyler's letter of 7 July (5), General St. Clair's letter on General Schuyler (4) and a letter from headquarters on the papers' prejudice against General St. Clair (4) are not chosen (X-1800-01). Contains those three groups.
label: The evacuation of Ticonderoga and Mount Independence, July and August 1777: the council of officers, General St. Clair's letter and Congress's inquiry

admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan (round three: stories once held back for framing, at the 6-paper threshold for 1793).
definition: Printings of the account given at New York by Captain John Fanning of the brig Union, 14 days from Cap Français (New York, 9 July 1793): on 18 June the civil commissioners Sonthonax and Polverel arrived at the Cape and suspended the governor, Galbaud; by his account they then encouraged 'a number of mulattoes' to come into town, who armed the enslaved people of the town 'to assist in destroying all the whites'; between 8 and 10 thousand people were killed from 20 June; and the town was plundered and burnt, with not more than 50 houses standing when he sailed on the 23rd with a fleet of 250 sail. One ship captain's account. Three papers print it under the heading 'HORRID NEWS!'.
label: Captain Fanning's account of Cap Français

admission_rule: Reviewed 1794 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from Fayetteville, dated the 6th: 'Two gentlemen just arrived here from Charleston (S. C.) report, that a French 20 gun ship, & an English 18 gun frigate had had a severe action near the harbour; that the English ship was taken and bro't into Charleston, in consequence of which a riot took place'. A report at second hand, as the letter-writer gives it.
label: A letter from Fayetteville, North Carolina, of 6 January 1794: a report from Charleston of an action between a French and an English ship

admission_rule: Reviewed 1803 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph credited by some papers to the Lancaster Journal and by others to the Washington Federalist: 'Fifteen millions of dollars (the price of Louisiana) calculating more than a ton to every waggon, would require 375 waggons to carry it; and (allowing 4 horses to each team) it would require fifteen hundred horses, they would make a string of five miles in length. The money would support 25 thousand soldiers for seven years and a half'. The National Intelligencer, the Republican Ledger and the New Hampshire Gazette follow it with a 'Counter statement' on what the territory contains. A policy argument against the price, as the papers printed it.
label: 'Fifteen millions of dollars (the price of Louisiana) ... would require 375 waggons to carry it': a calculation against the purchase, 1803

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a New York report of the fire-ship attack on the British ships in the Hudson on 16 August 1776.
label: Fire-ship attack

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the Austrian army's first bulletin, 'Dated Head Quarters Sacile, April 17', taken from London papers by way of Montreal and Boston: the Archduke John 'entered the territory of Frioule', and an action near Sacile 'terminated entirely to our advantage', with prisoners, cannon and eagles taken. The Austrian army's own account.
label: The first Austrian bulletin: the Archduke John in Friuli, April 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1779 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Fishkill (New York) report of 3 June 1779: 'The latter end of last week, a number of British vessels made their appearance in the North River; they consist of 13 ships, 3 brigs, 4 top-sail schooners, 3 galleys, 6 top-sail sloops, about 20 smaller vessels, and a great number of flat-bottom boats. Last Lord's day, (31st ult.) 1500 men landed eight miles below Peekskill...' It goes on with the enemy's batteries against Fort de la Fayette. A Fishkill paper's report.
label: Fishkill, 3 June 1779: 'a number of British vessels made their appearance in the North River'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1782 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Fish-Kill paragraph of 10 October 1782: 'We learn from Long-Island, that the enemy have evacuated their post at Lloyd's-Neck the 22d ult.—That the loyalists on that part of the island had the indulgence offered them of emigrating to Nova Scotia on certain terms of encouragement—That many of them chose rather to risk the forfeited mercy of their country...' Printed by all four newspapers that survive for its weeks; admitted by the rule's first part. A Fish-Kill paper's report.
label: Fish-Kill, 10 October 1782: 'We learn from Long-Island, that the enemy have evacuated their post at Lloyd's-Neck'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1781 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Fishkill paragraph of 1 November 1781: 'We have just heard from Albany, that a party of the enemy, upward of 500 strong, commanded by a Major Ross, came down the Oneida Lake, and committed depredations as usual; they burnt twenty dwelling and several out houses'. A Fishkill paper's report, from Albany news.
label: Fishkill, 1 November 1781: a report that a party of the enemy under Major Ross came down the Oneida Lake

admission_rule: Reviewed 1782 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Fish-Kill paragraph of 19 September 1782: 'On last Saturday his Excellency the Count De Rochambeau, commander in chief of the French army, arrived with his suite at Verplank's point; he was saluted on his approach by the American army, drawn up for that purpose in two lines fronting each other, and extending from Head-Quarters to the ferry...' Printed by all four newspapers that survive for its weeks; admitted by the rule's first part. A Fish-Kill paper's report.
label: Fish-Kill, 19 September 1782: 'his Excellency the Count De Rochambeau, commander in chief of the French army, arrived with his suite at Verplank's point; he was saluted on his approach by the American army'

admission_rule: Existing inspected selections only; additional candidates require an explicit documented admission.
definition: Later related account concerning the main body returning to Brest; no explicit retraction assigned.
label: Later fleet-return account

admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Boston report of May 1805, headed in most papers 'TOULON FLEET OUT': Captain Folgier (so printed in most papers; 'Folger' in the Oracle Post and the Virginia Argus, 'Foigier' in the National Intelligencer), arrived from Lisbon, 'is the bearer of the very interesting intelligence of the escape of the French fleet from Toulon'; a transport ship had brought Lisbon the news of the fleet off Cadiz. A ship captain's report of news at second hand.
label: Boston report: Captain Folgier's news that the Toulon fleet is out

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the report in part of the House committee on the part of the President's message concerning foreign relations (presented on 22 November 1808 by George W. Campbell): the choice lay between submission, war with both Britain and France, and continuing the embargo with stricter enforcement; with three resolutions.
label: The House committee's report on foreign relations

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the note of Charles James Fox, the British Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, to James Monroe, the American minister (Downing Street, May 1806): the King 'has thought fit to direct that the necessary measures should be taken for the blockade of the coasts, rivers and ports from the river Elbe to the port of Brest, both inclusive'. The British government's notice.
label: Fox's note to Monroe on the blockade from the Elbe to Brest

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Two French documents of February 1809 printed by American papers in May: a French imperial decree of 25 February releasing American vessels detained in French ports by the embargo, and General Armstrong's letter from Paris of 23 February reporting it. Contains those two groups. The French government's decree and the American minister's report.
label: France releases the American vessels held by its embargo, 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the declaration of Francis II, emperor of Austria, giving up 'the high office of emperor of Germany', from the Paris Moniteur of 14 August 1806: 'Since the peace of Presburg all our attention and all our care have been employed to fulfil with scrupulous fidelity all the engagements' of that treaty. A ruler's own declaration.
label: Francis II gives up the crown of the German Empire

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the American commissioners' letter to Lord Stormont of 2 April 1777: 'We did ourselves the honor of writing some time since to your Lordship on the subject of exchanging prisoners; you did not condescend to give us any answer'; they send depositions on the treatment of American prisoners in Europe. The papers add the reply they say was made: 'The king's ambassadour receives no letters from rebels, except when they come to ask mercy.' The commissioners' own letter.
label: Benjamin Franklin and Silas Deane to Lord Stormont, the British ambassador at Paris, 2 April 1777, on prisoners, and his reply

admission_rule: Reviewed 1774 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the declaration that Benjamin Franklin, agent of the Massachusetts House of Representatives in London, published in a letter of December 1773 to the printer of a London paper (the Morning Chronicle in one printing, the London Chronicle in another): 'Finding that two Gentlemen have been unfortunately engaged in a Duel, about a Transaction and its Circumstances of which both of them are totally ignorant and innocent, I think it incumbent on me to declare ... that I alone am the Person who obtained, and transmitted to Boston, the Letters in Question'; the letters, he says, were not of the nature of private letters between friends but were written by public officers on public affairs, to procure public measures. The New-Hampshire Gazette, the Pennsylvania Packet and Purdie and Dixon's Virginia Gazette print the letter; the Connecticut Courant and the Massachusetts Spy print a London report of the duel that gives the declaration in Franklin's words turned into indirect speech ('Benjamin Franklin, Esq; agent for the house of representatives of this province ... has published a declaration, That he alone was the person who obtained and transmitted to Boston the letters in question'). Counted together, a letter with a paragraph made from it (C-02, as X-1801-04): 5 papers, every paper that survives for its weeks. Franklin's own declaration.
label: Dr. Franklin's declaration that he alone obtained the Hutchinson letters and sent them to Boston, after the duel of Mr. Whately and Mr. Temple

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract from Natchitoches, 26 August 1806: 'Mr. Freeman returned to this place on Saturday last, after having ascended 430 miles above this place, where the Spaniards had been waiting for him'. One writer's account of the exploring party sent up the Red River.
label: Natchitoches, 26 August: Mr. Freeman's party turned back

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the French army's thirty-third bulletin of the army of Spain, from the Paris Moniteur of 2 March 1809 (translated for the Boston Chronicle from a paper brought by the letter of marque L'Esperance): 'The Duke of Dalmatia arrived at Tuy on the 10th Feb. The whole province is quiet', then the siege of Saragossa: 'More than one third of the houses were in our possession'. The Alexandria Daily Gazette printed the Saragossa part alone as an extract, under the Boston Recorder's introduction. The French army's own account.
label: The French thirty-third bulletin of the army of Spain: Tuy and Saragossa

admission_rule: Reviewed 1802 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Two items of March 1802 on the French expedition under General Leclerc, which reached St. Domingo (Saint-Domingue, now Haiti) early in February: the proclamation of the Consuls of the French Republic to the inhabitants of the island, which Leclerc published on landing, and a Baltimore report, from a ship's captain, of the burning of Cape François. Contains those two groups.
label: The French army arrives at St. Domingo, February 1802: the Consuls' proclamation and a report of the burning of the Cape

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the French army's thirtieth bulletin of the army of Spain, Valladolid, 21 January 1809, in two translations: 'The Duke of Dalmatia left Betanzos on the 12th inst. Having reached the Mero, he found the bridge of Burgo cut', then its account of the fighting before Corunna on the 16th. The French army's own account.
label: The French thirtieth bulletin of the army of Spain: Corunna

admission_rule: Reviewed 1788 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the act 'of King's Council of State, for the Encouragement of the Commerce of France with the United States of America. December 29, 1787. Extract from the Records of the Council of State. The King, desirous of encouraging the commerce of his subjects with the United States of America'; it sets the duties and privileges on American goods in France. An act of the French government, printed after the letter with which a French official sent it.
label: The King of France's Council of State, 29 December 1787: an act for the encouragement of the commerce of France with the United States

admission_rule: Reviewed 1783 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Portsmouth paragraph of 7 June 1783: 'Yesterday arrived here a French frigate in 44 days from France, with stores, &c. for the ship America, of 74 guns, now lying before this town. She brings nothing new.' A Portsmouth paper's report.
label: Portsmouth, New Hampshire, 7 June 1783: a French frigate arrives from France with stores for the ship America, of 74 guns

admission_rule: Reviewed 1803 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a translation of the note that the minister for foreign affairs of the French Republic addressed to the ambassador of his Britannic Majesty on 23 Floreal (13 May 1803), and that orators of the government communicated to the Conservative Senate: 'In the important and serious circumstances, in which the two nations find themselves, the undersigned the minister for foreign affairs of the French Republic, has received an order to place under the eyes of the British government the following note'; it answers the King's message to Parliament of March 1803 on 'formidable armaments ... preparing in the ports of France and Holland', and gives the French government's account of the negotiation over Malta. The papers print two translations ('are situated', 'find themselves'). The French government's own note.
label: The French minister for foreign affairs' note to the British ambassador, 13 May 1803, as communicated to the Conservative Senate

admission_rule: Reviewed 1802 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the account from the Paris papers of 3 and 4 August 1802, in two translations, of the Conservative Senate's audience with the First Consul: its president, Barthélemy, 'addressed Bonaparte in a speech of which the following are extracts: "Citizen First Consul, The French, grateful for the immense services you have rendered to them, wish that the First Magistracy of the State should be irrevocably placed in your hands"' ('A new career commences for the First Consul'), read the Senate's decree that, as the papers print it, 3,568,885 of 3,577,259 citizens had voted for Napoleon Bonaparte as Consul for life, and the First Consul replied. Five papers print the translation that begins 'At the Levee yesterday'; three print another ('The French people, as a mark of gratitude'), which the Alexandria Advertiser takes from the New York Mercantile Advertiser. Counted together as one item in two printed forms. The French Senate's and the First Consul's own words, as the papers translated them.
label: Paris, August 1802: the president of the Conservative Senate addresses Bonaparte, proclaimed First Consul for life, and the First Consul replies

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an English newspaper's summary of the French army's tenth bulletin, 'Ebersdorf, May 23': 'After describing the form of the Danube at Ebersdorf, the bulletin states, that on the night of the 20th, the Emperor crossed the Danube'; the summary gives the French account of the two days' fighting and the English writer's comments. The French army's account, as summarised in London.
label: The French tenth bulletin (Ebersdorf, 23 May 1809), as summarised in London

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the French army's twenty-fifth bulletin, 'Wolkersdorf, 8th July', translated from a Hamburg paper: the passage of the Danube from the island of Lobau on 4 July and the battles of 5 and 6 July. The French army's own account.
label: The French twenty-fifth bulletin: the battle of Wagram, July 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Four documents on the United States frigate Philadelphia, as the 1804 papers printed them: the President's message of 20 March sending Captain Bainbridge's letter, dated Tripoli, 1 November 1803, on the frigate's wreck on rocks near Tripoli and its capture; Commodore Preble's letter to the American consul at Gibraltar on its burning; Lieutenant Decatur's own report of 17 February 1804 that his party set the frigate on fire in the harbour of Tripoli; and the official notice of his promotion. Contains those four groups.
label: The frigate Philadelphia, lost before Tripoli and burned in its harbour, 1804

admission_rule: Reviewed 1779 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of two letters, as the papers published them in January and February 1779 with other papers from Georgia: 'In the morning of the 24th of November Colonel John M'Intosh, commanding officer in Fort Morris, received the following from Lieut. Col. Fuser, commanding a body of British troops, who had the night before taken possession of the upper end of the town of Sunbury': 'You cannot be ignorant that four armies are in motion to reduce this province... if you deliver me the fort which you command, lay down your arms, and remain neuter until the fate of America is determined, you shall, as well as all the inhabitants of this parish, remain in the peaceable possession of your property'; and the answer: 'We, Sir, are fighting the battle of America, and therefore disdain to remain neuter till its fate is determined.—As to surrendering the fort, receive this laconic reply.—Come and take it.' A British officer's summons and an American officer's answer, in an American publication.
label: Sunbury, Georgia, 25 November 1778: Lieutenant Colonel Fuser's summons to the fort, and Colonel McIntosh's answer, 'Come and take it'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1774 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Boston paragraph of August 1774: 'We hear that his Excellency Governor Gage desired the attendance of the Selectmen of this town at the Province House on Saturday last, when he informed them of that clause in the late act of parliament forbidding town-meetings without special leave of the Governor'; it reports that he told them he would give leave for a meeting if he judged it expedient, and, being told that the province law had been the rule of their conduct, that he was determined to carry the acts of parliament into execution and they must be answerable for any bad consequences. A Boston paper's report at second hand ('We hear').
label: Boston, August 1774: Governor Gage tells the selectmen of the clause of the new act that forbids town meetings without his leave

admission_rule: Reviewed 1774 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the letter of General Gage to Peyton Randolph, the president of the Continental Congress, dated Boston, 20 October 1774, in answer to the Congress's letter to him of 10 October: 'Representations should be made with Candour, and Matters stated exactly as they stand. People would be led to believe, from your Letter to me of the 10th Instant, that Works were raised against the Town of Boston, private Property invaded, the Soldiers suffered to insult the Inhabitants'; he answers that 'There is not a single Gun pointed against the Town, no Man's Property has been seized or hurt, except the King's', and that no troops have given less cause for complaint. General Gage's own letter.
label: General Gage's answer to the Congress, Boston, 20 October 1774: 'Representations should be made with candour, and matters stated exactly as they stand'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1774 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the proclamation of Thomas Gage, governor of Massachusetts Bay, dated 29 June 1774: 'A Proclamation, for discouraging certain illegal combinations. Whereas certain persons, calling themselves a Committee of Correspondence for the town of Boston, have lately presumed to make, or cause to be made, a certain unlawful instrument, purporting to be a solemn League and Covenant, intended to be signed by the inhabitants of this province; whereby they are most solemnly to covenant and engage, to suspend all commercial intercourse with the Island of Great-Britain'; it calls the covenant traitorous and orders magistrates to apprehend those who publish or sign it. The governor's own proclamation.
label: Governor Gage's proclamation of June 1774 'for discouraging certain illegal combinations' (the solemn league and covenant)

admission_rule: Reviewed 1774 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the proclamation of Governor Gage of July 1774: 'A Proclamation, for the encouragement of piety and virtue, and for preventing and punishing of vice, profanity and immorality. In humble imitation of the laudable example of our most gracious Sovereign George the third, who in the first year of his reign was pleased to issue his royal proclamation'; it exhorts all his Majesty's subjects 'to avoid all hypocrisy, sedition, licentiousness' and other immoralities, and commands judges and officers to see the laws against vice executed. The governor's own proclamation.
label: Governor Gage's proclamation of July 1774 'for the encouragement of piety and virtue, and for preventing and punishing of vice, profanity and immorality'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1810 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of Albert Gallatin's statement, signed by him and published in the National Intelligencer: 'Amongst the papers lately laid before the British Parliament, respecting American affairs, is a despatch from Mr. Erskine to Mr. Canning, dated 4th December, 1808, which principally relates to a conversation between Mr. Erskine and myself'; he says that the opinions the despatch ascribes to him were Mr. Erskine's own inference and that Mr. Erskine must have mistaken his meaning. Several papers print it after extracts of Mr. Erskine's despatches. The Secretary of the Treasury's own statement.
label: The Secretary of the Treasury's statement on Mr. Erskine's despatch of 4 December 1808, published in July 1810

admission_rule: Reviewed 1803 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a letter from Mr. Gascoigne, Member of Parliament for Liverpool, to the Mayor of Liverpool, dated London, 8 March 1803, which the ship Mercury, Captain Sterling, brought to New York in 31 days from Liverpool: 'War is expected—a message this day from the King to the House to that tendency—Militia expected to be called out to guard against invasion—Stocks down four per cent.—Mr. Pitt, it is supposed, will return soon to power'. The papers print it within two different New York reports of the Mercury's arrival (one from the New-York Gazette, 'Strong probability of a renewal of the War between Great-Britain and France', the other headed 'Symptoms of war in Europe'), and the New Hampshire Gazette within a third; the letter, which all of them print, is counted as the item. A Member of Parliament's letter, printed at second hand.
label: New York, April 1803: the ship Mercury brings Mr. Gascoigne's letter of 8 March from London, 'War is expected'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of General Gates's letter to the President of Congress (Ticonderoga, 5 November 1776), published by order of Congress, reporting that General Carleton's fleet and army had withdrawn from Crown Point.
label: Gates on Carleton's retreat

admission_rule: Reviewed 1779 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of extracts of Major General Gates's letter to the President of Congress, dated Newport, 27 October 1779: 'I have the honour to acquaint your Excellency, that this Island was evacuated by the enemy's troops on the night of the 25th instant, and the next morning the army under my command took possession of the town of Newport; I have further the pleasure to inform your Excellency, that the enemy did not commit any wanton destruction upon their leaving the Island...' An American general's own report.
label: General Gates to the President of Congress, Newport, 27 October 1779: 'this Island was evacuated by the enemy's troops on the night of the 25th instant'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1780 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of General Gates's letter to the President of Congress, Hillsborough, 20 August 1780: 'In the deepest distress and anxiety of mind, I am obliged to acquaint your Excellency with the defeat of the troops under my command ...', with Colonel Sumter's letter to him of 15 August; published by order of Congress. The commander's own letter.
label: General Gates to Congress, Hillsborough, 20 August 1780, on 'the defeat of the troops under my command' near Camden

admission_rule: Reviewed 1792 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a report of the General Advertiser of Philadelphia, 14 August 1792: 'By a courier arrived at Havre-de-Grace, just as an American vessel was about to sail for New-York, and which had but 27 days passage, the intelligence was received, that the army of M. la Fayette had taken the citadel of Namur'. A report at second hand, of news brought by a courier.
label: Philadelphia, August 1792, from the General Advertiser: by a courier at Havre, news that the army of M. la Fayette had taken the citadel of Namur

admission_rule: Reviewed 1780 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: General Arnold's letter to General Washington from the Vulture, 25 September 1780, and Congress's resolutions of 4 October and 3 November (his name erased from the register; the militiamen who intercepted Major Andre rewarded), as the papers printed them. Each counted by its own words. Contains those two groups.
label: General Arnold, September-November 1780: his letter to General Washington, and Congress's resolutions

admission_rule: Reviewed 1774 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a letter of 29 August 1774 that the papers print as 'a Copy of a Letter, said to be wrote by General Brattle, to the Commander in chief': 'Mr. Brattle presents his Duty to his Excellency Governor Gage, he apprehends it is his Duty to acquaint his Excellency from Time to Time with every Thing he hears and knows to be true & is of Importance in these troublesome Times'; it reports that a militia captain has been pressed to warn his company to meet at a minute's warning, and that the selectmen of Medford have taken their town's stock of powder from the arsenal on Quarry Hill, 'so that there is now therein the King's Powder only'. The papers printed it in early September among reports of the crowds that gathered at Cambridge on 2 September. The letter's own words, as printed by others; the excerpts end before it names militia officers.
label: Cambridge, 29 August 1774: a letter 'said to be wrote by General Brattle' to Governor Gage, on the militia and the province's powder

admission_rule: Reviewed 1783 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from General Clark, dated Lincoln, 27 November 1782, that the papers print from Richmond, 28 December: 'We left the Ohio the 4th inst. with 1050 men, surprised the principal Shawanese town on the evening of the 10th, and immediately detached parties to different quarters; in a few hours afterwards two thirds of their towns were laid in ashes, and every thing they were possessed of destroyed'.
