General Clark's own account of his expedition against the Shawnee towns, as the papers print it.
label: Richmond, December 1782: an extract of a letter from General Clark, dated Lincoln, 27 November 1782, on his expedition from the Ohio

admission_rule: Reviewed 1792 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of General Dumourier's letter to M. Servan of 1 October 1792: 'At length, my dear Servan, what I expected and predicted in my letters has taken place. The Prussians are in full retreat.' The general's own letter, in translation.
label: General Dumourier to M. Servan, Saint Menehould, 1 October 1792: the Prussians are in full retreat

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the paper General Hamilton left with his will, numbered No. 12 in the publication (No. 13 in the National Intelligencer, No. XII in Jenks' Portland Gazette): 'On my expected interview with Col. Burr, I think it proper to make some remarks explanatory of my conduct, motives and views', beginning 'My religious and moral principles are strongly opposed to the practice of duelling'. Most papers introduce it as 'inclosed with his will and some other papers in a packet addressed to one of his executors'. Hamilton's own words, written before the meeting.
label: General Hamilton's statement 'On my expected interview with Col. Burr', found with his will

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of Alexander Hamilton's will: 'In the name of God, Amen. I, Alexander Hamilton, of the city of New-York, Counsellor at Law, do make this my last Will and Testament', which names three executors, is signed on the ninth day of July 1804 and is certified at the New York Surrogate's Office on 16 July. Most papers print it after Hamilton's statement and the Evening Post's note 'On the foregoing letters and papers, the Editor will make no comment'. The document itself; the excerpts end before the executors' names.
label: General Hamilton's will, signed 9 July 1804

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Three items on General Moreau, held in the Temple at Paris in 1804 as an accomplice of Georges and Pichegru, as the American papers printed them: a letter to Bonaparte that the newsletter Les Nouvelles à la Main (No. II, 9 March 1804) attributed to him; the same newsletter's No. III (20 March), which says that letter was authentic with one exception and prints letters it says passed between Madame Bonaparte and Madame Moreau; and a London paragraph reporting that the Paris Moniteur had announced his banishment to America. Contains those three groups.
label: General Moreau in the papers, 1804: a letter attributed to him, a Paris newsletter's correction, and his banishment

admission_rule: Reviewed 1791 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of Brigadier General Charles Scott's account of the expedition against the towns on the Wabash in May and June 1791, in two forms counted together (C-02): his letter to the Secretary for the Department of War, dated Lexington, 20 June 1791 ('In prosecution of the enterprise, I marched four miles from the banks of the Ohio on the 23d of May, and on the 24th I resumed my march, and pushed forward with the utmost industry'), and the Lexington paper's 'detail of Facts, relative to the operations of the Expedition under Brig. Gen. Scott, against the Savages of the Wabash' of 25 June, which gives the same account in the third person ('The Army marched four miles from the bank of the Ohio on the 23d of last month'). The commander's own account, and a Lexington paper's version of it.
label: General Scott's account of the expedition against the towns on the Wabash, May and June 1791: his letter to the Secretary of War, and the Lexington 'detail of facts'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1791 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a circular letter of Brigadier General Scott to the county lieutenants in Kentucky, dated Lexington, 11 November 1791, first printed in the Kentucky Gazette: 'We have now received certain intelligence that the army have been defeated. The loss is very great. The Garrison at Fort Jefferson is intercepted and many, many have been wounded; gallant men are now left on the road, unable to travel, and without any provision but the flesh of the pack horses. This case requires immediate exertions.' He appoints a rendezvous for the 15th. The general's own circular.
label: Lexington, 11 November 1791: General Scott's circular letter to the county lieutenants of Kentucky, 'We have now received certain intelligence that the army have been defeated'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1791 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Two public papers on the defeat of the army under General St. Clair, as the papers printed them in November and December 1791: Brigadier General Scott's circular letter to the county lieutenants of Kentucky, dated Lexington, 11 November, and General St. Clair's letter to the Secretary of War, dated Fort Washington, 9 November, which the President sent to Congress in December. Contains those two groups.
label: The defeat of the army under General St. Clair, November 1791: General Scott's circular from Lexington and General St. Clair's report, as the papers printed them

admission_rule: Reviewed 1791 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the letter of Major General St. Clair to the Secretary of War, dated Fort Washington, 9 November 1791, which the President sent to Congress with a message in December: 'Yesterday afternoon the remains of the army under my command got back to this place, and I have now the painful task to give you an account of as warm and unfortunate an action as almost any that has been fought, in which every corps was engaged and worsted, except the first regiment—that had been detached upon a service I had the honor to inform you of in my last dispatch, and had not joined me.' The commander's own report.
label: Fort Washington, 9 November 1791: General St. Clair's letter to the Secretary of War, 'Yesterday afternoon the remains of the army under my command got back to this place'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: One affair in three printed documents, as the papers printed them from mid-August to early September 1793: John Jay and Rufus King's statement that the French minister, Genêt, had said he would appeal to the people from certain decisions of the President; Genêt's letter to the President asking him to declare that he had never said so to him; and the Secretary of State's answer for the President. Contains those three groups. The statement is an allegation and the letter the minister's own account; whether he said it is not settled here.
label: Genêt and the President: the 'appeal to the people', 1793

admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the letter of Citizen Genêt, minister plenipotentiary of the French Republic, to President Washington (New York, 13 August 1793), printed with the Secretary of State's answer, as published in New York (the National Gazette credits the New York Diary of 21 August): persons were saying that he had threatened to appeal to the people from the President's decisions, and he asked the President for an explicit declaration that he had never intimated such an intention to him. The minister's own account.
label: Genêt's letter to the President, 13 August 1793

admission_rule: Reviewed 1774 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a short extract of a letter from a gentleman in England to his friend in Philadelphia, printed from Philadelphia in March 1774: 'The warlike preparations of the French I imagine will alarm all Europe; what their designs are, time must bring forth. The insurrection at Petersburg, we imagine is set on foot by them, and that his Prussian Majesty is at the bottom of scheme'; it expects fleets and armies to be sent to different parts. A private letter printed at second hand, with the writer's conjectures.
label: 'A gentleman in England writes his friend in Philadelphia: The warlike preparations of the French I imagine will alarm all Europe'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of George Johnstone's declaration dated New York, 26 August 1778, in answer to Congress's declaration: having seen the declaration of Congress of 11 August and its resolution, 'The said George Johnstone for himself says, That he is far from considering the said resolution of the Congress as offensive to him; That he rather receives it as a mark of distinction'; he declares that 'the subscriber, George Johnstone, thinks proper to decline acting as a Commissioner, or otherwise interfering in any message, answer, agreement, negotiation, matter or thing that may regard the said Congress, which he does with so much the more pleasure as he is perfectly satisfied the business will be left in more able and sufficient hands', reserving the liberty of publishing a justification of his conduct. Mr. Johnstone's own declaration.
label: George Johnstone's declaration of 26 August 1778: he declines to act as a commissioner in anything that regards Congress

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from a gentleman in Georgia (14 March 1808): the embargo had left the citizens of Mobile and Pensacola 'almost in a state of starvation', with the prices of corn and flour there. It is one unnamed correspondent's report.
label: A Georgia letter: Mobile and Pensacola

admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan (round three: stories once held back for framing, at the 6-paper threshold for 1793).
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter dated German Creek, Territory South of the Ohio, 16 August 1793, written to the editor of a Winchester paper (2 September) and printed from it: the writer reports that on 4 August Colonel Daugherty of Jefferson county crossed the Tennessee with 180 men to 'the valley Indian towns', where by his account they killed nine men and two women, took seven prisoners, burnt twenty towns and villages and destroyed crops, with five of their own men wounded. He adds that the frontier inhabitants are 'in close forts', and argues for a large company raised 'under the sanction of government' to give the towns, in his words, 'a severe flogging, in order to bring them to a sense of their duty, and teach them to pay some respect to treaties'. One writer's account.
label: A letter from German Creek, 16 August 1793: an expedition across the Tennessee

admission_rule: Reviewed 1782 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph of foreign news dated 10 August 1782: 'The attention of all Europe is now turned with infinite apprehension and solicitude to the fate of Gibraltar. On this theatre the greatest exploits are shortly expected to take place. The fame acquired by the Duke de Crillon in his siege of Minorca, on the one hand, and the tried and determined bravery of General Elliot, on the other, must produce a contest...' A single paragraph from a run of foreign news (C-09), printed by all four newspapers that survive for its weeks; admitted by the rule's first part. A writer's expectation, from the European papers.
label: 10 August 1782: 'The attention of all Europe is now turned with infinite apprehension and solicitude to the fate of Gibraltar'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1803 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a report from Raleigh, North Carolina, of early December 1803 (a Raleigh paragraph of 5 December in most papers, a letter dated 8 December in the National Intelligencer): 'A bed of Gold Ore has been lately discovered in Cabarrus County, in this state, in a Creek running through the land of' a farmer, 'which promises to be a source of great riches to the proprietor'; his children found the first pieces while fishing. The papers name the landowner; the excerpts end before his name. A report at second hand.
label: Raleigh, December 1803: 'A bed of Gold Ore has been lately discovered in Cabarrus County'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an eyewitness account of the attack by American row galleys (gondolas) on the Phoenix and the Rose on 3 August 1776.
label: Row galleys attack the warships

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the oration Gouverneur Morris delivered at General Hamilton's funeral in New York, as the Evening Post gave it, saying that those who heard it 'all agree that it comes near enough to what was actually delivered, to be presented as the oration at length': 'Fellow-citizens, If on this sad, this solemn occasion, I should endeavour to move your commiseration, it would be doing injustice to that sensibility which has been so generally and so justly manifested.' The speaker's words as reported; two papers name him 'Governor Morris'.
label: Gouverneur Morris's oration at General Hamilton's funeral: 'If on this sad, this solemn occasion'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of extracts from the message of William Livingston, Governor of New Jersey, to the General Assembly of the state: 'Gentlemen, I heartily congratulate you upon the agreeable news we have received from France, since I had the pleasure of meeting you last in this place'; it lays before the Assembly the resolution of Congress of 23 April recommending pardon for those who return, and argues against receiving back Tories who have taken part with the enemy. The Governor's own message, as the New-Jersey Gazette printed it.
label: Governor Livingston's message to the General Assembly of New Jersey, May 1778, on the news from France and on the Tories

admission_rule: Reviewed 1782 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of General Greene's letter to the President of Congress, Head-Quarters near Bacon's Bridge, South Carolina, 21 May 1782: 'I do myself the honor to enclose to your Excellency a copy of a resolution of the British House of Commons, and the King's reply, which were sent out to me last evening by Lieutenant-General Leslie, through Major Skelly, his Aid de Camp, accompanied with a verbal message, that as those changes of measures seemed to lead directly to a peace, he would agree to a cessation of hostilities on their part, provided we would on ours...'; 'As the proposition for a cessation of hostilities did not come with the necessary forms, I gave no written answer.' A sub-story (C-01): in 4 of the 5 newspapers that survive for its weeks. The general's own letter.
label: General Greene to the President of Congress, near Bacon's Bridge, 21 May 1782: 'I do myself the honour to enclose to your Excellency a copy of a resolution of the British House of Commons, and the King's reply'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1782 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of General Greene's letter to the President of Congress of 31 May 1782 ('I had the honor to address your Excellency on the 21st inst. on the subject of a verbal message from Lieut. Gen. Leslie, proposing a cessation of hostilities in this country. Since then I have received...'), with the letter it encloses from General Wayne, Ebenezer, 24 May 1782: 'On the 21st inst. I received intelligence of the enemy being out in force from Savannah, in consequence of which White's dragoons and Posey's infantry were put in motion...'. The letter and its enclosure are counted as one item (as X-1810-01), and the enclosure printed alone with it (as 1779's General Putnam letter, X-1779-03): four papers print the letter, three of them with General Wayne's letter; the New-Hampshire Gazette prints General Wayne's letter alone, 'extracted' from a Philadelphia paper, and later a paragraph of General Greene's letter ('Flying parties of the British cavalry are frequently making excursions into the country from Charlestown'), which is not counted again. In all five newspapers that survive for its weeks; admitted by the rule's first part. The generals' own letters. The New-Jersey Gazette dates General Greene's letter 21 May.
label: General Greene to the President of Congress, near Bacon's Bridge, 31 May 1782, with General Wayne's letter of 24 May: 'On the 21st inst. I received intelligence of the enemy being out in force from Savannah'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1782 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of extracts of General Greene's letters from Ashley Hill, South Carolina: of 28 August 1782 ('The inclosed copy of a letter from Lieutenant General Leslie, contains an extraordinary requisition for a supply of provision, which was refused. I cannot but consider it as an evidence of the intention of the enemy to seduce and lull the people of this country...'), with General Leslie's letter from Charlestown ('I hope these considerations will induce you to accept a proposal so evidently advantageous to the interests of your own party; and that you will in consequence, order rice and other provisions to be sent into town...'); and of 29 August ('I have the honour to transmit your excellency the report of brigadier general Gist, relative to the operations of the troops under his command... It is very unfortunate that we have to lament the loss of so valuable and distinguished an officer as lieutenant colonel Laurens, who was killed in the skirmish on the 27th instant'), with General Gist's report and a list of the killed and wounded. Printed together by all four newspapers that survive for their weeks; admitted by the rule's first part (the letters and their enclosures as one item, as X-1810-01). The generals' own letters.
label: General Greene's letters of 28 and 29 August 1782, with General Leslie's letter on provisions and General Gist's report of the skirmish of 27 August

admission_rule: Reviewed 1782 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Two letters of the commander of the southern army, printed together in July 1782: the first on a verbal message from the British general at Charlestown proposing a cessation of hostilities, the second sending General Wayne's report of an action near Savannah.
label: General Greene's letters to the President of Congress of 21 and 31 May 1782, near Bacon's Bridge, South Carolina

admission_rule: Reviewed 1781 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of General Greene's proclamation: 'By Nathaniel Greene, Esquire, Major-General, commanding the American army in the southern department. A Proclamation. Whereas on the fourth day of the present month, colonel Isaac Hayne, commanding a regiment of militia in the service of the United States, was captured by a party of British troops'. General Greene's own words.
label: General Greene's proclamation after the execution of Colonel Isaac Hayne, 1781

admission_rule: Reviewed 1781 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of General Greene's letter to the President of Congress of 10 March 1781: 'Since I had the honour of addressing your excellency last, there have been some changes in our circumstances. On the second, Lieut. Col. Lee, with a detachment of riflemen, attacked the advance of the British army, under col. Tarleton, near Allamance'. General Greene's own account.
label: General Greene to the President of Congress, Head Quarters, Iron Works, North Carolina, 10 March 1781

admission_rule: Reviewed 1781 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of General Greene's letter to the President of Congress of 11 September 1781: 'In my dispatch of the 25th of August I informed your Excellency, that we were on our march for Friday's Ferry, to form a junction with the State troops and a body of militia collecting at that place'; it reports the action of the 8th at Eutaw. General Greene's own account.
label: General Greene to the President of Congress, Martin's Tavern, near Ferguson's Swamp, 11 September 1781

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the resolution offered in the House by Mr. Gregg of Pennsylvania on 29 January 1806: 'Whereas Great Britain impresses citizens of the United States, and compels them to serve on board her ships of war, and also seizes and condemns vessels belonging to citizens of the United States', no goods of Great Britain or its colonies should be imported 'until equitable and satisfactory arrangements on these points shall be made'. A proposal in Congress.
label: Mr. Gregg's resolution, 29 January

admission_rule: Reviewed 1782 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Hague paragraph of 1 October 1782 with a letter from Paris of late September: 'We have just received the following private intelligence from Paris, the contents of which are sufficient to excite the tears of every humane person. Paris, September 26. Sir, I here send you the melancholy relation of the disasters which happened at the siege of Gibraltar. On the 9th the land batteries began to play on the place...' Printed by all four newspapers that survive for its weeks; admitted by the rule's first part. A private letter from Paris, as a Hague paper printed it.
label: Hague, 1 October 1782: 'the following private intelligence from Paris, the contents of which are sufficient to excite the tears of every humane person': the disasters at the siege of Gibraltar

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph from Dutch papers (the Hague, 17 October 1806), translated in New York: 'Last night his excellency the Secretary of State received the important intelligence, that hostilities have commenced between the French and Prussians'. A first report of the war, through the Dutch papers.
label: The Hague, 17 October 1806: war between France and Prussia

admission_rule: Reviewed 1780 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph from the Hague, 23 March 1780, as Rivington's Royal Gazette printed it from the Carteret packet: 'Sir Joseph Yorke, Ambassador Extraordinary from his Britannic Majesty, presented a memorial to the States-General on the 21st inst. which, after a recapitulation of many matters ... concludes thus: His Majesty has ordered the under-written, to declare ...'. The British ambassador's memorial, as the paragraph gives it.
label: The Hague, 23 March 1780: Sir Joseph Yorke's memorial to the States General of 21 March

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the proclamation done 'at the head-quarters, Fort Dauphin, November 29, 1803' and signed by Dessalines, Christophe and Clerveaux, under the heading 'PROCLAMATION of Dessalines, Christophe and Clerveaux, Chiefs of St. Domingo': 'In the name of the black people and men of colour of St. Domingo. The independence of St. Domingo is proclaimed. Restored to our primitive dignity, we have claimed our rights; we swear never to yield them to any power on earth.' The three generals' own words, in the English translation the papers received from New York and Philadelphia.
label: The proclamation of Dessalines, Christophe and Clerveaux, chiefs of St. Domingo, 29 November 1803: 'The independence of St. Domingo is proclaimed'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a report of December 1775: 'A person lately from Halifax to Cape Cod, reports, That he saw at Halifax a particular account of the loss in the several harbours of Newfoundland, on the 9th of September, amounting in the whole to more than 4000 men, who had nearly finished their fishing voyage'. A report at second hand.
label: December 1775: a person from Halifax reports the loss of more than 4000 men in the storm of 9 September at Newfoundland

admission_rule: Reviewed 1772 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from Hamburg of 25 August 1772: 'The day before yesterday two express were dispatched from Stockholm, and passed through this city ... it is no longer a secret here. The following is the intelligence they brought: "The four great cities, namely, Christianstadt, Joenkjoeping, Landscrona, and Gothenburgh, have declared his Majesty, the King of Sweden, as their absolute sovereign ..."'. A letter at second hand. Rind's Virginia Gazette prints the same letter in other words ('A letter from Hambourg, dated August 25, says ... two couriers, dispatched from Stockholm ...'), counted with it (C-02).
label: Hamburg, 25 August 1772: 'The day before yesterday two express were dispatched from Stockholm ... The four great cities ... have declared his Majesty, the King of Sweden, as their absolute sovereign'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Papers on the claim of Hamet Caramalli, 'ex-bashaw of Tripoli', on the United States after the peace with Tripoli, as the papers printed them in 1806: the President's message of 13 January, two documents sent with it (the convention Hamet made with William Eaton, and Hamet's letter to the President), and the report of the Senate committee of 17 March. Contains those four groups.
label: Hamet Caramalli's claim on the United States, 1806

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a letter from Hamet ('Achmet Bashaw') to the President, sent to Congress with the message of 13 January 1806: 'For nearly eleven years, I have been labouring under the weight of misfortune'. His own account of the war against Tripoli and of his part in it with General Eaton.
label: Hamet's letter to the President

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the publication that began in the New York Evening Post of 16 July 1804: an address 'TO THE AMERICAN PUBLIC' ('The shocking catastrophe which has recently occurred, terminating the life of Alexander Hamilton, and which has spread a gloom over our city that will not be speedily dissipated, demands that the circumstances which led to it, or were intimately connected with it, should not be concealed from the world'), then 'the correspondence that passed between General Hamilton and Colonel Burr', the letters numbered from No. 1 (Burr's letter of 18 June 1804: 'I send for your perusal a letter signed Charles D. Cooper'), with the statement agreed by the two seconds. Most papers printed it over one or two issues; the National Intelligencer and the New Hampshire Gazette begin with the correspondence itself. The two men's own letters, and the seconds' account.
label: The correspondence between General Hamilton and Colonel Burr, published at New York, July 1804

admission_rule: Reviewed 1782 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a text the papers call the 'Translation of the Hand-Bill, printed in Amsterdam' ('Extra tidings from the United States of Holland, to the United States of North-America, that is to say, the Seven Provinces of Holland have declared America free and independent States'): 'We the United States of Holland, have these twenty-five years past seen the iniquity of the British administration to the American colonies, and finding ourselves in gratitude to the calls of religion, freedom and virtue...' A handbill, as the papers describe it, in their translation.
label: Translation of a handbill printed in Amsterdam: 'A Declaration of Independence from the United States of Holland to the United States of America', 'done at the Hague' 28 March 1782

admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a London paragraph of January 1807: Sir Harford Jones, back from the Russian headquarters, had never seen an army in a higher state of discipline or more eager to meet the enemy, with news of the Russian columns and of the French crossing the Vistula. It is one witness's account. Two versions circulated, dated London 6 January and 'From the Liverpool Advertiser'.
label: Sir Harford Jones on the Russian army

admission_rule: Reviewed 1802 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a circular dated 'American Consulate, Havanna, December 25, 1801' and signed by the consul of the United States there: 'By an order of the government of this island, published this day, the admission of American, and all other foreign vessels into its ports, is prohibited from this date. You will be pleased, Sir, to give immediate publicity to this information, for the government of the merchants and traders of your district.' The papers print copies sent to the collectors of different ports (Baltimore, Philadelphia, New York); the Oracle's adds a postscript of 31 December. The American consul's own notice of a Spanish colonial order.
label: The American consul at Havana's circular of 25 December 1801: the ports of Cuba closed to American and all foreign vessels

admission_rule: Reviewed 1797 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Charleston report (September 1797) that more than a hundred American vessels had been carried into Havana by French privateers.
label: French captures at Havana

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from a gentleman at Havana, 26 January 1809, first printed at Charleston: 'by the arrival yesterday of the ship Fortune from Liverpool ... the news from Spain is of a very disagreeable nature. Bonaparte is at the head of his armies, which appear to be victorious in all directions'. One writer's report at second hand.
label: A Havana letter on the news from Spain, January 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a New York report (24 July 1776) that the men of war lie in Haverstraw Bay, that a tender was fired on, and that a landing party was attacked at Peekskill.
label: Warships in Haverstraw Bay

admission_rule: Reviewed 1794 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a letter 'from a gentleman now in France to his friend in this town, received by the brig Dolphin, just arrived at Providence, dated Havre, Dec. 30, 1793': 'I then told you of the success of the Armies of the Republic in the taking of Toulon and Valenciennes; this day, being the Decadi, we have been celebrating the event'. A letter-writer's account, as the papers printed it.
label: A letter from Havre of 30 December 1793, received at Providence: the French celebrate the retaking of Toulon

admission_rule: Reviewed 1803 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a London paragraph of 8 August 1803 on French preparations to invade England, headed 'Invasion of England' in the Portland Gazette: 'From Havre de Grace, say letters, 70,000 men, on board a fleet consisting of gun-boats and other vessels of various denominations, sail in a direction, as nearly as possible, for the Sussex Coast. They are to land, if possible near Brighton. From Boulogne, Calais, Dunkirk, Ostend, and Holland, the several flotillas are to proceed to the opposite shores'. A report at second hand, from letters.
label: London, 8 August 1803: 'From Havre de Grace, say letters, 70,000 men, on board a fleet ... for the Sussex Coast'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan (round two: stories once held back for framing, at the year's 7-paper rule).
definition: Printings of a Baltimore paragraph of 3 February 1807: from papers brought by a gentleman from St. Thomas, an account of 'operations' in 'the republic of Hayti' down to 27 December 1806, 'on which day the new Republican Constitution was adopted'. It says that General Christophe came before Port-au-Prince on 5 December with about 10,000 men 'to compel' the assembly to make him emperor, fired on General 'Pichon', the commander there, who had come out to meet him, and was driven from the town; and that news received at Jacmel on 15 January had him defeated and in flight. Six papers add, after the first sentences, the editor's promise to give the constitution 'without further loss of time than is necessary for a correct translation'. A report at second hand, from papers and news from the republic's side.
label: News from Hayti by way of St. Thomas, February 1807

admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Norfolk paragraph first found in the Norfolk Gazette of 6 May 1805: 'By a Gentleman from St. Thomas we are obligingly informed of some circumstances respecting the defeat of the Haytians before the city of St. Domingo, by the garrison under command of the brave Ferrand'. It quotes a summons from 'Jean Jacques, the first, Emperor of Hayti, to General Ferrand' and tells of an action of 28 March. A report at second hand ('it is said'), told from the side of the French garrison; its words are the paper's.
label: Norfolk report from St. Thomas on the Haytian army before St. Domingo

admission_rule: Reviewed 1782 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the army's orders dated 'Head Quarters, Philadelphia, Thursday, January 10, 1782. ORDERS': 'As it is expected, that in the course of the present winter, many of the officers and men belonging to the army of the United States, will be indulged with leave of absence from their corps for a limited time: and as it is absolutely necessary the strictest punctuality should be observed, in returning at the expiration of the time for which leave is given...'; 'The general, however, cannot but hope, by taking the precaution of causing this public notice of his intention to be given to the army, the disagreeable consequences will be...' The Pennsylvania Packet printed them in six issues. The commander's own orders.
label: Head Quarters, Philadelphia, 10 January 1782: orders on the officers and men 'indulged with leave of absence from their corps' for the winter

admission_rule: Reviewed 1782 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the orders of Head-Quarters, Verplank's Point, 24 October 1782, which a correspondent sent to the editor ('as it exhibits the army in so respectable a point of view, he presents it with pleasure to the public'): 'Before the army marches from this ground, the Commander in Chief orders it to be signified to the several corps...' Printed by all four newspapers that survive for its weeks; admitted by the rule's first part. The army's own orders, with a correspondent's introduction.
label: Head-Quarters, Verplank's Point, 24 October 1782: orders 'Before the army marches from this ground'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1787 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of 'the Heads of the Treaty of Peace concluded betwixt the Americans and the Emperor of Morocco, July 24, 1786': 'If the Americans are at war with any other nation, their vessels are to be allowed to take refuge in any of the ports belonging to his Imperial Majesty'; the articles on prisoners, salutes, merchants and consuls follow. A summary of the treaty's articles as the papers printed it.
label: The heads of the treaty of peace between the United States and the Emperor of Morocco, concluded in July 1786

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the letter of William Heath to the Senate and House of Representatives of Massachusetts, June 1806: 'I have been notified by a very respectable committee of both Houses, that I have been elected Lieutenant Governor of the Commonwealth'; he declines the office. A public man's own statement.
label: General Heath declines to be Lieutenant Governor of Massachusetts

admission_rule: Reviewed 1797 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Reports of the mutiny on the British frigate Hermione (September 1797) and her delivery to the Spanish at La Guaira: first rumours, the detailed 'Particulars', and a follow-up.
label: Hermione mutiny

admission_rule: Reviewed 1797 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the detailed account of the Hermione mutiny first printed in Philadelphia on 16 November 1797.
label: 'Particulars of the mutiny'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1773 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from St. George's Key, Bay of Honduras, of 4 June 1773 ('another letter from the same place' in two papers, 'a letter from the same place' in the Massachusetts Spy), printed with New York news of 5 August: 'This day they bring us from Sherboon the following account: That a few days ago came into that river a species of tigers, not like any ever known in this country ...'. A letter at second hand, as the papers reprinted it.
label: St. George's Key, Bay of Honduras, 4 June 1773: a letter: 'This day they bring us from Sherboon the following account: That a few days ago came into that river a species of tigers, not like any ever known in this country'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of Commodore Esek Hopkins's letter of 9 April 1776 to the President of Congress, on the fleet's expedition to New Providence in the Bahamas.
label: Hopkins's report from New Providence

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter to the editor of a Natchez paper, dated 2 August 1806 and headed 'HOSTILE APPEARANCE': 'On or about the 18th of July ult. a detachment of Spanish troops' came toward Natchitoches. The papers give the writer's place as Natchez or Natchitoches. One writer's account.
label: 'Hostile appearance': a letter of 2 August on Spanish troops

admission_rule: Reviewed 1800 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the address of the House of Representatives in answer to the speech: 'The House of Representatives have received with great respect, the communication which you have been pleased to make to the two Houses of Congress, at the commencement of the present session'. The House's own address.
label: The House of Representatives' address in answer to the President's speech, November 1800

admission_rule: Reviewed 1801 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the report of the committee of the House of Representatives 'instructed ... to wait on the President elect, and notify him of his election', made on 19 February 1801: 'That they have, according to order, performed that service, and addressed the President elect, in the following words to wit: The committee beg leave to express their wishes for the prosperity of your administration; and their sincere desire that it may promote your own happiness and the welfare of your country.' Mr. Jefferson's answer follows: 'I receive, gentlemen, with profound thankfulness, this testimony of confidence from the great representative council of our nation. It fills up the measure of that grateful satisfaction, which had already been derived from the suffrages of my fellow-citizens themselves'; 'In deciding between the candidates, whom their equal vote presented to your choice, I am sensible that age has been respected, rather than more active and useful qualifications.' The House committee's report, with Mr. Jefferson's own answer.
label: The House committee's report of 19 February 1801 on notifying Mr. Jefferson of his election, with his answer

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph of the House of Representatives' proceedings of Monday 12 November 1804, in the National Intelligencer's words: 'Mr. Griswold stated that some inconvenience had been felt by some of the merchants of the Atlantic ports in making shipments to New Orleans, as they were not authorized to obtain drawbacks on a re-shipment from that port to a foreign country', and moved 'That the committee of Commerce and Manufactures be instructed to enquire into the expediency of allowing, under proper regulations, a drawback of duties on goods, wares and merchandise, imported into the port of New Orleans from any port of the United States, and from thence exported to any foreign port or place'; 'The resolution was carried nem. con.' The papers printed it inside their reports of the House's proceedings; it is counted as an item, as 1806 counted Mr. Gregg's resolution and 1800 Mr. Livingston's. A member's motion and the House's vote, as reported.
label: A motion in the House, 12 November 1804: Mr. Griswold asks for an inquiry into drawbacks of duties on goods shipped on from New Orleans

admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the address of thanks for the King's speech that the Speaker of the House of Commons presented in December 1774: 'Most gracious Sovereign, We, your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal subjects, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, return your Majesty our humble thanks for your most gracious speech from the throne'; the address answers the speech's points on America. The House of Commons' own address.
label: The House of Commons' address of thanks to the King for his speech, December 1774

admission_rule: Reviewed 1794 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a report of the debate: 'HOUSE OF COMMONS. May 26. Embargo laid on Foreign Ships by the AMERICAN STATES. Mr. Sheridan said, there was a paper which has created a general alarm, and on account of which the States of America had laid an Embargo on foreign ships. The paper he alluded to, purported to be an answer given by the Lord Dorchester to the Indians'. A report of a debate in Parliament.
label: House of Commons, 26 May 1794: the embargo laid by the American States (Mr. Sheridan's motion)

admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a London account of the debate in the House of Lords on 20 November 1777, at the opening of the session: 'As soon as his Majesty had left the House, the Earl of Harcourt and Lord Percy were introduced, and took their seats; the Lord Chancellor then read his Majesty's speech'; Lord Percy moved an address of thanks, Lord Coventry opposed it and recommended withdrawing the troops from America, and the account goes on with the Earl of Chatham's amendment and the Earl of Sandwich's reply. The Newport Gazette prints it from papers brought by the ship Tom from Liverpool. A London account of the debate, with the speakers' words as reported.
label: House of Lords, 20 November 1777: the debate on the address of thanks for the King's speech, as a London account printed it

admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the House of Lords' proceedings on its address in answer to the King's speech: the motion to add that the Lords would ask for full information on the state of America before the House committed itself was rejected ('Contents 13, Non-contents 63' in one printing), and the Lords who voted for it entered a protest: 'Dissentient, Because we cannot agree to commit ourselves with the careless facility of a common address of compliment, in expressions which may lead to measures in the event fatal to the lives, properties and liberties of a very great part of our fellow subjects'. Counted by the protest. A report of the Lords' vote with the dissenting Lords' own protest.
label: The House of Lords on the address of thanks, December 1774: an amendment asking for the papers on America rejected, and the protest of the Lords who dissented

admission_rule: Reviewed 1794 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the address: 'SIR, THE House of Representatives, calling to mind the blessings enjoyed by the people of the United States, and especially the happiness of living under constitutions and laws, which rest on their authority alone, could not learn, with other emotions than those you have expressed, that any part of our fellow-citizens should have shewn themselves capable of an insurrection'. The House's own words.
label: The House of Representatives' address to the President, 29 November 1794, in answer to his speech

admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the replication of the House of Representatives to the answer of Samuel Chase, reported by its managers and adopted by the House in February 1805: 'The House of Representatives of the United States have considered the answer of Samuel Chase, one of the associate justices of the supreme court of the United States, to the articles of impeachment'. The accusers' own reply.
label: The House's replication to Judge Chase's answer

admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a summary of the report made to the House on 17 November 1807 by Mr. Blount for the committee on the part of the President's message relating to aggressions, with the report's conclusion quoted: the outrage on the Chesapeake 'has been stamped with circumstances of indignity and insult' with scarcely a parallel.
label: The House committee's report

admission_rule: Reviewed 1803 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the resolution that the House of Representatives agreed to with closed doors on 7 January 1803, on a motion Mr. Randolph had made on the 5th: 'Resolved, That this House receive with great sensibility the information of a disposition in certain officers of the Spanish government at New Orleans to obstruct the navigation of the river Mississippi, as secured to the United States by the most solemn stipulations'; 'willing, at the same time, to ascribe this breach of compact to the unauthorized misconduct of certain individuals, rather than to a want of good faith on the part of his Catholic Majesty', the House will wait the issue of the executive's measures, and declares 'their unalterable determination to maintain the boundaries, and the rights of navigation and commerce through the river Mississippi, as established by existing treaties'. Printed in the papers' reports of the House's proceedings. Pages that quote it later in essays and reviews of the session are not counted (C-07). The House's own resolution.
label: The House of Representatives' resolution of 7 January 1803 on the navigation of the Mississippi

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the journal of the House of Representatives' proceedings with closed doors in December 1805 and January 1806 on the President's message of 6 December 1805 about Spain, made public at the beginning of April 1806 when 'the injunction of secrecy' was taken off: the committee's report ('The committee have beheld with just indignation the hostile spirit manifested by the court of Madrid'), the resolutions and the votes. Six papers printed the journal as the National Intelligencer gave it; three printed a shorter account with the report or the resolutions. An official record.
label: The House's secret journal on Spanish affairs, published in April

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of Congress's resolution of 19 July 1776 ordering that Lord Howe's circular letter to the former royal governors (20 June 1776) and the declaration it enclosed be published, 'that the good people of these United States may be informed of what nature are the Commissioners, and what the terms', followed by the letter and the declaration offering pardons.
label: Lord Howe's declaration, published by Congress

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the declaration of Lord Howe and General William Howe, the King's commissioners, of 19 September 1776: Congress had disavowed every purpose of reconciliation, the King would revise his instructions and the acts complained of, and the inhabitants were invited to consider whether to trust their fate to Congress.
label: The declaration of 19 September

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: The declarations of Lord Howe and General William Howe as the King's commissioners for restoring peace, as the American papers printed them: Lord Howe's declaration of June 1776, published by order of Congress in July, and the brothers' declaration of 19 September. Contains those two groups; their declaration of 14 July (printed in the New-York Gazette) and their proclamation of 30 November (printed in the Freeman's Journal) are not included.
label: The Howe brothers' declarations

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of General Howe's letter to General Washington of 21 April 1777, which Congress ordered published on 16 June with the other letters on the subject: 'I have received your letter of the 9th instant, concerning the requisition of Lieutenant Colonel Walcot, a copy of which came inclosed. Though I observe that officer has meant to insist very strongly on the justice of the claim for the return of prisoners in your possession'; he answers the charge on the usage of the prisoners. The British commander's own letter.
label: General Howe to General Washington, New York, 21 April 1777, on the exchange of prisoners

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Reports of the British warships that went up the Hudson on 12 July 1776: lying in Haverstraw Bay, boats driven off at Tappan, the attack by American row galleys (3 August) and the fire-ship attack (16 August). Contains those four groups; the wider coverage is not included.
label: British warships in the Hudson

admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of 'a copy of a letter from capt. Hull, of the Argus, to commodore Barron, dated Argus, (Derne) April 28' (1805), released with Commodore Rodgers's letter in September: 'I have the honor to inform you, that at nine o'clock in the morning of the 27th, being about ten miles to the eastward of the town of Derne, with the Hornet in company, we discovered the Nautilus at anchor'. An officer's own account of the attack on Derne.
label: Captain Hull's letter on the attack on Derne

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Documents of the House of Representatives' impeachment of Samuel Chase, one of the associate justices of the Supreme Court, as the 1804 papers printed them: the articles of impeachment its committee reported on 26 March 1804, the judge's memorial on the proceedings, published in April, and the articles its committee reported again on 30 November 1804. His trial before the Senate in 1805 is a reviewed story of 1805. Contains those three groups.
label: The impeachment of Judge Chase, 1804: the articles reported to the House, and the judge's memorial

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a French imperial decree of 25 February 1809: 'American vessels which have been detained in the ports of the Empire, solely by the (French) Embargo, are permitted to return directly to the U. States. This favor is not extended to such vessels as have been detained on account of irregular papers, or from any other cause.' The French government's decree.
label: The French decree of 25 February 1809 on American vessels

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the National Intelligencer's leading article of 15 November 1809: 'All negotiation with the British government at this place is suspended by one of those events which we should call extraordinary'; it says the minister offered 'the grossest insult' to the nation, and quotes Vattel on what a sovereign may do when a foreign minister offends him. The government paper's argument.
label: The National Intelligencer, 15 November 1809: 'All negotiation … is suspended'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph of the National Intelligencer of 16 August 1809, the government paper's account: 'Mr. Secretary Smith received on the 14th inst. from Mr. Erskine a long and very satisfactory letter', in which Mr. Erskine explains why he did not lay his instructions before the American government; the paper adds its own view of Mr. Canning's dispatch.
label: The National Intelligencer on Erskine's letter of explanation, August 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph of the National Intelligencer of 13 November 1809, the government paper's account: 'In the course of the correspondence, which, it seems, has taken place between the Secretary of State and Mr. Jackson', the British minister repeated what the paper calls a 'gross insinuation', and the Secretary informed him 'that no further communications would be received from him'.
label: The National Intelligencer's statement of 13 November 1809 on the correspondence with Jackson

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Three items of November 1809 on the end of the correspondence between the Secretary of State and the British minister, Francis James Jackson: the National Intelligencer's statement of 13 November, its article of 15 November that 'All negotiation with the British government at this place is suspended', and Jackson's circular of 13 November to the British consuls. Contains those three groups. The Intelligencer's paragraphs are the government paper's account; the circular is the British minister's own.
label: The British minister Jackson and the end of the correspondence, November 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a letter headed 'CIRCULAR', Washington, 13 November 1809, from the British minister F. J. Jackson to the British consuls: 'I have to inform you with much regret, that the facts which it has been my duty to state in my official correspondence with Mr. Smith, have been deemed by the President of the United States to afford a sufficient motive for breaking off an important negotiation'; he says he gave no offence and will withdraw to New York. The British minister's own account.
label: Jackson's circular to the British consuls, 13 November 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a card of John Jay and Rufus King to the printers of the New York Diary (August 1793): a report having reached New York from Philadelphia that Mr. Genêt, the French minister, had said he would appeal to the people from certain decisions of the President, they had been asked on their return whether he had said so, and 'we answered, that he had'. An allegation by two named men.
label: Jay and King: Genêt said he would appeal to the people

admission_rule: Reviewed 1794 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the memorial: 'The undersigned Envoy of the United States of America has the honor of representing to the Right Honorable Lord Grenville, his Britannic Majesty's Secretary of State for the Department of foreign affairs. That a very considerable number of American vessels have been irregularly captured, and as improperly condemned'. The American envoy's own words, printed as official documents with the answer.
label: Mr. Jay's memorial to Lord Grenville of July 1794 on the captures of American vessels, with the answer

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of President Jefferson's answer to the petition of the Boston town meeting, which had asked him to suspend the embargo: he could not suspend it while the belligerents' edicts stood, and only the legislature could prescribe its course. The Portland Gazette prints the same text as the answer to Portland's petition.
label: Jefferson's answer to the petitions against the embargo

admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the Secretary of State's answer to Genêt for the President (Philadelphia, 16 August 1793): the diplomatic characters residing here should not correspond directly with the President, the Secretary of State being the organ of their communications, and the President did not think it within the line of propriety or duty to bear evidence against a declaration, so he declined to interfere. An official document.
label: Jefferson's answer for the President, 16 August 1793

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of President Jefferson's answer to the address of the New Hampshire legislature of 14 June 1808, which had approved the measures of his administration, the embargo among them.
label: Jefferson's answer to the New Hampshire legislature

admission_rule: Reviewed 1801 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Three addresses of Thomas Jefferson as the papers printed them in February and March 1801, after the House of Representatives chose him President on 17 February 1801: the report of the House's committee that notified him of his election, with his answer; his address to the Senate on leaving its chair, 28 February; and his inaugural address of 4 March. Contains those three groups.
label: Mr. Jefferson chosen President and inaugurated, February and March 1801: his answer to the House's committee, his farewell to the Senate and his inaugural address

admission_rule: Reviewed 1801 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the address that the Vice President delivered to the Senate on Saturday 28 February 1801, when he 'took leave of that body': 'Gentlemen of the Senate, To give the usual opportunity of appointing a President pro tempore, I now propose to retire from the chair of the Senate; and as the time is near at hand, when the relations will cease, which have for some time subsisted between this honorable house and myself, I beg leave before I withdraw, to return them my grateful thanks for all the instances of attention and respect with which they have been pleased to honour me'; 'I may have erred at times. No doubt I have erred. This is the law of human nature.' Mr. Jefferson's own address.
label: Mr. Jefferson's address to the Senate on leaving its chair, 28 February 1801

admission_rule: Reviewed 1801 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the address that Thomas Jefferson delivered in the Senate Chamber before taking the oath of office as President on 4 March 1801: 'Friends and Fellow Citizens, Called upon to undertake the duties of the first Executive office of our country, I avail myself of the presence of that portion of my fellow citizens which is here assembled to express my grateful thanks for the favor with which they have been pleased to look towards me'; it goes on 'We have called by different names brethren of the same principle', and states 'the essential principles of our government'. Pages that print part of it, or quote it in essays, are not counted (C-06, C-07): the Rhode-Island Republican's extract of 17 October and quotations in the Republican Gazette. The President's own address.
label: Mr. Jefferson's inaugural address, 4 March 1801

admission_rule: Reviewed 1801 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a letter that Thomas Jefferson, then Vice President and a candidate for President, wrote at Monticello on 4 September 1800 in reply to a letter of August: 'Your favor of August 26th, has been duly received, and is entitled to my thankfulness for the personal considerations you are pleased to express in it. How far the measure proposed might have the expected effect, you can best judge: however, in the great exercise of right in which the citizens of America are about to act, I have, on mature consideration, seen, that it is my duty to be passive'; 'The great question which divides our citizens is, whether it is safest that a preponderance of power should be lodged with the monarchical, or the republican branch of our government?' The papers head it as Mr. Jefferson's letter 'in reply to one addressed to him by a citizen of Berkeley', and print it with their own introductions: the National Intelligencer's correspondent values it because 'it contains the spontaneous effusions of his heart'; Jenks's Portland Gazette prints it as 'Jefferson's Second Letter', which 'will serve as a second part of his Mazzei Letter'. Mr. Jefferson's own letter, published by others, each paper with its own heading.
label: Mr. Jefferson's letter of 4 September 1800 in reply to a citizen, as the papers printed it in 1801

admission_rule: Reviewed 1780 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of Governor Jefferson's letter to the President of Congress, Richmond, 15 October 1780: 'I do myself the pleasure of congratulating your Excellency on the small dawn of good fortune which at length appears in the South, as you will find by the dispatches I have the honour of inclosing ...', with the letters it enclosed (an officer's letter of 2 October on Colonel Clarke at Augusta; letters on the defeat of Major Ferguson at King's Mountain). The Virginia Gazette prints the enclosed letters without the Governor's (one item, X-1810-01). The writers' own letters.
label: Governor Jefferson to Congress, Richmond, 15 October 1780, with dispatches from the south (Augusta; Major Ferguson defeated at King's Mountain)

admission_rule: Reviewed 1802 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a letter from Thomas Jefferson, President of the United States, to Thomas Paine, which a New York paper took from a London paper in August 1802 ('about which so much has been said'): 'You expressed a wish in your letter to return to America by a national ship; Mr. Dawson, who brings over the treaty, and who will present you this letter, is charged with orders to the Captain of the Maryland to receive and accommodate you back, if you can be ready to depart at such a short warning'; it ends with the wish that Paine 'may long live to continue your useful labours, and to reap their reward in the thankfulness of nations'. Papers of both parties printed it, some with hostile introductions; two printed it again in essays and columns of the President's letters. The President's own letter, as the papers printed it.
label: 'You expressed a wish in your letter to return to America by a national ship': the President's letter to Thomas Paine, published August 1802

admission_rule: Reviewed 1797 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Reports (January 1797) that Jefferson wrote to Madison about the election result, and a later report giving a different account of the letter.
label: Jefferson's letter to Madison

admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the speech President Thomas Jefferson delivered on taking the oath of office for a second term, 4 March 1805: 'Proceeding, fellow citizens, to that qualification which the constitution requires, before my entrance on the charge again conferred on me'. He gives his account of his first term: taxes and the debt, Louisiana, 'the aboriginal inhabitants of these countries', religion and the press. The President's own account (a policy argument).
label: President Jefferson's second inaugural address

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a letter of the former President John Adams, Quincy, 13 March 1809, answering a letter of 3 March from two men of Northampton: 'Nothing remains to me but the right of private judgment ... I am, totis viribus [with my whole strength], against any division of the Union, by the North River, or by Delaware River, or by the Potomac, or any other river, or by any chain of mountains.' Some papers print the letter at length, others extracts. His own opinion.
label: John Adams's letter of 13 March 1809: 'against any division of the Union'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1801 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Boston paragraph of October 1801: 'Mr. JOHN APPLETON, the official bearer of the ratified treaty between the United States and France, arrived here yesterday in the brig Reward, from Dieppe.' The treaty is the convention of 30 September 1800 with the French Republic, which the Senate ratified with conditions in February 1801 and the First Consul in July. A Boston paper's notice.
label: Boston, October 1801: 'Mr. John Appleton, the official bearer of the ratified treaty between the United States and France, arrived here yesterday'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1800 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the resolutions that the joint committee of Congress reported through Mr. Marshall and both houses passed: 'That a Marble Monument be erected by the United States, in the Capitol, at the City of Washington, and that the family of General Washington be requested to permit his body to be deposited under it'; that there be a funeral procession and an oration before both houses on 26 December; that the people be recommended to wear crape on the left arm for thirty days; that the President send a copy to Mrs. Washington; and that he issue a proclamation. The weekly papers printed them in January 1800 with the proceedings; three papers printed them again from July to October among the laws and resolutions of the session. Congress's own resolutions.
label: The joint resolutions of Congress of 23 December 1799 on the death of Washington

admission_rule: Reviewed 1780 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a letter of Jonathan Williams, at Nantes, 8 February 1780, 'To the gentlemen merchants and other persons in America, who remit bills of exchange to Europe': 'Of the many bills which have been sent from America to me, few whole sets have arrived ...'; how bills should be endorsed and sent; 'Every Printer on the continent is requested to insert this Letter'. The writer's own notice.
label: Jonathan Williams at Nantes, 8 February 1780, to the merchants and others in America who remit bills of exchange to Europe

admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of President Jefferson's proclamation of 2 July 1807, which recited the attack on the Chesapeake and required all armed vessels bearing commissions under the British government to leave the harbours and waters of the United States, forbidding all intercourse with them.
label: The President's proclamation of 2 July

admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the letter of Captain Michael Kalteisen, commandant of Fort Johnson in Charleston harbour (2 May 1807), to the commander of the British sloop of war Driver, which a proclamation of the President had barred from American harbours: she must leave within twenty-four hours. Most papers printed it inside a Charleston report of the Driver's arrival, reprinted from New York; the papers give the proclamation different dates.
label: Fort Johnson orders the Driver out

admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an account from Lexington, Kentucky (June 1805): 'The party of discovery, under the command of captains Lewis and Clark, left the mouth of the Missouri on the 19th of May, 1804'; it tells, from the party's dispatches and letters, of its winter quarters at Fort Mandan, the river, the country, its animals and the Indian nations the party met. A report at second hand; its words about the Indian nations are the party's and the paper's.
label: A Kentucky account of the party of discovery at Fort Mandan

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph from the Scioto Gazette (Chillicothe, 13 November 1806) headed 'IMPORTANT COMMUNICATION': 'By a gentleman of the highest respectability from Kentucky, we are furnished with the following intelligence'; the substance of an affidavit of the United States attorney for Kentucky (printed 'Davies' or 'Daveiss') that Aaron Burr 'had formed an Association for making war against Spain, invading Mexico, and forming a distinct Empire in the Western country'. An allegation, reported at second hand.
label: Chillicothe, 13 November: the Kentucky affidavit against Colonel Burr

admission_rule: Reviewed 1800 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the speech with which King George III opened Parliament on 11 November 1800: 'My tender concern for the welfare of my Subjects, and a sense of the difficulties with which the poorer classes particularly have to struggle, from the present high price of provisions, have induced me to call you together at an earlier period than I had otherwise intended'; it speaks of the scarcity of grain, the negotiations for peace, and the war. The papers give two different introductions. The King's own speech.
label: The King's speech to Parliament, 11 November 1800

admission_rule: Reviewed 1803 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the message that Lord Hawkesbury presented to the House of Commons: 'His Majesty thinks it right to inform the House of Commons, that, from an anxious desire to prevent the calamities of war being extended to the Batavian Republic, he communicated to that Government his disposition to respect their neutrality, provided that a similar disposition was manifested on the part of the French Government', and that, this not having been admitted, he directed his minister to leave the Hague and gave orders for letters of marque and reprisals. The Oracle heads it 'War with Holland'. The King's own message.
label: The King's message to the House of Commons on the Batavian republic, 1803

admission_rule: Reviewed 1794 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a declaration: 'DECLARATION Of the King of Prussia against a general armament of the inhabitants of the empire. I. When the proposition for a general armament of the subjects of the empire was made at the assembly of the Diet, the king of Prussia represented such essential difficulties against this measure'. An act of the King of Prussia, as the papers printed it from London papers.
label: London, 19 March 1794: the King of Prussia's declaration against a general armament of the inhabitants of the Empire

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the King's proclamation for a general fast: 'George R. We, taking into our most serious consideration the just and necessary measures of force which we are obliged to use against our rebellious subjects in our colonies and provinces in North America, and putting our trust in almighty God'; it commands a public fast and humiliation to be observed in England, Wales and Berwick upon Tweed on Friday 13 December 1776. The King's own proclamation.
label: The King's proclamation for a general fast, 1776: 'the just and necessary measures of force which we are obliged to use against our rebellious subjects'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: The King's proclamation of a public fast for the war in America, and the remarks Mr. Burke made on it in the House of Commons, which the papers printed together in March and April 1777. Contains those two groups.
label: The King's proclamation for a general fast, 1776, and Mr. Burke's remarks on it

admission_rule: Reviewed 1779 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a proclamation of George III given at St. James's on 9 July 1779, as the papers took it from London papers: 'Whereas we have received intelligence that preparations are making by our enemies to invade this our kingdom... and to the intent that they may not, in case of their landing, strengthen themselves by seizing the horses, oxen and cattle of our subjects...' It charges the officers of the coasts to have the cattle and provisions driven inland 'upon the first approach of the enemy'. The King's own proclamation.
label: The King's proclamation of 9 July 1779: 'Whereas we have received intelligence that preparations are making by our enemies to invade this our kingdom'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the King's speech closing the session of Parliament, 6 June 1777: 'My Lords and Gentlemen, The conclusion of the public business, and the consideration of the inconvenience which I fear you must have suffered by so long an attendance, call upon me to put an end to this session of Parliament'; he thanks them for their 'steady perseverance in maintaining the rights' of the crown and the nation. The King's own speech.
label: The King's speech at the close of the session of Parliament, 6 June 1777

admission_rule: Reviewed 1773 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a London paragraph of 1 July 1773 with the King's speech closing the session of Parliament: 'This day his Majesty went to the House of Peers, made a speech to both houses, and put an end to the present session of parliament. His Majesty's speech was substantially as follows: "My Lords and Gentlemen, ..."'. A London report with a published speech, as the papers reprinted it.
label: London, 1 July 1773: 'This day his Majesty went to the House of Peers, made a speech to both houses, and put an end to the present session of parliament'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1782 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of George III's speech at the close of the session of Parliament on 11 July 1782, as the papers took it from London papers in September: 'My Lords and Gentlemen, The unwearied assiduity with which you have persevered in the discharge of your duty in parliament, during so long a session, bears the most honourable testimony of your zeal and industry in the service of the public...' The King's own words.
label: The King's speech to both Houses of Parliament, 11 July 1782: 'The unwearied assiduity with which you have persevered in the discharge of your duty'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of George III's speech closing the session of Parliament on 23 May 1776.
label: The King's speech of May 1776

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of George III's speech opening the session of Parliament in October 1775, which the American papers printed from January 1776. The printings date the speech differently: the 26th in one, the 27th in another.
label: The King's speech of October 1775

admission_rule: Reviewed 1780 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the King's speech at the opening of Parliament, 25 November 1779: 'My Lords and Gentlemen, I meet you in Parliament at a time when we are called upon by every principle of duty, and every consideration of interest, to exert our united efforts in the support and defence of our country, attacked by an unjust and unprovoked war ...'; it speaks too of the kingdom of Ireland. A letter to a printer that quotes the speech is not counted (C-07). The King's own speech.
label: The King's speech to both Houses of Parliament, 25 November 1779

admission_rule: Reviewed 1773 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the King's speech to both Houses of Parliament at the opening of the session, 26 November 1772: 'My Lords and Gentlemen, I should most willingly have consulted your private convenience, by allowing you a longer recess from business, if I had not thought, that some very important parts of the public service required the immediate attention of Parliament ...' (the affairs of the East India Company, the dearth of corn, the war in the east of Europe). A published speech, as the papers reprinted it; the two Houses' addresses in reply and paragraphs that quote it are other texts.
label: Westminster, 26 November 1772: the King's speech opening the session: 'My Lords and Gentlemen, I should most willingly have consulted your private convenience, by allowing you a longer recess from business'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1779 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of George III's speech to both Houses of Parliament at the opening of the session on 26 November 1778, as the papers took it from London papers ('From the London General Advertiser and Morning Intelligencer of November 27, 1778'): 'My Lords and Gentlemen, I have called you together in a conjuncture which demands your most serious attention. In the time of profound peace, without pretence of provocation or colour of complaint, the Court of France hath not forbore to disturb the public tranquillity, in violation of the faith of treaties and the general rights of Sovereigns, at first by the clandestine supply of arms and other aid to my revolted subjects in North-America...' Printed by all seven newspapers that survive for its weeks; admitted by the rule's first part. The King's own words.
label: The King's speech at the opening of Parliament, 26 November 1778: 'I have called you together in a conjuncture which demands your most serious attention'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1782 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of George III's speech to both Houses of Parliament on 27 November 1781, at the opening of the session, as the papers took it from London papers in February 1782: 'My Lords and Gentlemen, When I last met you in Parliament, I acquainted you with the arduous situation of public affairs at that time, and I represented to you the objects which I had in view, and the resolution with which I was determined to persevere in the defence of...' The Pennsylvania Packet printed it twice. The King's own words. The addresses of the two Houses in answer and the King's answer to the Lords are listed as not chosen (the same affair and weeks).
label: The King's speech at the opening of Parliament, 27 November 1781: 'When I last met you in Parliament, I acquainted you with the arduous situation of public affairs'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the speech of George III to both Houses of Parliament, 31 October 1776, as the American papers printed it in February 1777: 'My Lords and Gentlemen, Nothing could have afforded me so much satisfaction as to have been able to inform you, at the opening of this session, that the troubles which have so long distracted my colonies in North America were at an end'; it says that the colonies' leaders 'have now openly renounced all allegiance to the crown'. Purdie's Virginia Gazette heads it 'Speech of George III. tyrant of Great Britain, to his venal parliament'. The King's own speech.
label: The King's speech at the opening of Parliament, 31 October 1776

admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the King's answer to the address and petition of the Common Council of London: 'I am always ready to listen to the dutiful petitions of my subjects, and ever happy to comply with their reasonable requests, but while the constitutional authority of this kingdom is openly resisted by a part of my American subjects', he owes it to the rest of his people to enforce obedience. The King's own answer.
label: The King's answer to the Common Council of London: 'I am always ready to listen to the dutiful petitions of my subjects'
