admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the King's answer to the address, remonstrance and petition of the Livery of London, April 1775: 'It is with the utmost astonishment that I find any of my subjects capable of encouraging the rebellious disposition which unhappily exists in some of my colonies in North America'; he says he will continue to pursue the measures of Parliament. The King's own answer.
label: The King's answer to the Livery of London: 'It is with the utmost astonishment that I find any of my subjects capable of encouraging the rebellious disposition'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1781 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the King's manifesto: 'MANIFESTO. GEORGE R. Through the whole course of our reign, our conduct towards the States General of the United Provinces has been that of a sincere friend and faithful ally'; it sets out the King's complaints against the Republic. The King's own words, from the London Gazette Extraordinary of 21 December 1780.
label: The King's manifesto against the States General of the United Provinces (London Gazette Extraordinary, 21 December 1780)

admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the King's message to the House of Lords, delivered by Lord Weymouth on 17 March 1778, as a London account printed it with the paper delivered by the French ambassador: 'His Majesty having been informed, by order of the French King, that a treaty of amity and commerce has been signed between the court of France and certain persons employed by his Majesty's revolted subjects in North-America, has judged it necessary to direct, that a copy of the declaration delivered by the French Ambassador to Lord Viscount Weymouth be laid before the House of Lords'; the King says he has sent orders to his ambassador to withdraw from the French court, and is determined to be prepared to exert all the force and resources of his kingdoms. The papers printed it in May from a Philadelphia paper of 9 May, which had it by the Porcupine frigate. The King's own message, with the French ambassador's paper.
label: The King's message to Parliament of 17 March 1778 on the French ambassador's declaration of a treaty with the United States

admission_rule: Reviewed 1774 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the King's proclamation, from the London Gazette of 1 October 1774: 'A Proclamation, For dissolving the present Parliament, and declaring the calling of another. George R. Whereas we have thought fit, by and with the advice of our privy council, to dissolve the present Parliament, which now stands prorogued to Tuesday the fifteenth day of November next'; it declares that writs for calling a new Parliament will be issued. The King's own proclamation.
label: The King's proclamation of 30 September 1774 for dissolving the present Parliament and calling another (London Gazette, 1 October)

admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the King's proclamation of 23 August 1775, 'By the King, A Proclamation, For suppressing Rebellion and Sedition': 'Whereas many of our subjects in divers parts of our colonies and plantations in North America, misled by dangerous and ill-designing men, and forgetting the allegiance which they owe', have proceeded to open and avowed rebellion, all officers and subjects are to exert themselves to suppress it and to disclose traitorous conspiracies. The King's own proclamation.
label: The King's proclamation for suppressing rebellion and sedition, 23 August 1775

admission_rule: Reviewed 1783 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the King's proclamation: 'By the King. A Proclamation, Declaring the Cessation of Arms, as well by Sea as Land, agreed upon between His Majesty, the Most Christian King, the King of Spain, the States General of the United Provinces, and the United States of America, and enjoining the Observance thereof. George R. Whereas Provisional Articles were signed at Paris, on the Thirtieth Day of November last, between Our Commissioner for treating of Peace with the Commissioners of the United States of America, and the Commissioners of the said States'. London reports of its reading at the Royal Exchange, which name its title, are not counted (C-07). The King's own proclamation.
label: The King's proclamation declaring the cessation of arms, as well by sea as land, agreed upon between him, the Most Christian King, the King of Spain, the States General and the United States

admission_rule: Reviewed 1774 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the King's speech at the opening of the session of Parliament on 13 January 1774: 'My Lords and Gentlemen, The unusual length of the last session of Parliament made me desirous of giving you as long a recess as the public service would admit'; it regrets that 'the Peace so long expected, and so very desirable, is not yet effected between Russia and the Porte', says that the other foreign powers continue in the same pacific disposition, and that Parliament will have full leisure to attend to 'the Preservation and the Advancement of the Revenue and Commerce of the Kingdom'. The King's own speech.
label: The King's speech to both Houses of Parliament, 13 January 1774

admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the King's speech of 3 June 1778: 'My Lords and Gentlemen, After so long and laborious an application to the public business, I think it proper at this season of the year to give you some recess. I come at the same time to return you my particular thanks for the zeal you have shewn in supporting the honour of my crown'. The papers printed it in August from the June mail. The King's own speech.
label: The King's speech to both Houses of Parliament, 3 June 1778, giving them a recess after a long session

admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the speech from the throne with which the King opened the new Parliament on 30 November 1774: 'It gives me much concern, that I am obliged, at the opening of this Parliament, to inform you, that a most daring spirit of resistance and disobedience to the law still unhappily prevails in the province of the Massachusetts Bay, and has in divers parts of it broke forth in fresh violences of a very criminal nature'; he says he has taken measures for carrying into execution the laws of the last session and will withstand every attempt to weaken his authority over the colonies. The King's own speech.
label: The King's speech to both Houses of Parliament, 30 November 1774: 'a most daring spirit of resistance and disobedience to the law still unhappily prevails in the province of the Massachusetts Bay'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1781 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the King's speech opening the new Parliament: 'My Lords and Gentlemen, It is with more than ordinary satisfaction that I meet you in Parliament, at a time when the late elections may afford an opportunity of receiving the most certain information of the disposition and the wishes of my people'. The King's own words, as the papers printed them from London papers.
label: The King's speech to both Houses of Parliament at the opening of the new Parliament, 6 November 1780

admission_rule: Reviewed 1792 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph of the Knoxville Gazette of 10 October 1792: 'It is an undoubted truth, (strange as it may appear)' that the governor of Louisiana and the governor of Pensacola 'have opened the stores of the King of Spain, in West Florida, to the Creeks and Cherokees, and delivered them arms and ammunition in abundance, advising and stimulating them to go to war against the frontier inhabitants of the United States'. Two papers print it without '(strange as it may appear)'. The Knoxville paper's allegation.
label: Knoxville, 10 October 1792: the Knoxville paper states as 'an undoubted truth' that the governors of Louisiana and Pensacola have opened the King of Spain's stores to the Creeks and Cherokees

admission_rule: Reviewed 1801 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph dated Knoxville, Tennessee, 19 September 1801 (9 September in three papers): 'We hear from South West Point that the treaty with the Cherokees is broken up, the commissioners not being able to effect the object of their appointment. The Cherokees refuse to sell lands, or to permit roads being cut through their country. Doublehead concluded his last talk with saying "That the Indians do not wish to be spoken to on that subject." He then addressed the people of Tennessee, and said "That the white people owed them three lives: that they had waited some time for satisfaction, and would wait yet longer, but were determined on retaliation."' The Alexandria Advertiser and the Providence Journal print 'do not wish to be again spoken to'; the three Portsmouth papers (the New Hampshire Gazette, the Oracle and the Republican Ledger) date the paragraph 'Sept. 9' and print 'did not wish to be again spoken to' and 'the white people owed them their lives' (read on the scans). A Knoxville paper's report at second hand ('We hear'), with Doublehead's words as the paper gives them; not the Cherokees' own account. It is in 6 papers, below the rule, and stands as a sub-story under a parent that reaches 7 (C-01), so that both sides of the affair show (the owner's decision of 23 November 2026). A paragraph that reports the rumour in other words (the Republican Gazette, 29 October) is not counted (C-07).
label: Knoxville, 19 September 1801: 'We hear from South West Point that the treaty with the Cherokees is broken up'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1797 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Philadelphia item (September 1797): Kościuszko is offered a land warrant and back pay for his Revolutionary War service and declines the money.
label: Kościuszko's land warrant

admission_rule: Reviewed 1781 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the Marquis de Lafayette's letter to General Greene dated 'Mr. Tyree's plantation, 20 miles from Williamsburg, June 27, 1781': 'My letter of the 28th informed you of the enemy's retrograde movement to Richmond, where they had made a stop'; it goes on to the action of the advanced corps under Colonel Butler. The Marquis's own account; the Pennsylvania Packet prints it after his covering letter to the President of Congress.
label: The Marquis de Lafayette to General Greene, near Williamsburg, 27 June 1781, sent to Congress with his letter of 28 June

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of news from Lisbon papers of December 1807, brought by the brig Perseverance: decrees of the French general in chief after the occupation, forbidding the use of arms to all but the military, confiscating English property and making French and Spanish money current.
label: Lisbon under the French, December 1807

admission_rule: Reviewed 1803 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a translation of the proclamation that Laussat, the colonial prefect sent by the French Republic to take over Louisiana from Spain, addressed to its inhabitants in 1803: 'Your separation from France marks one of the most shameful epochs of her annals, under an enfeebled and corrupt government, after an ignominious war, and a disgraceful peace'; it praises the First Consul and announces the mission of 'your captain general Victor, your colonial prefect and your chief judge'. The French prefect's own proclamation, in translation.
label: Proclamation of Laussat, French colonial prefect, to the Louisianians, 1803

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings after a cannon shot from the British ship Leander killed an American seaman near the entrance of New York harbour on 25 April 1806, which the President's proclamation calls 'a murder': the resolutions of a meeting at New York and the President's proclamation of 3 May. Contains those two groups.
label: The Leander off New York, 1806

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter 'from a gentleman on board the Leander', dated Jacmel, 1 March 1806: 'General Miranda has explained to us his plan'. One member of the expedition's own account.
label: A letter from on board the Leander at Jacmel, 1 March

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the circular of Tobias Lear, American consul general at Algiers (16 December 1807), received at Salem in February 1808: three American vessels detained by an Algerine frigate, because the annuities were two years in arrears, had been released after he settled with the Dey.
label: Lear's circular: peace with Algiers

admission_rule: Reviewed 1802 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the proclamation of the French general in chief at St. Domingo, dated at the Cape, 20 Prairial, year 10 (8 June 1802), and signed by Leclerc, in two translations. Six papers print the one that begins 'General Toussaint not being contented with enjoying the amnesty which had been granted him, attempted again to kindle the flames of civil war. I have thought proper to cause him to be arrested'; three print another: 'Gen. Toussaint did not wish to enjoy the amnesty which had been granted to him; he has continued to conspire; he was just going to rekindle a civil war. I thought it necessary to have him arrested'. Both promise that the proofs will be published and that the measure should not alarm those who have laid down their arms. Counted together as one item in two printed forms. The French commander's own proclamation, as the papers translated it.
label: General Leclerc to the citizens of St. Domingo, June 1802: 'I have thought proper to cause him to be arrested'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of General Lee's note from the headquarters at Cambridge, 11 July 1775: 'General Lee's compliments to General Burgoyne. Would be extremely happy in the interview he so kindly proposed. But as he perceives that General Burgoyne has already made up his mind on this great subject', he declines it, lest it give rise to jealousies. General Lee's own letter.
label: General Lee's answer to General Burgoyne, Cambridge, 11 July 1775, declining the interview

admission_rule: Reviewed 1810 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the resolutions that Mr. Leib submitted to the Senate for consideration on 8 March 1810, as the papers reported the Senate's proceedings: 'Resolved, That the President of the United States be required to instruct our minister at the court of Great Britain, to demand of the British government an immediate compliance with the arrangement made by their minister, Mr. Erskine, with this government, comprising atonement for the attack upon the frigate Chesapeake, and a relinquishment of the orders in council'; a further resolution concerns what is to follow the failure or refusal of the British government to carry the arrangement into effect. Counted as a paragraph of the proceedings by its own words (X-1800-08, X-1804-04). A senator's resolutions, submitted for consideration: a policy argument.
label: Mr. Leib's resolutions in the Senate, 8 March 1810: the President to instruct our minister to demand of the British government compliance with the arrangement made by Mr. Erskine

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an item from the newsletter Les Nouvelles à la Main, No. II, Paris, 9 March 1804, under headings such as 'Letter from Moreau to Bonaparte': 'The letter which we now publish, has been circulated all over Paris for this week, and many thousand copies have been sent into the departments'; the letter, 'addressed to Monsieur Bonaparte, the First Consul, by Citizen Moreau', is dated from the dungeon of the Temple and opens 'Since your ambition requires more victims, strike, but do not calumniate those you butcher.' A letter the newsletter attributes to Moreau; its No. III (another group) qualifies it.
label: A letter to Bonaparte 'from the dungeon of the Temple', attributed to General Moreau by Les Nouvelles à la Main, March 1804

admission_rule: Reviewed 1773 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from 'a gentleman of character in London', 'per the last Packet' ('by the last Packet' in the Virginia papers), printed with New York news of 4 January 1773: 'I hear your militia are put on a good footing, and that you are marching and counter-marching: It is well; but I am most desirous you should fortify; as sure as you live if you do not, the town will be burnt about your ears in the next war ...'. A letter at second hand, as the papers reprinted it.
label: A letter 'per the last Packet', January 1773: 'I hear your militia are put on a good footing, and that you are marching and counter-marching: It is well; but I am most desirous you should fortify'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1794 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a letter 'from an officer in the legion of the United States, dated Camp, 12 miles advance of Greenville, 28th July': 'I hope by the time this reaches you that we shall be able to give a good account of the Indian war. We have about 1700 or 1800 Kentucky volunteers with us'. An officer's letter, as the papers printed it.
label: A letter from an officer of the legion, dated near Greenville, 28 July 1794

admission_rule: Reviewed 1782 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter 'from Camden, South Carolina, to a gentleman in this town' (Philadelphia), dated 5 February 1782 (on the Pennsylvania Packet's scan the day is faded, and its transcription reads 25): 'I imagine by this time your expectations are great with respect to news in our quarter. I have only to inform you that general Greene's army still remain quiet at... (thirty miles from Charlestown)...' A private correspondent's account, at second hand.
label: A letter from Camden, South Carolina, February 1782: 'general Greene's army still remain quiet'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1782 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from Fort Pitt dated 3 September 1782: 'From the middle to the last of July, the Indians have been very troublesome on the frontiers of this country—Hanna's town was burned, several inhabitants killed and taken, and about the same time Fort Wheeling was blockaded for several days; for two weeks the inhabitants were in such consternation that a total evacuation of the country was to be dreaded...' Printed by all four newspapers that survive for its weeks; admitted by the rule's first part. A correspondent's account from Fort Pitt.
label: A letter from Fort Pitt, 3 September 1782: 'From the middle to the last of July, the Indians have been very troublesome on the frontiers of this country—Hanna's town was burned'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1782 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter 'from a gentleman at General Greene's camp, dated September 2, 1782': 'Orders have been repeated for the evacuation of Charlestown: they have not transports enough to convey their stores, and provide for the refugees who are to go to East Florida. We have good information they have fallen upon this method:—they will evacuate Charlestown in a few days, and leave the refugees at Beaufort on Port Royal Island...' Printed by all four newspapers that survive for its weeks; admitted by the rule's first part. A correspondent's account.
label: A letter from a gentleman at General Greene's camp, 2 September 1782: 'Orders have been repeated for the evacuation of Charlestown'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1770 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from London dated 6 September 1770: 'Mr. Hutchinson is Governor.—The province I am sure ought to be very thankful for the having one born among themselves ...'. A letter at second hand, as the papers print it; the Virginia papers print it after a paragraph on Dr. Franklin.
label: A letter from London, 6 September 1770: 'Mr. Hutchinson is Governor.—The province I am sure ought to be very thankful for the having one born among themselves'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1788 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from L'Orient, 'received by the Brig Lively ... dated July 17': 'In this unfortunate and unhappy country we cannot depend upon any thing. The King is now at WAR with his subjects, & there are many regiments of infantry that have refused'. A letter-writer's account; the New-Hampshire Gazette heads it 'SERIOUS and ACTUAL TROUBLES in FRANCE.'
label: A letter from L'Orient of 17 July 1788 on troubles in France

admission_rule: Reviewed 1780 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from 'an intelligent gentleman in the neighbourhood of Morristown', 9 June 1780: 'Although extremely fatigued, I catch a moment to inform you that I have just returned from Elizabeth-Town, where I have been reconnoitring the enemy's situation and strength ...'; the letter goes on to the burning of Connecticut Farms and General Washington drawing the army back above Springfield. The New-Hampshire Gazette prints only the later part of the letter and is not counted (C-06). A private letter: the writer's account.
label: A letter from near Morristown, 9 June 1780: the British incursion from Elizabethtown

admission_rule: Reviewed 1781 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter dated 'Newcastle, 18 miles this side of Richmond, May 28, 1781': 'Yesterday was a week since Cornwallis joined Arnold (Philips being dead of a fever) at Petersburg; the latter had 3500 men, the former 1500'. A letter-writer's account, as a Philadelphia paper printed it.
label: A letter from Newcastle, Virginia, 28 May 1781: Lord Cornwallis has joined General Arnold at Petersburg

admission_rule: Reviewed 1791 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a letter from Paris of 10 March 1791 on the duties the National Assembly decreed on foreign importations: 'The importation of oil from any country, but the United States of America, shall be prohibited. The oil imported from the United States of America, in French or American vessels, shall pay a duty of twelve livres per quintal.' The New-Hampshire Gazette and the New Hampshire Gazetteer print an extract of the letter ('Our Assembly has at last decreed the duties which are to be paid upon foreign importations'); the Gazette of the United States and the Patowmac Guardian report what it contains ('A letter from Paris, of March 10, ... contains the following information'), counted with it (C-02). A correspondent's report of a decree.
label: A letter from Paris of 10 March 1791: the National Assembly decrees that 'the importation of oil from any country, but the United States of America, shall be prohibited'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1781 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from St. Eustatius dated 14 February 1781: 'The strictest discipline and decorum is kept up by the military here; a bomb battery and several new fortifications are constructing'. The Royal Gazette of Charleston prints it under 'Basseterre, (St. Christopher) Feb. 15'. A letter-writer's account from the island.
label: A letter from St. Eustatius of 14 February 1781, after the island was taken by the British

admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from the Hague dated 4 June 1778, in London news: 'The proposals for a treaty between the Americans and the United Provinces now lie before the States; the answer I am told the Americans received on the delivery of them was, that the business required a very serious attention'. The New-York Gazette and the Newport Gazette print it in August; three American papers print it in November as 'a letter from Holland, dated in June'. A correspondent's letter, as the London papers gave it.
label: A letter from the Hague of 4 June 1778: American proposals for a treaty lie before the States of the United Provinces

admission_rule: Reviewed 1774 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph of the London news of 26 January 1774: 'A letter from the Lower Elbe, dated Jan. 13, says, "The insurrection in Russia is at present the topic of every conversation. It seems to have happened in the most critical time, when fresh troops were greatly wanted"'; it says that troops on their march for Moldavia have been recalled, that troops about Warsaw have orders to march for Petersburg, and that 'a total Revolution' is suspected to be the consequence. A report at second hand, from a letter, in the papers' London news.
label: London, 26 January 1774: a letter from the Lower Elbe, 'The insurrection in Russia is at present the topic of every conversation'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1782 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter 'dated Uxbridge, near Charlestown, South-Carolina, October 5, 1782': 'To write news I have none scarce worth communicating, except that the fleet of transports from Jamaica are arrived, and which, with the fleet arrived a few days before, make upwards of ninety sail: they have threatened to carry away the 1500 negroes they have collected; but if they do, our government is determined to confiscate every marriage settlement of their friends...' Printed by all four newspapers that survive for its weeks; admitted by the rule's first part. A South Carolina correspondent's account.
label: A letter dated Uxbridge, near Charlestown, 5 October 1782: 'To write news I have none scarce worth communicating, except that the fleet of transports from Jamaica are arrived'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1810 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter 'from a gentleman of the first respectability at Washington, Mississippi Territory, to his friend in this city, bearing date October 30, 1810': 'The situation of Florida most certainly claims the earliest possible attention of our government, for, unless they are adopted into our family of governments, there is much room to fear that one of the great belligerents of Europe will attempt to lay violent hands on it'; it reports that men of the territory were crossing the line in expectation of military employment and that the convention would meet again at Baton Rouge. A private letter printed at second hand.
label: A letter from Washington, Mississippi Territory, 30 October 1810: 'The situation of Florida most certainly claims the earliest possible attention of our government'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1791 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the letter of the King of France to the National Assembly accepting the constitution, from the Paris papers of September 1791, in three translations counted as one item (C-02): 'Gentlemen, I have attentively examined the Constitutional Act which you have presented to me. I do accept it, and will cause it to be executed. This simple declaration might at another time have been sufficient: but now I am bound to make my motives known; it is a duty which I owe to the Nation and to myself' (the National Gazette, from a Paris paper of 14 September, and the Patowmac Guardian and the Kentucky Gazette); 'I have attentively examined the Constitutional Act, which you have presented for my acceptance. I accept it, and I shall cause it to be executed' (the New-Hampshire Gazette and the New Hampshire Gazetteer); 'I have examined with attention the Constitution which you presented me for acceptance. I accept it, and shall see it executed' (the Gazette of the United States). The King's own letter, in translation.
label: The King of France's letter to the National Assembly accepting the constitution, September 1791: 'I have attentively examined the Constitutional Act which you have presented to me. I do accept it'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1788 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter 'of a late date, from the illustrious President of the late Federal Convention, to his friend in Frederickburgh, Virginia', taken from Mr. Green's Virginia Herald: 'I thank you for your kind congratulation on my safe return from the Convention'; the writer gives his view of the Constitution the Convention proposed. The letter-writer's own words, as the papers printed them.
label: A letter of the President of the late Federal Convention to a friend in Fredericksburg, Virginia, on his return from the Convention

admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from a gentleman at Albany, 2 September 1775: 'By an Express arrived last Evening, we hear there has been a Skirmish near St. John's, between a reconnoitering Party of our Men in a Boat, and a Boat of Regulars, Canadians, and Indians'; it gives the general's account of the skirmish and says General Montgomery has set off with 1200 men for St. John's, to muster on the Isle aux Noix. A private letter at second hand, giving the general's letter.
label: A letter from Albany, 2 September 1775: 'we hear there has been a skirmish near St. John's'; General Montgomery sets off toward St. John's

admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Two items printed in July and August 1805 about the party of discovery on the Missouri under Captains Lewis and Clark: a Kentucky account of the party's winter at Fort Mandan, and Captain Lewis's letter to the President of 7 April 1805. Contains those two groups.
label: News from Lewis and Clark's party at Fort Mandan, 1805

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: The first printed news of the return of Captain Lewis, Captain Clark and their party to St. Louis from the Pacific, in September 1806: the National Intelligencer's announcement and Captain Clark's letter to his brother. Contains those two groups.
label: The return of Lewis and Clark, 1806

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the National Intelligencer's paragraph of 27 October 1806: 'It is with the sincerest pleasure, that we announce to our fellow citizens, the arrival of CAPTAIN LEWIS, with his exploring party, at St. Louis'; the President had a letter from him dated 23 September. The government paper's report.
label: The National Intelligencer announces Captain Lewis's arrival at St. Louis

admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of 'A letter from Captain Meriwether Lewis to the President of the United States. Fort Mandan, April 7th, 1805': 'Herewith inclosed you will receive an invoice of certain articles, which I have forwarded to you from this place'; he describes the party and its plans for going on. The writer's own account.
label: Captain Lewis's letter to the President from Fort Mandan

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a letter from Lewistown, Delaware, of 12 April 1777: 'Yesterday morning the ship Morris, Capt. Anderson was chased into the mouth of our Bay by a frigate; the Roebuck, laying in the Road, made sail after her. Capt.
