Mr. Lyons is appointed by the Board of Longitude to make observations ...'. A London report, as the papers reprinted it.
label: London, May 1773: 'The Racehorse and Carcass are fitting out for an expedition to the North Pole, under the command of the Honourable Captain Phipps'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1773 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a London paragraph of June 1773: 'The French Ambassador observed at Portsmouth that he had now seen two of the finest sights in the world, "The King of Prussia, at the head of his army, and the King of England at the head of his fleet." ...'. A London report, as the papers reprinted it.
label: London, June 1773: 'The French Ambassador observed at Portsmouth, that he had now seen two of the finest sights in the world, "The King of Prussia, at the head of his army, and the King of England at the head of his fleet"'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1773 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a London paragraph of early 1773 in two wordings: 'The Hotel Dieu, (one of the finest hospitals in the world) was burnt down at Paris the beginning of January last, and between seven and eight hundred sick persons perished in the flames ...' (the Virginia papers: 'The Hotel Dieu at Paris is burnt down, with twelve houses ...'). A London report, as the papers reprinted it; letters from Paris on the same fire are other texts.
label: London, early 1773: 'The Hotel Dieu, (one of the finest hospitals in the world) was burnt down at Paris the beginning of January last, and between seven and eight hundred sick persons perished in the flames'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1772 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a London paragraph of November 1771 (dated 11 and 13 November in the Virginia papers): 'A very great Personage last Thursday, in Council, after expressing the most tender concern for the Duke of Gloucester, thought proper to take notice, that the late act of the Duke of Cumberland would cause an eternal separation between himself and the Duke. Upon which tears being seen to gush, a motion was made to adjourn the Council; but the great Personage, resuming his wonted firmness, told the Council, that no private concerns respecting himself should ever retard the public business of the kingdom ...'. A London paper's report, as the papers reprinted it.
label: London, November 1771: 'A very great Personage last Thursday, in Council, after expressing the most tender concern for the Duke of Gloucester, thought proper to take notice, that the late act of the Duke of Cumberland would cause an eternal separation between himself and the Duke'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1773 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a London paragraph of 26 June 1773 (another wording in the New-Hampshire Gazette): 'His Majesty set out from the Commissioner's house, on his return to Kew, at three quarters after six o'clock, having been graciously pleased to order the following sums to be distributed, viz. To the artificers, workmen, and labourers of the Dock-yard ...' (after the King's visit to the fleet at Portsmouth). A London report, as the papers reprinted it.
label: London, 26 June 1773: 'His Majesty set out from the Commissioner's house, on his return to Kew, at three quarters after six o'clock, having been graciously pleased to order the following sums to be distributed'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1773 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a London paragraph of 24 and 25 June 1773: 'Yesterday being midsummer day, there was a very numerous and respectable appearance of the livery of London, in Common-Hall assembled, for the annual purpose of electing Sheriffs for the city of London, and county of Middlesex, for the year ensuing ...'. A London report, as the papers reprinted it.
label: London, 25 June 1773: 'Yesterday being midsummer day, there was a very numerous and respectable appearance of the livery of London, in Common-Hall assembled, for the annual purpose of electing Sheriffs for the city of London, and county of Middlesex'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1773 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a London paragraph of 8 December 1772: 'Yesterday Serjeant Glynn sat for the first time as Recorder of London. His charge to the grand jury was exceedingly pathetic, elegant and instructive, accompanied with copious eulogiums on the blessings this country enjoys over all others, in having the freedom of trial by a jury of their peers.' A London report, as the papers reprinted it.
label: London, December 1772: 'Yesterday Serjeant Glynn sat for the first time as Recorder of London. His charge to the grand jury was exceedingly pathetic, elegant and instructive'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1773 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a London paragraph of 22 April 1773, one of them without its first sentence: 'Lord North did not come yesterday from St. James's to the House of Commons till near four o'clock. As soon as his Lordship arrived, the Speaker rose, and acquainted the House that he had received a letter from the Sheriffs of Middlesex, signed "Richard Oliver" and "Watkin Lewes", in answer to a circular letter he had written to them by order of the House ...'. A London report of proceedings in the House of Commons, as the papers reprinted it.
label: London, 22 April 1773: 'Lord North did not come yesterday from St. James's to the House of Commons till near four o'clock. As soon as his Lordship arrived, the Speaker rose, and acquainted the House that he had received a letter from the Sheriffs of Middlesex'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1801 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a London paragraph of 15 August 1801: 'The intelligence of the surrender of Cairo is confirmed. Two messengers arrived yesterday with dispatches from Constantinople and Vienna to government and the East India Company. The dispatches to government are from Lord Minto, who continues to congratulate his majesty's ministers on the fall of Cairo. The dispatches, however, to the East India Company, place the intelligence beyond all doubt.' Five of the papers print after it the letter it introduces, from Peter Tooke at Constantinople of 19 July ('I had the honor to address you, on the 17th inst. by an express courier, in order to inform you of the reduction of the castle and city of Cairo by his majesty's and the Ottoman armies'), which is in 7 papers with the Rhode-Island Republican and the Republican Gazette and is not counted with it (see the README). A London paper's report at second hand.
label: London, 15 August 1801: 'The intelligence of the surrender of Cairo is confirmed'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1791 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a London paragraph of 3 June 1791: 'Accounts were received yesterday at the Secretary of State's office, by way of France, that the plague rages with dreadful havoc in that part of Turkey nearest to the Mediterranean, inasmuch, that in a small district a thousand persons have died in a day.' The New-Hampshire Gazette prints it twice (C-08). A London report of accounts received by way of France.
label: London, 3 June 1791: 'Accounts were received yesterday at the Secretary of State's office, by way of France, that the plague rages with dreadful havoc in that part of Turkey nearest to the Mediterranean'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1794 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a London paragraph: 'By an American Gentleman who left Brest on Friday last we learn, that there were one and thirty sail, besides a great number of frigates, lying at single anchor, ready to put to sea at the shortest warning'. A report from London papers.
label: London, 15 March 1794: thirty-one sail of the line ready at Brest

admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph of the London news of December 1774: 'A number of transports are sailed for Ireland, to receive on board the 22d, 49th, 55th, and 63d regiments. Major General Howe and Sir William Draper, are going out as Brigadiers on the Staff.' A London report, a single paragraph of the papers' London news.
label: London, December 1774: transports sail for Ireland to take on four regiments; Major General Howe and Sir William Draper to go out as brigadiers

admission_rule: Reviewed 1772 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a London paragraph of September 1772: 'Orders are stuck up at the War-Office for all persons (commissioned and private) absent from regiments on duty in the West Indies and America to join them without delay.' A London report of an order.
label: London, September 1772: 'Orders are stuck up at the War-Office for all persons (commissioned and private) absent from regiments on duty in the West Indies and America to join them without delay'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph of the London news of 7 January 1775: 'Lord North has publicly declared, that so far from the meetings of the American and West India Merchants being disagreeable to him, he, on the contrary, wishes for nothing more than as much information as possible on the American business to be laid before Parliament as soon as possible.' A London report of Lord North's words, a single paragraph of the papers' London news.
label: London, 7 January 1775: Lord North is said to have declared that, far from the merchants' meetings being disagreeable to him, he wishes for as much information as possible on America

admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: The two bills that Lord North brought into the House of Commons in February 1778, as copies printed in New York reached the papers in April (the New-York Gazette heads them 'Copies of two bills presented and read in the House of Commons, on the 19th of February last'), and Congress's report of 22 April 1778 on 'a certain printed paper sent from Philadelphia, purporting to be the draught of a bill'. Contains those three groups.
label: Lord North's conciliatory bills and Congress's answer, as the papers printed them in April and May 1778

admission_rule: Reviewed 1774 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph of the London news of 21 January 1774: 'Lord Viscount Pitt, son to the Earl of Chatham, is to embark next month for North America, to make the tour of the British colonies on that continent.' A report from London, a single paragraph of the papers' London news.
label: London, 21 January 1774: 'Lord Viscount Pitt, son to the Earl of Chatham, is to embark next month for North America'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the proclamation of Louis Napoleon as King of Holland (June 1806), 'read this day to the military, and announced to the people': 'Louis Napoleon, by the Grace of God and the constitutional laws of the state, King of Holland, to all who shall see and read this, greeting'. A ruler's own proclamation.
label: Louis Napoleon proclaimed King of Holland, 1806

admission_rule: Reviewed 1803 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph of news from Rotterdam of April 1803, in runs of European news (dated 12 April in four papers and 8 April, under the heading 'Expedition to Louisiana', in three): 'By an express order from the First Consul, the Louisiana expedition is definitively suspended. The French General began the day before yesterday to debark the troops that were on board the vessels; they will proceed, with the other troops newly arrived in this Republic, to different destinations both on the frontiers and elsewhere'. The Kentucky Gazette gives it in shorter words ('By an express order of Bonaparte, the Louisiana expedition is suspended, and the troops are debarked'), counted with the others. A report at second hand.
label: Rotterdam, April 1803: 'By an express order from the First Consul, the Louisiana expedition is definitively suspended'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Two documents of the handing over of New Orleans and Louisiana to the United States in December 1803, as the papers printed them in January 1804: General Wilkinson's orders to the American troops before New Orleans, 17 December 1803, and Governor Claiborne's proclamation that the government of Spain and France over the province has ceased. Contains those two groups.
label: The United States take possession of Louisiana, December 1803: General Wilkinson's orders and Governor Claiborne's proclamation

admission_rule: Reviewed 1803 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the treaty between the United States of America and the French Republic: 'The President of the United States of America, and the First Consul of the French Republic, in the name of the French people, desiring to remove all source of misunderstanding relative to objects of discussion mentioned in the second and fifth articles of the convention of the 8th Vendemiaire, an. 9, (30th September, 1800.) relative to the rights claimed by the United States, in virtue of the treaty concluded at Madrid'; its articles cede Louisiana as the French Republic acquired it from Spain. The National Intelligencer printed it on 21 October and again on 2 November with the President's proclamation. The two governments' treaty, as printed after the Senate's vote.
label: The treaty for the cession of Louisiana, signed at Paris on 30 April 1803

admission_rule: Reviewed 1779 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from Brigadier General Lovell (the papers print 'Lovell' or 'Lovel'), commanding the Massachusetts expedition against the British post at Majorbagaduce on the Penobscot, to Jeremiah Powell, President of the Council: 'The army under my command having arrived in Penobscot River on the 25th instant—I the same evening attempted to make a lodgment on Majorbaggaduce, but the wind springing up very strong, I was obliged to desist...' An American commander's own report.
label: Brigadier General Lovell to the President of the Council of Massachusetts, Majorbagaduce, 28 July 1779: 'The army under my command having arrived in Penobscot River'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a report from Lübeck (9 or 10 November 1806) of the French attack of 6 November, which took the town from the Prussians: 'the most dreadful day in the annals of Lubeck'.
label: Lübeck stormed

admission_rule: Reviewed 1810 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an address that Lucien Bonaparte, the Emperor's brother, is said to have had distributed at Rome after he sailed in 1810 and that, the papers say, was suppressed by an official order: 'To the Roman Citizens. In the bosom of retirement, occupied with no other cares than those of my family'; he says that he had no choice between unconditional submission and immediate flight. Lucien Bonaparte's own words, as the London papers gave them.
label: Lucien Bonaparte's address to the citizens of Rome, 1810, as the papers printed it in November

admission_rule: Reviewed 1791 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the recital that M. Drouet, one of the two citizens who stopped the King, gave before the National Assembly: 'I am the Postmaster of Sainte Menehould, formerly a dragoon in the regiment of Conde. My comrade, William, was formerly a dragoon of the Queen's regiment. On the 21st of June, at half past seven o'clock in the evening, two carriages and eleven horses baited at my house—I thought I recognized the Queen; and perceiving a man at the back part of the carriage, on the left, I was struck with the resemblance of his countenance to the King's effigy on an assignat of 50 livres.' M. Drouet's own account, as the papers print it.
label: M. Drouet's recital before the National Assembly of France: 'I am the Postmaster of Sainte Menehould', on how the King was stopped in June 1791

admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan (round two: stories once held back for framing, at the year's 7-paper rule).
definition: Printings of a Norfolk paragraph of 29 June 1807: Robert MacDonald, 'one of the seamen wounded on board the Chesapeake frigate', died at the Marine Hospital, and his funeral the day before was 'attended by nearly four thousand citizens', with a procession of boats, minute guns, colours at half mast and a sermon at Christ Church; the paper prints the order of the procession. A local report of a public funeral.
label: Robert MacDonald's funeral at Norfolk, June 1807

admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Philadelphia paragraph of 14 August 1793: by the brig Molly, Capt. Morris, from Madeira, word that a frigate from Falmouth had brought English papers to about 24 June with an account of a very bloody battle near Lisle, to the advantage of the French, in which 17,000 men fell; Morris said the account was believed at Madeira. A report at third hand of what newspapers said; the Gazette of the United States and the American Herald of Liberty add that the consul's letter from Madeira of 4 July said there was nothing new.
label: By the brig Molly from Madeira: a battle near Lisle reported

admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the Secretary of State's letter of 10 July 1805 to the president of the South Carolina Insurance Company at Charleston: 'I have received your letter of the 22d ult. inclosing the memorial of the insurance company of which you are President, and of the merchants and others, interested', on the capture of the ship Two Friends by a French privateer and on French privateers off Charleston bar. The government's own answer; the memorial it answers is the merchants' complaint.
label: Madison's answer to the Charleston memorial on the ship Two Friends

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the address James Madison delivered on taking the oath as President, 4 March 1809: 'Unwilling to depart from examples of the most revered authority, I avail myself of the occasion now presented, to express the profound impression made on me, by the call of my country'.
label: Madison's inaugural address, 4 March 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the report of the Secretary of State to the Senate, sent with a message of the President, 'respecting "new principles interpolated into the law of nations"': 'The most important of the principles interpolated into the law of nations, is that which appears to be maintained by the British government and its prize courts'. The American government's account and argument.
label: The Secretary of State's report on 'new principles' in the law of nations

admission_rule: Reviewed 1794 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the resolutions Mr. Madison read in the committee of the whole house: 'Resolved, as the opinion of this committee, that the interest of the United States would be promoted by further restrictions and higher duties, in certain cases, on the manufactures and navigation of foreign nations, employed in the commerce of the United States, than those now imposed'; later printings give the first resolution as the house debated it. Resolutions moved in Congress, as the papers printed them.
label: Congress, January 1794: Mr. Madison's resolutions for further restrictions and higher duties on the commerce of foreign nations

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the Secretary of State's letter to David Erskine, the British minister (25 March 1808), sent to Congress with the President's message: the Orders in Council of November 1807 could not be justified as retaliation for the French decrees.
label: Madison to Erskine on the Orders in Council, 25 March

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the letter of the Secretary of State to the Marquis de Casa Yrujo of 15 January 1806: 'In consequence of the just objections which your conduct has furnished against your continuance here, as the organ of communication on the part of his Catholic Majesty', the President expects that his departure 'will not be unnecessarily postponed'; with the Marquis's answers. Each side's own words, printed by the papers with their own remarks.
label: Madison's letter to Yrujo of 15 January and Yrujo's answers

admission_rule: Reviewed 1802 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a short letter from Madrid dated in August 1802 (15 August in most papers), which some papers call a circular of the American consul general at Madrid and others a letter 'from an official character at the Spanish court': 'On the 11th instant the plenipotentiaries of the United States and Spain signed a convention for the appointment of commissioners who are to form a board, and sit at Madrid, for the indemnification of those who have sustained losses, damages, or injuries in consequence of the excesses of individuals of either nation, during the late war, contrary to the existing treaty or the law of nations. The convention to have no force or effect, until it be ratified by the contracting parties.' An official's letter, as the papers printed it.
label: Madrid, August 1802: 'the plenipotentiaries of the United States and Spain signed a convention' for a board of commissioners on losses

admission_rule: Reviewed 1783 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Philadelphia paragraph of 16 January 1783: 'On Tuesday evening major Burnet, aide-camp to the honourable major general Greene, arrived here, in twenty-one days from Charlestown, with dispatches from the General; of which the following is an extract', and the extract of General Greene's letter to the president of Congress, dated headquarters, 19 December 1782: 'I have the honour to communicate to your excellency the agreeable information of the evacuation of Charlestown'. A Philadelphia paper's report, with the general's own letter.
label: Philadelphia, January 1783: Major Burnet arrives from Charleston with General Greene's dispatches on the evacuation of the town

admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of Chief Justice Marshall's opinion of 1 April 1807 at Richmond on the motion to commit Aaron Burr on two charges: he committed him for setting on foot an expedition against Spanish territory, a misdemeanor, but not for treason, finding no proof yet that war had been levied. Includes one printing of a summary of the opinion.
label: Marshall's opinion on committing Burr

admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of Chief Justice Marshall's opinion of 20 October 1807 at Richmond, after the treason trial, on the motion to commit Burr, Blennerhassett and Israel Smith to be tried elsewhere for treason and misdemeanor: he held it improper to commit them on the charge of treason, and committed Burr and Blennerhassett for preparing and providing the means for a military expedition. Includes printings of a Richmond report that quotes the opinion's conclusion.
label: Marshall's opinion of 20 October

admission_rule: Reviewed 1782 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a translation from the Martinico Gazette of 18 April 1782, brought to Newbury by the brig Swan, of an account of a sea engagement in the West Indies in April 1782: 'The following account of a sea engagement between the French fleet under the command of his Excellency the Count de Grasse, and the British fleet, under the orders of Sir George B. Rodney, is translated from the Martinico Gazette, of April 18...' The French side's published account, as Boston papers translated it; the Royal Gazette of Charleston prints it too. Accounts from the British side in the same weeks are listed as not chosen.
label: Boston, 16 May 1782: 'The following account of a sea engagement between the French fleet under the command of ... the Count de Grasse, and the British fleet, under ... Sir George B. Rodney, is translated from the Martinico Gazette'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1782 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter of a merchant at Fort St. Pierre, Martinique, as Boston and Richmond papers published it in March 1782: 'You have no doubt been informed of the reduction of the island of St. Kitts, which capitulated on the 12th ult. at ten o'clock, P. M. Nevis surrendered immediately, and Monserrat had the same fate...' The papers date the letter 1 March (Boston) or 3 March (the Royal Gazette, from Richmond) and call the island St. Kitts or St. Christopher. A merchant's account; the articles of capitulation, printed in the same weeks, are listed as not chosen.
label: A merchant's letter from Fort St. Pierre, Martinique, March 1782: 'You have no doubt been informed of the reduction of the island of St. Kitts'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1783 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Philadelphia paragraph of 10 June 1783: 'The general assembly of Maryland, at their last session, passed an act to invest the United States in Congress assembled, with a power to levy for the use of the said states, certain duties on imported foreign goods, wares and merchandizes, as a fund for the payment of the debt contracted by Congress during the late war.' A Philadelphia paper's report.
label: Philadelphia, 10 June 1783: the general assembly of Maryland passes an act to invest Congress with a power to levy duties on imported goods

admission_rule: Reviewed 1773 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the resolutions of the Massachusetts House of Representatives of 28 May 1773 answering the Virginia resolutions of 12 March: 'Whereas the Speaker hath communicated to this House a letter from the truly respectable House of Burgesses in his Majesty's ancient colony of Virginia, enclosing a copy of the resolves entered into by them on the 12th of March last ...'. A published document, as the papers printed it.
label: Boston, 28 May 1773: the House of Representatives' resolutions: 'Whereas the Speaker hath communicated to this House a letter from the truly respectable House of Burgesses in his Majesty's ancient colony of Virginia'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the address of the Provincial Congress of Massachusetts Bay to Charles Lee, major general of the Continental army, on his arrival at Cambridge: it congratulates him on his safe arrival and says 'We admire and respect the character of a man who, disregarding the allurements of wealth and distinction his merit might procure, engages in the cause of mankind, in defence of the injured, and relief of the oppressed'. The Provincial Congress's own address.
label: The Massachusetts Provincial Congress's address to General Lee, July 1775

admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the address of the Provincial Congress of Massachusetts Bay 'To his Excellency George Washington, Esq; General and Commander in Chief of the Continental Army': 'The Congress of the Massachusetts Colony, impressed with every sentiment of gratitude and respect, beg leave to congratulate your Excellency on your safe arrival'; it describes the state of the province and of its army. The Provincial Congress's own address.
label: The Massachusetts Provincial Congress's address to General Washington on his arrival at Cambridge, July 1775

admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of resolves of the Provincial Congress of Massachusetts Bay of February 1775, with the address to the inhabitants that some papers print before them: since a large reinforcement of troops is expected and the province's destruction appears intended, 'RESOLVED, That the great Law of self Preservation, calls upon the Inhabitants of this Colony, immediately to prepare against every Attempt that may be made to attack them by Surprise'; the militia and the minute men are to perfect themselves in military discipline, and the towns to encourage persons skilled in making fire-arms and bayonets. Counted by the resolves. The Provincial Congress's own resolves.
label: The Massachusetts Provincial Congress, February 1775: the militia and minute men to perfect themselves in discipline, and the towns to encourage the making of fire-arms

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a report from the Massachusetts Senate of 2 February 1809: its committee 'on the several Memorials from the people of a number of towns in this state, praying the interposition of the Legislature' reports resolves, the first that the act of 9 January to enforce the embargo 'is, in the opinion of the legislature, in many respects unjust, oppressive and unconstitutional, and not legally binding on the citizens of this state'. A state legislature's report and policy argument.
label: Report to the Massachusetts Senate on the act enforcing the embargo, 2 February 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1800 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of General Massena's letter to General Bonaparte dated Genoa, 7 June 1800: 'MY GENERAL, I HAVE the honour to give you an account of the evacuation of Genoa, conformable to the annexed convention. I hope you will find it worthy of the obstinate resistance of the brave army you have entrusted to me', in most papers with the convention for the evacuation and his letter to the Consuls. A commander's own report.
label: Massena's report to the First Consul on the evacuation of Genoa, 7 June 1800

admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the answer of Richard E. Lee, Mayor of Norfolk, to Commodore Douglas (4 July 1807): 'the American people are not to be intimidated by menace'; the ban was an act of individuals, not of the government, and the inhabitants would protect themselves against any aggression.
label: The Mayor's answer of 4 July

admission_rule: Reviewed 1800 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the letter in which the Austrian general Melas, 'on summoning Massena to surrender the city of Genoa, wrote to him in the following terms: General, Fortune has not crowned your bravery, which entitles you to my esteem, and to that of the whole world'. The Austrian commander's own letter, as the London papers gave it.
label: General Melas's letter summoning Massena to surrender Genoa, 1800

admission_rule: Reviewed 1774 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Boston report of October 1774, printed with the members' resolves: 'Wednesday last the members chosen in consequence of Governor Gage's writ for calling a General Assembly, met at the court-house in Salem pursuant to the precepts; and after waiting a day without being admitted to the usual oath, which should have been administered by the Governor or other constitutional officers; and having chosen the Honourable John Hancock, Esq; to be their Chairman ... they proceeded to business, and passed the following Resolves'; the resolves, dated at Salem on 7 October, say that the governor's proclamation discharging them was unconstitutional, and resolve that they form a provincial congress, to meet at Concord. A Boston paper's report, with the members' own resolves.
label: Boston, October 1774: the members chosen for the General Court meet at Salem without the governor, and resolve themselves into a provincial congress

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of President Jefferson's message to Congress of 13 January 1806: 'I lay before Congress the application of Hamet Caramalli, elder brother of the reigning bashaw of Tripoli, soliciting from the United States attention to his services and sufferings in the late war against that state'. The executive's own account of its dealings with him.
label: The President's message of 13 January on Hamet Caramalli

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of President Jefferson's message to Congress of 17 January 1806: 'In my message to both Houses of Congress, at the opening of their present session, I submitted to their attention, among other subjects, the oppression of our commerce and navigation by the irregular practices of armed vessels, public and private'. The executive's account, with documents.
label: The President's message of 17 January on British seizures and impressment

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of President Jefferson's message to Congress of 17 January 1809: 'I communicate to Congress certain letters which passed between the British Secretary of State, Mr. Canning, and Mr. Pinkney, our minister plenipotentiary at London', with the two letters: Mr. Canning writes that he was 'desirous to ascertain whether in fact the Orders in Council of November had been known to the government of the United States previous to the message of the President proposing the Embargo', and Mr. Pinkney answers. Official documents; each letter is its writer's own account.
label: The President's message of 17 January 1809 with letters of Canning and Pinkney

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of President Jefferson's message to Congress of 3 December 1806: 'I have the satisfaction to inform you that the negotiation depending between the United States and the government of Great Britain is proceeding in a spirit of friendship', and that 'a temporary suspension of the act of last session, prohibiting certain importations, would, as a mark of candid disposition on our part' help it. The executive's own account and request.
label: The President's message of 3 December on suspending the act

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: President Jefferson's last annual message, at the opening of the second session of the Tenth Congress on 8 November 1808, and three of the diplomatic papers sent with it, which the papers printed in later issues and in instalments: Canning's note to Pinkney, an extract of Armstrong's letter from France, and Madison's letter to Erskine. Contains those four groups.
label: The President's message of 8 November and its documents

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of President Jefferson's annual message to Congress of 8 November 1808: the overtures to Britain and France had failed, their edicts stood, and Congress was to decide what course to take on the embargo.
label: The President's message of 8 November

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the President's message to the Senate of 10 January 1806, sending 'documents and papers ... relative to complaints by the government of France, against the commerce carried on by American citizens to the French Island of St. Domingo': letters of General Turreau, the French minister, to the Secretary of State, and of Talleyrand to General Armstrong. The complaints are the French government's own account, in its own words (Turreau writes of trade 'with the rebels of every color').
label: The President's message with the French complaints on trade with St. Domingo

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of President Madison's message to the Senate of 15 June 1809, in compliance with its resolution of the 13th: 'I transmit extracts from letters from Mr. Pinkney to the Secretary of State, accompanied by letters and communications to him, from the British Secretary of State for the Foreign Department', with Mr. Canning's letter of 24 December 1808 ('I stated to you the probability that some alterations might be made in the orders in council'). One paper prints the documents without the message. Official documents; each letter is its writer's own account.
label: The President's message to the Senate of 15 June 1809, with letters of Mr. Pinkney and Mr. Canning

admission_rule: Reviewed 1781 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from an officer commanding militia, dated 'New-London, Friday, 9 o'clock September 7, 1781': 'Yesterday morning at 10 o'clock, I received advice that the enemy were landing at New-London Harbour's mouth---I immediately ordered the regiment under my command to march to New-London for its defence'. The officer's own account, as a Hartford paper printed it.
label: New London, 7 September 1781: a militia officer's letter on the enemy's landing and attack on New London

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Boston paragraph of November 1806 headed 'MIRANDA DEFEATED': Captain Foster, arrived from Trinidad, 'informs, that three days previous to his sailing, a Mr. Taylor, who had embarked in the expedition with Miranda, reached that place with the unpleasant intelligence of their defeat'. A report at second hand.
label: 'Miranda defeated': Captain Foster's report from Trinidad

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings about the expedition that General Francisco de Miranda fitted out at New York in the ship Leander for the coast of Caracas, as the papers printed them through 1806: questions put to the Secretary of State in February, a letter from on board the Leander in April, Miranda's proclamation of 28 June, and a report of the expedition's defeat in November. Contains those four groups.
label: General Miranda's expedition, 1806

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the proclamation that General Miranda issued on 28 June 1806 ('published at Trinidad', in one paper's words): 'FRIENDS AND COUNTRYMEN, The glorious opportunity now presents itself of relieving from oppression and arbitrary government, a people who are worthy of a better fate'. The expedition's own appeal.
label: General Miranda's proclamation of 28 June: 'Friends and Countrymen'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph headed 'MOREAU' in most papers, from a London paper: 'It has been announced in the Paris Moniteur, (the government paper) that this General has been banished to America—to what part is not suggested. Other papers mention that he left his prison on the 21st June, and proceeded for Perpignan'. A report at second hand of the French government paper's announcement.
label: 'It has been announced in the Paris Moniteur ... that this General has been banished to America': a London paragraph on Moreau, 1804

admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the letter of James Monroe and William Pinkney from London, 27 December 1806, to the Secretary of State: they had agreed with the British commissioners to conclude a treaty on all the points of their negotiation, on terms they trusted the government would approve. The President sent it to Congress on 19 February 1807. Several papers printed it again in October and November, after the treaty had been set aside.
label: Monroe and Pinkney: a treaty agreed

admission_rule: Reviewed 1803 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from a gentleman in the suite of Mr. Monroe, the envoy extraordinary sent to France early in 1803, to a friend in New York, dated Paris, 16 April 1803: 'Mr. Monroe was presented to the Minister for foreign affairs on the 14th, by whom he was received with every mark of attention ... Mr. M. will not be presented to the First Consul until ten days hence'; it adds that General Bernadotte had left Paris to embark for the United States as the French minister, and that 'It is the general opinion that war is at no great distance'. A private letter's account, as a New York paper printed it.
label: Paris, 16 April 1803: a letter from a gentleman in Mr. Monroe's suite, 'Mr. Monroe was presented to the Minister for foreign affairs on the 14th'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the letter of James Monroe, the American minister in London, to Lord Mulgrave of the British government, dated Great Cumberland Place, 23 September 1805, sent to Congress with the President's message of 17 January 1806: 'I flattered myself, from what passed in our last interview, that I should have been honored' with an answer. The American minister's case against the British courts' decisions on neutral trade.
label: Monroe's letter to Lord Mulgrave, 23 September 1805

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of General Montgomery's letter to Governor Carleton from before Quebec, dated December 1775, calling on him to surrender the town.
label: Montgomery's letter to Carleton

admission_rule: Reviewed 1801 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the letter of Moreau, general in chief of the French Army of the Rhine, to the Minister of War, from his head-quarters at Anzing, 12 Frimaire of the year 9 (2 or 3 December 1800), in three translations: 'I have the pleasure of giving you an account, my dear general, of an action most glorious for the army which I command, and of the greatest advantage to the republic' (the Alexandria Advertiser and the National Intelligencer, from London prints); 'I HAVE the pleasure, General, to give an account of an event very glorious for the army which I command, and of great advantage to the Republic' (the Oracle, the Portland Gazette, the New Hampshire Gazette and the Republican Ledger, from Paris papers brought to Boston by the Governor Strong); and a shorter form, 'An event has happened as glorious for the army which I command, as it is greatly advantageous to the Republic' (the Providence Journal). The forms are counted together (C-02). The letter reports the battle at Hohenlinden in Bavaria, the prisoners and the cannon taken. A French general's own report of a battle.
label: General Moreau's report to the Minister of War on the battle of Hohenlinden, December 1800

admission_rule: Reviewed 1781 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of General Morgan's letter to General Greene of 19 January 1781: 'The troops I have the honor to command, have gained a compleat victory over a detachment from the British army, commanded by lieutenant colonel Tarleton. The action happened on the 17th instant, about sun-rise, at a place called the Cowpens, near Pacolet river'. General Morgan's own account, sent to Congress by General Greene.
label: General Morgan to General Greene, Camp near Cain Creek, 19 January 1781: his account of the action at the Cowpens

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from Moses Creek of 26 July 1777: 'We have just had a brush with the enemy at Fort Edward, in which Lieut. Van Veghten was most inhumanly butchered and scalped. Two serjeants and two privates were likewise killed and scalped'; the letter goes on to tell that a young woman was taken from a house at Fort Edward and killed and scalped, and that another woman was killed near the same place. The excerpts end before the young woman's name (C-12). A report at second hand.
label: A letter from Moses Creek, 26 July 1777: 'We have just had a brush with the enemy at Fort Edward'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a letter dated 'Algiers, September 9, 1805', from Mr. Mountford, 'secretary of Mr. Lear, and now our charge d'affaires at Algiers', which General Eaton gave to the Enquirer: 'I have only a few moments to inform you, our affairs here are well. On the 30th ult. the soldiers rose in a body and murdered the Dey and his prime minister.' An American official's own short report; the words are his.
label: Mountford's letter from Algiers, 9 September

admission_rule: Reviewed 1787 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a letter of John Jay, New York, 1 December 1787, sent to the Independent Gazetteer of Philadelphia by the man he wrote to: 'I thank you for your obliging letter of the 24th ult. enclosing a paragraph respecting me in Mr. Oswald's paper of the same date'; he authorises its denial, 'and to declare, that, in my opinion, it is advisable for the people of America to adopt the Constitution proposed by the late Convention'. A letter and the note that sends it are counted as one item (X-1810-01). Mr. Jay's own letter.
label: Mr. Jay's letter of 1 December 1787, from the Independent Gazetteer: he authorises the denial of sentiments imputed to him against the proposed Constitution

admission_rule: Reviewed 1783 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Philadelphia paragraph of 14 January 1783: 'In the Ostend cutter, which arrived at Baltimore on Wednesday last, came passenger Mr. Miller, late printer of the London Evening Post, and also of the London Courant, who for these fifteen years past, has so freely exercised the liberty of the press, to the advantage of his country and honour to himself; but particularly in asserting and defending the cause of America.' A Philadelphia paper's report.
label: Philadelphia, January 1783: 'In the Ostend cutter, which arrived at Baltimore on Wednesday last, came passenger Mr. Miller, late printer of the London Evening Post'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1783 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the letter of Mr. Morris, superintendent of finance, to Congress, dated Office of Finance, 24 January 1783, which the papers print in March, 'the resignation of the superintendant of finance having occasioned much conversation': 'As nothing but the public danger would have induced me to accept my office, so I was determined to hold it until the danger was past, or else to meet my ruin in the common wreck'; he writes that funding the public debts on solid revenues was 'the last essential work of our glorious revolution'. Mr. Morris's own letter.
label: Office of Finance, 24 January 1783: Mr. Morris's letter to Congress, 'As nothing but the public danger would have induced me to accept my office'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1792 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a letter of James Seagrove, agent of Indian affairs in the southern department, to the citizens of Georgia, from St. Mary's, 4 October 1792, as a Savannah paper gave it: 'It being (in my opinion) of some consequence to the citizens of Georgia to know the disposition of the Creek Indians towards them at this time, I have therefore taken this mode of assuring them, that, from the whole of my late communications, and the investigation of matters, I do not find any disposition in the chiefs of the Creek nation to be unfriendly to any part of the United States'; more mischief, he writes, is to be dreaded from the ill-disposed among ourselves. Mr. Seagrove's own letter. A Philadelphia paragraph that sums it up ('By the latest accounts from Georgia, received from Mr. Seagrove'), in three papers, is not counted (C-07).
label: Mr. Seagrove, agent of Indian affairs in the southern department, to the citizens of Georgia, St. Mary's, 4 October 1792: the chiefs of the Creek nation not unfriendly

admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the British answer, a letter from Lord Mulgrave to Talleyrand, the French minister of foreign affairs (January 1805): 'His Majesty has received the letter which has been addressed to him by the chief of the French government'; the King cannot answer it more particularly before communicating with the powers of the continent, in particular the Emperor of Russia. Britain's own letter.
label: Lord Mulgrave's answer to Talleyrand

admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the letter of the Emperor Napoleon to the King of England, Paris, 12 Nivose year 13 (2 January 1805): 'Sir, my brother, Called to the throne of France by Providence, by the suffrages of the senate, the people and the army, my first sentiment is the wish of peace.' France's own letter: a proposal of peace and its argument.
label: Napoleon's letter to the King of England

admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: The two letters that the French minister of foreign affairs laid before the French Senate on 4 February 1805, as the papers printed them from April: the Emperor Napoleon's letter to the King of England of 2 January 1805, proposing peace, and Lord Mulgrave's answer to Talleyrand. Contains those two groups; each is one government's own letter.
label: Napoleon's letter to the King of England and the British answer

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the Emperor Napoleon's proclamation to his army after the battle of 2 December 1805, dated Austerlitz, 12 Frimaire: 'Soldiers, I am satisfied with you'; an army of 100,000 men 'has been in less than four hours cut to pieces and dispersed'. A commander's address to his own army.
label: The Emperor's proclamation to the army after the battle

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the speech of the Emperor Napoleon at the opening of the French Legislative Body in March 1806: 'Since your last session, the greatest part of Europe has entered into a coalition with England. My armies have never ceased to conquer'. A head of state's own account.
label: The Emperor Napoleon's speech opening the Legislative Body, March 1806

admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the speech of the Emperor Napoleon to the French Senate in September 1805, from Paris papers: 'Senators, In the present circumstances of Europe, I feel the necessity of appearing in the midst of you, and of making known to you my sentiments'; he is about to leave his capital to put himself at the head of the army. A head of state's own account. The Norfolk Gazette prints another translation ('I come among you to communicate my sentiments'), counted with the others.
label: Napoleon's speech to the French Senate, September 1805

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the Nashville Clarion's account of 20 October 1809: 'To record the untimely end of a brave and prudent officer, a learned scholar and scientific gentleman this column of the Clarion is ushered to the world in black. On the night of the 10th instant Meriwether Lewis, esq. Governor-general of Upper Louisiana, on his way to Washington city', died at a house on the road; the paper says 'he had shot himself', and adds a sketch of his career. A newspaper's account.
label: The Nashville Clarion on the death of Governor Meriwether Lewis, October 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1801 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph from Nashville, Tennessee, of 12 August 1801: 'On Monday last, arrived in this town, major general Wilkinson, commander in chief of the army of the United States, and one of the commissioners for treating with the Southern Indians, and yesterday he set off for South West point, where a treaty is to be holden with the Cherokees—one of the objects of negotiation, we learn, is to obtain from the Indians a relinquishment of the tract of country, lying between the Cumberland and Holston settlements, an event so desirable to the citizens of Tennessee'; it adds that the fourth regiment is to open a road from Nashville to the Natchez. A Nashville paper's account of what the commissioners were to seek; the Cherokees' answer is not in it (the Knoxville paragraph of September, the sub-story beside this one, reports their refusal).
label: Nashville, 12 August 1801: General Wilkinson sets off for South West Point, 'where a treaty is to be holden with the Cherokees'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1797 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a letter from a gentleman at Nassau, New Providence, dated 26 September 1797, as a Columbia (South Carolina) paper printed it on 3 November: 'We have lately very providentially escaped a most hellish plot.—A parcel of French negroes who had been captured and sold here, and who had ran away from their owners, entered into a conspiracy (about thirty in number) to burn the town and make a general massacre of the whites.' By his account one of them told his master a few hours before, five were taken and condemned and three executed. One correspondent's account, written from the side of those who held the accused; the accused are heard only through it, and it names no one.
label: A letter from Nassau, New Providence, 26 September 1797: the writer's account of a 'plot'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter dated 7 August 1804, published at Natchez on 10 August: 'Returning this morning from the vicinity of Little Bayou-Sara, I met not far from the line, 21 armed men;—on passing a house within my view, they sounded a French horn, and unfurled a flag composed of four white and three blue stripes'. Two papers print it under the heading 'Unpleasant Symptoms'. An unsigned letter-writer's own account.
label: Natchez, August 1804: a letter of 7 August on armed men with a flag near Bayou Sara

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Natchez report of 14 August 1804: 'By a gentleman arrived here yesterday from the neighbourhood of Bayou Sarah, we have been favored with the following information. That Mr. Nathan Kemper, with a party of about 30 men, with colors flying and horns sounding, marched from the neighbourhood of the line of demarcation between this Territory and West-Florida, on the 7th inst. against the fort of Baton Rouge' (the wording varies a little between papers); it gives a paper posted at the party's headquarters: 'For a people to be free, it is sufficient that they will it.' A report at second hand from a traveller, with the party's own declaration.
label: Natchez, 14 August 1804: 'Mr. Nathan Kemper, with a party of about 30 men, with colors flying and horns sounding' marches on Baton Rouge

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the National Intelligencer's paragraph of 19 April 1809, the government paper's own account: 'Since the arrival of Mr. Oakeley at Washington, Mr. Smith, Secretary of State, and Mr. Erskine, the British Minister, have been, we understand, every day engaged in discussions in relation to two points of difference between the United States and Great Britain', which had been settled; the notes that follow 'shew the happy result of these discussions'.
label: The National Intelligencer's paragraph of 19 April 1809 on the arrangement

admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan (round two: stories once held back for framing, at the year's 7-paper rule).
definition: Printings of a Washington paragraph of 29 July 1807 from the National Intelligencer: 'Much error having appeared in the accounts circulated' of what passed between the government and the British minister, Erskine, 'in the case of the seamen, to obtain whom the Leopard made the late attack on the Chesapeake', it states that his application for their surrender was refused, that naval commanders had orders not to recruit British deserters, and that the government had reason to believe the seamen were native citizens of the United States. The National Intelligencer's own account; it adds a note with the seamen's names and particulars as Captain Barron reported them.
label: The National Intelligencer on the seamen the Leopard sought

admission_rule: Reviewed 1803 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the National Intelligencer's paragraph of 18 July 1803, printed after the President's proclamation of 16 July: 'Dispatches from the American ministers at Paris were received by the Executive on Thursday evening. They were brought by Mr. Hughes of Baltimore, as confidential bearer, and contain the Treaty signed April 30th which conveys Louisiana to the United States. The extent of the territory ceded is defined by a general reference to that in which Louisiana was ceded to France'; the terms follow: '11,250,000 dollars to be paid to France in six per cent stock', the assumption of the debts and captures due by France to citizens of the United States, not to go beyond 3,750,000 dollars, and privileges for French and Spanish vessels in the ports of the ceded territory. The Oracle heads it 'Louisiana—[Official.]'. The government paper's statement, before the treaty was published.
label: Washington, July 1803: 'Dispatches from the American ministers at Paris ... contain the Treaty signed April 30th which conveys Louisiana to the United States', with its terms

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the National Intelligencer's paragraph of 19 March 1806 on the House vote of 17 March: 'The House of Representatives, the immediate organs of the people, have, after mature deliberation, taken ground in vindication of our violated rights, on which we congratulate the nation'; with Mr. Nicholson's resolution and the yeas and nays. The Washington paper's own report and judgement.
label: The National Intelligencer on the vote of 17 March

admission_rule: Reviewed 1801 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the letter of Vice-Admiral Lord Nelson to the commander in chief, Admiral Sir Hyde Parker, dated on board the Elephant, off Copenhagen, 3 April 1801, which the London Gazette published with the admiral's own dispatches: 'In obedience to your directions to report the proceedings of the squadron named in the margin, which you did me the honor to place under my command, I beg leave to inform you that having, by the assistance of that able officer Capt. Riou ... buoyed the channel of the Outer Deep, and the position of the middle ground, the squadron passed in safety', and engaged 'the Danish line'. Several papers head it 'Extract from Lord Nelson's Letter'. A British admiral's own report of a battle, as the London Gazette published it.
label: Lord Nelson's letter on the battle of Copenhagen, 3 April 1801, as the London Gazette published it

admission_rule: Reviewed 1801 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the remonstrance addressed 'To THOMAS JEFFERSON, Esq. President of the United States' by merchants of New Haven: 'The undersigned merchants, residing at the port and within the district of New-Haven, respectfully remonstrate against the late removal of Elizur Goodrich, Esq. from the office of Collector for the District of New-Haven, and the appointment of Samuel Bishop, Esq. to fill his vacancy. As the ground of our remonstrance we represent that the office while filled by Mr. Goodrich was conducted with a promptness, integrity and ability, satisfactory to the mercantile interest of this district—promptness and ability not to be found in his successor'; it goes on to Mr. Bishop's age ('seventy-eight years old in November next') and infirmities, says that the business would have to be done by his son, whom it calls 'so entirely destitute of public confidence' that no partisan would have recommended him, and asks the President to reconsider the appointment. It is 'Signed by' four merchants 'and others, to the number of eighty persons', with a certificate, signed by the president of the bank and of the chamber of commerce in New Haven and the president of its insurance company, that the signers own more than seven eighths of the port's shipping. Six papers print it before the President's reply; the New Hampshire Gazette prints the reply without it. It is in 6 papers, below the rule, and stands as a sub-story under a parent that reaches 7 (C-01), so that both sides of the exchange show (the owner's decision of 23 November 2026). The merchants' own remonstrance: an argument against an appointment, with their allegations about the new Collector's fitness and about his son.
label: The remonstrance of the merchants of New Haven to the President against the removal of their Collector, 1801

admission_rule: Reviewed 1801 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Two documents that six papers printed together in July and August 1801: the remonstrance in which merchants of New Haven, Connecticut, objected to the President's removal of Elizur Goodrich from the office of Collector of the port and to the appointment of Samuel Bishop, and the President's reply of 12 July 1801. Each side's own words. Contains those two groups.
label: The New Haven remonstrance and the President's reply, 1801: the merchants' remonstrance against the removal of their Collector, and the President's answer of 12 July

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a New London paragraph of 24 January 1777: 'We are informed, that Captain Phips, who lately escaped from the fleet at Newport, heard a letter read by an Hessian officer; another Hessian, who stood by, heard it, and could speak English, told Phips, that the contents were to recall the Hessian troops, for the dominions of the Prince of Hesse were invaded by the French King.' A report at second hand of what a Hessian soldier said.
label: New London, 24 January 1777: Captain Phips heard a letter read by a Hessian officer at Newport, that the Hessian troops were to be recalled

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an unsigned account from New Orleans, dated 16 July 1809 (10 July in two papers), of 'a transaction' at the army's camp of Terre-aux-Boeufs: a lieutenant had reported 'that a general revolt was intended as soon as the men had received their pay', and the commanding general 'resolved as on a former occasion to anticipate the conspirators', had men drawn out on parade and ordered a court martial. In four papers it is a letter that opens by accusing two named men of 'exciting sedition among the troops'. One side's account; it names soldiers as accused.
label: An account from New Orleans of a planned revolt at the camp of Terre-aux-Boeufs, July 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1781 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a New York paragraph of 24 September 1781: 'The following is said to be a pretty accurate Account of the Engagement off the Chesapeake the 5th inst. between the British and French Fleets: The first certain notice our Admiral received of the enemy's fleet being actually upon the coast'. A New York paper's account, from the British side; the Connecticut Courant and the New-Hampshire Gazette print it under an introduction of their own, from 'The first certain notice'.
label: New York, 24 September 1781: an account of the engagement of 5 September off the Chesapeake between the British and French fleets

admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract from the votes and proceedings of the General Assembly of New York of 23 February 1775: 'A Motion was made by Mr. Thomas, in the Words following, viz. Mr. Speaker, I Move that the Sense of this House be taken, on the Necessity of appointing Delegates for this Colony, to meet the Delegates of the other Colonies on this Continent, in General Congress, on the 10th Day of May next'; the debates that followed and the vote, in which the motion was rejected. The Assembly's own votes.
label: The New York General Assembly, 23 February 1775: Mr. Thomas's motion on the necessity of appointing delegates to the next Continental Congress, and the vote

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the resolutions of 'a meeting of Federal Republicans' at the Tontine Coffee House, New York, in late April 1806, called 'to take into consideration the defenceless state of our harbor': 'Resolved, That the citizens of the U. S. are of right, and according to the constitution and laws of the land, entitled to the enjoyment of life, liberty, and property'. A party meeting's own resolutions.
label: Resolutions of a New York meeting after the Leander shot

admission_rule: Reviewed 1794 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a New York paragraph: 'By the brig Mary, Capt. Haley, in 48 days from Brest, we have received the following important intelligence: About the 20th of March an engagement took place between the French and Prussian armies, which ended in a signal victory on the side of the Republicans'. A report brought by a ship, in the papers' words.
label: New York, 19 May 1794: news from Brest by the brig Mary

admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the address of the Provincial Congress of New York 'To his Excellency, George Washington, Generalissimo of all the Forces raised and to be raised in the confederated Colonies of America': 'At a time when the most loyal of his Majesty's subjects, from a regard to the laws and constitution, by which he sits on the throne, feel themselves reduced to the unhappy necessity of taking up arms', the Congress welcomes him and trusts that he will lay down his command when an accommodation is made. The Provincial Congress's own address.
label: The New York Provincial Congress's address to General Washington, June 1775

admission_rule: Reviewed 1802 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a report from the New York Gazette of 16 July 1802, from the captain of a schooner arrived in 38 days from Gibraltar: 'From Capt. Dawson we have received an account of an engagement between two Algerine cruisers and a Portuguese man of war off Malaga, wherein the former were victorious. The force of the Algerines was a frigate of 32 guns (the same which was presented by the American government to the Dey) and a xebec'; the Portuguese frigate struck after an action of three hours and was carried into Algiers. The Virginia Argus prints a Philadelphia form of the report that opens in other words ('The Captain of an American vessel arrived at New-York from Gibraltar, has given an account of the engagement') and goes on in the same words; counted with the others as a printed form. A ship captain's report at second hand.
label: New York, July 1802: from Captain Dawson, 'an engagement between two Algerine cruisers and a Portuguese man of war off Malaga'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1772 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a New York paragraph of February 1772: 'Captain Prince, from Cayenne, on his passage, touched at the Windward Islands, where he was informed, that on the 27th of December last, a most terrible fire broke out in the Island of Grenada, which burnt down no less than 600 houses; and that not more than 40 were left standing in the whole town of Grenada.' A shipmaster's report at second hand. Letters from the islands on the same fire, in other words, are other texts.
label: New York, February 1772: 'Captain Prince, from Cayenne, on his passage, touched at the Windward Islands, where he was informed, that on the 27th of December last, a most terrible fire broke out in the Island of Grenada, which burnt down no less than 600 houses'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a New York report of 18 July 1809: the master of the sloop Henry, from Bermuda, 'informs us' that when he left Martinique on 27 June 'advices were received there of the capture of the Toulon fleet by lord Collingwood, consisting of 5 sail of the line, 6 or 7 frigates, and 30 transports'. A report at third hand; one paper said it did not believe it.
label: A report from Martinique that the Toulon fleet was captured, July 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1802 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a New York report of 3 November 1802, in two forms: 'One of the most alarming Fires that has ever happened in this city, within our recollection, broke out last evening, between 8 & 9 o'clock, in a stable in Bridge-street, between Whitehall & Broad-streets' (two papers), or 'Last evening one of the most alarming Fires that has ever happened in this city, broke out in a stable in Bride-street, between Whitehall and Broad-streets' (five papers; the street is printed 'Bride-street' in some papers and 'Bridge-street' in others); in less than an hour and a half about fifty buildings, mostly dwelling houses, were burnt, pulled down or gutted. The report goes on to name some of the sufferers; the excerpts end before their names. Counted together as one report in two printed forms. A New York paper's report.
label: New York, 3 November 1802: 'one of the most alarming Fires that has ever happened in this city'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a New York report of 3 or 4 June 1804 under the heading 'MASSACRE OF ALL THE WHITES AT CAPE FRANCOIS' (in some papers 'AT ST. DOMINGO', in one 'OF CAPE-FRANCOIS'): 'By the Pilot Boat Grey-Hound, Capt. Sandford, in 16 days from Cape Francois we have a confirmation of the massacre and pillage at that and other places of the Island by Gen. Dessalines' troops, which commenced on the 19th of April' (the Rhode-Island Republican prints the 10th; the captain's name is also printed Sanford and Stanford). A report at second hand, from the people who arrived on the pilot boat, in the New York paper's words. Dessalines's own proclamation on these events, printed in four papers, is listed among the items not admitted.
label: A New York report by the pilot boat Grey-Hound, June 1804: 'MASSACRE OF ALL THE WHITES AT CAPE FRANCOIS'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a New York report of 4 October 1809: 'Late last night the Spanish frigate Cornelia … arrived at the quarantine ground. She sailed from Cadiz on the 20th of August. This vessel has brought out his excellency Don Lewis de Onis, minister plenipotentiary and envoy extraordinary from his Catholic majesty Ferdinand the 7th'. A report.
label: New York, 4 October 1809: the Spanish frigate Cornelia brings Don Onis

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

The new Spanish Minister, Don Onis, has not been received by our government'; it says the President would not receive him while Spain remained 'in its present unsettled state'. A newspaper's report.
label: New York, 25 October 1809: Don Onis 'has not been received by our government'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1773 printings, checked against the scan.

A New York report, as the papers reprinted it.
label: New York, 2 December 1773: 'Letters were received by the Packet appointing the Honourable Henry White, Esq; Abraham Lott, Esq; and Mr. Benjamin Booth, Merchant of this City, to be Agents for the Sale of the Tea shipped for this Province'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1773 printings, checked against the scan.

label: New York, 4 January 1773: 'Several letters from London by the Packet, say, "that the ministry are determined to use their influence in parliament for a repeal of the act imposing a duty on all teas exported to the colonies from Great-Britain"'

A New York report of what letters say, as the papers reprinted it.
label: New York, October 1773: 'By letters from London, and from good authority, we are assured that the East-India Company have determined upon sending three vessels with tea, one of them for Boston, another for Philadelphia, and the third for this port'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan (round three: stories once held back for framing, at the 6-paper threshold for 1793).

admission_rule: Reviewed 1794 printings, checked against the scan.

A report from a letter, in the papers' words.
label: Philadelphia, 11 November 1794: news from the westward (General Wayne's army at the Miami towns)

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

label: The act of 1 March 1809 to interdict commercial intercourse with Great Britain and France

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

label: The act of 28 June 1809 continuing the non-intercourse act

admission_rule: Reviewed 1794 printings, checked against the scan.

A report from Norfolk.
label: Norfolk, February 1794: the French fleet arrives in Hampton Roads

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.

Five papers print it under the heading 'Deplorable and Distressing Fire!!', two in a shorter form. A local paper's report. The excerpts end before the name of the owner of the warehouse where the fire began.
label: A Norfolk report of 25 February 1804: 'DEPLORABLE AND DISTRESSING FIRE!!'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.

label: The Secretary of State's notice that the amendment on electing the President and Vice-President has been ratified, 1804

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the newsletter's No. III, Paris, 20 March 1804, under headings such as 'Letters between Madame Bonaparte and Madame Moreau': 'In a preceding number we published a letter from General Moreau to the First Consul. We are now informed from good authority, that it was authentic, with the exception that General Moreau, instead of acknowledging himself guilty of the pretended conspiracy, says, that had he conspired ...', followed by two letters it attributes to Madame Bonaparte and Madame Moreau. The newsletter's own correction of its earlier item, and letters it attributes to the two women; the Berkeley and Jefferson Intelligencer prints the letters without the correction.
label: Les Nouvelles à la Main, No. III, March 1804: the letter attributed to Moreau 'authentic, with the exception' of one passage, and letters it says passed between Madame Bonaparte and Madame Moreau

admission_rule: Reviewed 1788 printings, checked against the scan.

A report of a suspicion, in the papers' own words (an allegation).
label: From Nova Scotia, September 1788: a report that Benedict Arnold is suspected of setting fire to his own house or store

admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.

An American official's own account.
label: O'Brien's letter from Malta on the attacks on Tripoli

admission_rule: Reviewed 1782 printings, checked against the scan.

Published by order of congress. Extract from the Registers of the Council of State...' Printed by all four newspapers that survive for its weeks; admitted by the rule's first part. The French council's decree, in Congress's translation.
label: Office for Foreign Affairs, 30 September 1782: 'Translation of an Arret of his most christian majesty's council of state, prescribing the formalities to be observed in the shipping of prize goods'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1779 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter 'from an officer in the western army commanded by Major General Sullivan', dated Konadasagea (the papers spell it several ways), 9 September 1779: 'Since the action of the 29th of last month, the Indians have fled at the approach of our army, and left their settlements to our mercy—New-Town, Konowarohala, French Katherines, Candai, Skayes, Gagheonghwa, and Konadasagea, are great heaps of ruin: besides these, we have burnt a number of scattering houses; and destroyed a large country of corn...' An American officer's own account of his army's burning of the towns; it is not the account of the Six Nations.
label: A letter from an officer in General Sullivan's army, Konadasagea, 9 September 1779: 'Since the action of the 29th of last month, the Indians have fled at the approach of our army'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1779 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an account of General Lincoln's attack on the British post at Stono Ferry, South Carolina, on 20 June 1779, which four papers print as an 'Extract of a letter from an officer of rank, in South-Carolina, June 22, 1779' and the Virginia Gazette as 'Authentic intelligence received by his Excellency the Governor from South Carolina': 'General Lincoln having received such intelligence of the intention, strength, and position of the enemy, as rendered it advisable to attack them at Stono Ferry, did so on the 20th instant about 7 in the morning, with great vigour; they were advantageously posted and covered by three strong redoubts...' An American officer's account.
label: South Carolina, 22 June 1779: 'General Lincoln having received such intelligence of the intention, strength, and position of the enemy, as rendered it advisable to attack them at Stono Ferry'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Three papers of the new Parliament's first days, as the colonial papers printed them from the London papers in January and February 1775: the King's speech from the throne of 30 November 1774, the House of Lords' rejection of an amendment to its address and the protest of the Lords who dissented, and the House of Commons' address of thanks. The King's and the Houses' own words.
label: The opening of Parliament, 30 November 1774: the King's speech, the Lords' debate and protest on the address, and the Commons' address of thanks

admission_rule: Reviewed 1781 printings, checked against the scan.

His Majesty having taken into consideration the many injurious proceedings of the States General of the United Provinces, and their subjects, as set forth in his royal manifesto of this date ... is pleased ... to order, and it is hereby ordered, That general reprisals be granted against the ships, goods, and subjects, of the States General of the United Provinces'. An order of the King in Council.
label: The King in Council, 20 December 1780: general reprisals to be granted against the ships, goods and subjects of the States General of the United Provinces

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

The British government's order.
label: The British order in council of 24 May 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Britain's order in council of 26 April 1809, which revoked the orders of November 1807 and put the ports of France, Holland and Italy under blockade, the Board of Trade's explanation of it to the merchants trading to America, and the papers that President Madison sent to the Senate on 15 June: extracts of Mr. Pinkney's letters and Mr. Canning's, and Mr. Erskine's note on the order with the Secretary of State's answer. Contains those four groups.
label: The British order in council of 26 April 1809 and the papers sent to the Senate

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
