definition: Printings of General St. Clair's letter to Congress of 14 July 1777: 'Congress may probably think it extraordinary that so much time should have elapsed before they heard from me, after a step of such consequence as the evacuation of the posts that had been intrusted to my care'; he gives the reasons that induced it. Published by order of Congress. The commander's own report.
label: General St. Clair to Congress, Fort Edward, 14 July 1777, on the evacuation of the posts entrusted to him

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Philadelphia paragraph of 10 May 1806: 'We learn from a gentleman who arrived in this city a day or two ago, from St. Domingo, that at the time of his departure there were very general movements among the subjects of the black emperor Dessalines'; the cause was not known, 'but it was said that some advices had been received by way of Jamaica'. A traveller's report at second hand, in the paper's words.
label: A Philadelphia report of movements in St. Domingo, May 1806

admission_rule: Reviewed 1772 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a notice from St. James's of 1 September 1772: 'The King has been pleased to grant unto George James Williams and Francis North, Esqrs. the office of Receiver General of all his Majesty's revenues within his colony and dominion of Virginia.' An official notice of an appointment, as the London papers gave it.
label: St. James's, 1 September 1772: 'The King has been pleased to grant unto George James Williams and Francis North, Esqrs. the office of Receiver General of all his Majesty's revenues within his colony and dominion of Virginia'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1773 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a St. Vincent paragraph of 27 February 1773, from the Royal Grenada Gazette: 'On Wednesday the 17th instant a number of Charibs came into the Grand Camp at Macarican, and a TREATY of PEACE and FRIENDSHIP was then concluded by his Excellency General Dalrymple ...'. A report from the island, as the papers reprinted it; the papers spell the Caribs and the camp in several ways.
label: St. Vincent, 27 February 1773: 'On Wednesday the 17th instant a number of Charibs came into the Grand Camp at Macarican, and a TREATY of PEACE and FRIENDSHIP was then concluded by his Excellency General Dalrymple'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Reports of the meeting of a committee of Congress (Franklin, John Adams and Edward Rutledge) with Lord Howe on Staten Island in September 1776: their setting off, and the committee's report to Congress. Contains those two groups.
label: Staten Island peace conference

admission_rule: Reviewed 1779 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Three public acts on the night attack on the British post at Stony Point on the Hudson, 15 and 16 July 1779, as the papers printed them in July and August: General Washington's letter of 16 July sending General Wayne's first note, his letter of 21 July sending Wayne's report, and the resolutions of Congress of 26 July thanking the commanders, officers and soldiers.
label: Stony Point, July 1779: General Washington's two letters to Congress with General Wayne's reports, and the thanks of Congress

admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the speech of Caleb Strong, Governor of Massachusetts, to the two houses of the legislature, June 1805: 'I embrace with pleasure the opportunity of congratulating you on the return of the anniversary, established by our Constitution'. He speaks of debtors, land disputes in the eastern counties, banks, and Kentucky's proposed amendment on the federal courts. A governor's own policy argument.
label: Governor Strong's speech to the Massachusetts legislature

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan (round three: stories once held back for framing, at the year's 7-paper rule).
definition: Printings of a letter to the settlers on the Watauga and Nolachucky rivers, signed 'Henry Stuart, Deputy Superintendent', for the British superintendent of Indian affairs in the southern district, with a sworn statement that a stranger delivered it on 18 May 1776. The letter invites those 'willing to join his Majesty's forces, as soon as they arrive at the Cherokee nation' to sign a paper of allegiance, and says that the King will land an army in West Florida and march it through the Creek nation to the Chickasaws, 'where 500 warriors from each nation are to join them', and on by the Cherokees, 'who have also promised their assistance'. The papers printed it in June and July as a letter delivered to the frontier inhabitants, and from late August among papers sent from Augusta, Georgia, as 'an intercepted letter'. One side's letter, as printed.
label: Henry Stuart's letter to the frontier inhabitants, May 1776

admission_rule: Reviewed 1774 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the resolves of a convention of delegates of every town and district of Suffolk County: 'At a meeting of the Delegates of every town and district in the county of Suffolk on Tuesday the 6th of September, at the house of Mr. Richard Woodward of Dedham, and by adjournment at the house of Mr. Vose of Milton, on Friday the ninth instant ... the following being several times read, and put paragraph by paragraph, was unanimously voted'; the resolves declare 'That no obedience is due from this province to either or any part of the acts above mentioned, but that they be rejected as the attempts of a wicked administration to enslave America', recommend that the people appear under arms at least once every week, and recommend withholding all commercial intercourse with Great Britain, Ireland and the West Indies. Several papers print them as they were laid before the Continental Congress at Philadelphia, which approved them on 17 September. The convention's own resolves.
label: The resolves of the delegates of the towns of Suffolk County, Massachusetts Bay, 6–9 September 1774 (the Suffolk resolves)

admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph of the London Sun of 10 April 1793: it was rumoured that Dumouriez, having found reason to doubt his army's promises to support his plan of marching to Paris and placing young Louis on the throne, had left it at the head of a regiment of cavalry. A rumour, labelled as one. Several papers print it with a New York introduction ('In the Sun, of the 10th April, which is the latest paper received'), the others among London paragraphs.
label: The Sun of 10 April: Dumouriez rumoured to have left his army

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a 'Swedish bulletin' from the headquarters of the Swedish army, April 1806, from London papers: reports 'received from adjutant general count Lowenhielm' said the Prussians had taken several villages near Lauenburg, and on the 23rd 'the Prussians passed the Lauenburg frontier'. One army's own account.
label: A Swedish bulletin: the Prussians cross into Lauenburg

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a New York report (end of July 1776) that about fifteen inhabitants drove off five boats from the men of war trying to land on Tappan meadows.
label: Boats driven off at Tappan

admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the report of Littleton W. Tazewell to the Mayor of Norfolk (5 July 1807) on delivering the Mayor's answer on board the Bellona: Douglas said his letter had been misapprehended and that he intended no menace. Includes one shorter account of the report.
label: Tazewell's report to the Mayor

admission_rule: Reviewed 1783 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a notice signed 'An American': 'To all Printers of Public News-Papers. Tell it to the whole World, and let it be published in every News-Paper throughout America, Europe, Asia and Africa, to the everlasting disgrace and infamy of the British King's Commanders at New-York, That during the late War, it is said, Eleven Thousand Six Hundred and Forty Four American Prisoners, have suffered death by their inhumane, cruel, savage and barbarous usage on board the filthy and malignant British Prison Ship called the Jersey, lying at New-York.' An anonymous writer's allegation, of a number that 'it is said'.
label: 'To all Printers of Public News-Papers. Tell it to the whole World': a notice signed 'An American' on the American prisoners said to have died in the prison ship at New York

admission_rule: Reviewed 1773 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from Temeswar of 23 May 1773: 'Since hostilities have recommenced between the Turks and Russians, they have had several skirmishes and severe conflicts, in which victory has indifferently declared herself for either party ...'. A letter at second hand, as the papers reprinted it.
label: Temeswar, 23 May 1773: a letter: 'Since hostilities have recommenced between the Turks and Russians, they have had several skirmishes and severe conflicts'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1797 printings of this report, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Norfolk report, from a passenger on the Danish ship Christian Haven, that the British attack on Santa Cruz de Tenerife (July 1797) was driven off. Other Tenerife accounts in the collection are different texts and are not included.
label: Tenerife defeat report

admission_rule: Reviewed 1791 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Two acts of the third session of the first Congress, as the papers printed them from February to April 1791: the act declaring the consent of Congress that a new State be formed within the jurisdiction of Virginia and admitted into the Union by the name of the State of Kentucky, and the act for the admission of the State of Vermont into the Union. Contains those two groups.
label: The acts of Congress of February 1791 on the admission of Kentucky and Vermont into the Union

admission_rule: Reviewed 1783 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Five public papers of the peace, as the papers printed them in the spring of 1783: the provisional articles agreed at Paris on 30 November 1782 between the King's commissioner and the commissioners of the United States; the preliminary articles between Great Britain and France signed at Versailles on 20 January 1783; the King's proclamation of the cessation of arms; the proclamation of the United States in Congress assembled of 11 April; and General Washington's orders of 18 April for proclaiming the cessation of hostilities to the army. Contains those five groups.
label: The articles of peace and the cessation of arms, as the papers printed them from March to May 1783

admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Two public papers on the battle fought near Monmouth Court-House, New Jersey, on 28 June 1778, as the British army marched from Philadelphia to New York: General Washington's letter to Congress of 1 July, and the resolution of thanks of Congress of 7 July. Contains those two groups.
label: The battle of Monmouth, 28 June 1778: General Washington's account to Congress, and the thanks of Congress

admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Three public declarations on one of the British commissioners, George Johnstone: Congress's declaration of 11 August 1778 that it is incompatible with the honour of Congress to hold any correspondence with him, and the two declarations of 26 August answering it, one by the other three commissioners and one by Mr. Johnstone. Contains those three groups.
label: George Johnstone and Congress, August and September 1778: Congress's declaration, the commissioners' declaration and Mr. Johnstone's declaration

admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: The two manifestos of October 1778: the British commissioners' manifesto and proclamation of 3 October, addressed to the members of Congress, the assemblies and all the inhabitants, and the manifesto of Congress of 30 October. Contains those two groups.
label: The British commissioners' manifesto and proclamation of 3 October 1778, and the manifesto of Congress of 30 October

admission_rule: Reviewed 1780 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of The Crisis, Number IX (by the author of Common Sense, June 1780): 'Had America pursued her advantages with half the spirit she resisted her misfortunes, she would, before now, have been a conquering and a peaceful people ...'. An essay, its author's argument.
label: The Crisis, Number IX: 'Had America pursued her advantages with half the spirit she resisted her misfortunes'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1791 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph of July 1791: 'The English papers give an account of the first pitched battle to which the French revolution has given rise; it was fought near Carpentras, between 10,000 patriots and about 7000 counter-revolutionists. The latter were completely routed, and Carpentras, in which was a garrison of 4000 men invested by the patriotic troops. On the 21st of April a capitulation was proposed by the besieged.' A report at second hand from the English papers.
label: 'The English papers give an account of the first pitched battle to which the French revolution has given rise': a battle near Carpentras

admission_rule: Reviewed 1780 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: A Boston paragraph of 29 June 1780 that the French fleet with 12,000 troops had sailed from Brest, and General Washington's general orders of 20 July on its arrival at Rhode Island, as the papers printed them. Each counted by its own words. Contains those two groups.
label: The French fleet and army for America, 1780: news of its sailing, and General Washington's orders on its arrival

admission_rule: Reviewed 1791 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph of the English news of July 1791: 'The Insurgents of Birmingham had made a gridiron of immense size, which they brought to Dr. Priestley's house, where they said they meant to broil an Anti-constitutional Philosopher by the blaze of his own writings, and light the fire with the Rights of Man.' The Gazette of the United States and the Patowmac Guardian print it among the London reports of the riots, the New-Hampshire Gazette at the end of an account of the riot. An English paper's report.
label: 'The Insurgents of Birmingham had made a gridiron of immense size': a paragraph of the English news on the riots at Birmingham, July 1791

admission_rule: Reviewed 1794 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: The President's proclamation of 25 September 1794 calling forth the militia against the combinations in the western counties of Pennsylvania, and the meeting of delegates at Parkinson's Ferry on 2 October, as the Pittsburgh paper reported it and as its resolutions were printed: one affair's separate public acts (X-1800-01).
label: The insurrection in the western counties of Pennsylvania, September and October 1794: the President's proclamation and the meeting at Parkinson's Ferry

admission_rule: Reviewed 1792 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the President's letter of 16 January 1792 to the Secretary of War: 'As the circumstances which have engaged the United States in the present Indian war may some of them be out of the public recollection, and others perhaps be unknown, it may appear adviseable that you prepare and publish, from authentic documents, a statement of those circumstances, as well as of the measures which have been taken, from time to time, for the re-establishment of peace and friendship'; the Secretary of War's statement of the causes of the hostilities with the Indian tribes north-west of the Ohio follows. Printed together, counted as one item (X-1810-01). The President's and the Secretary's own words.
label: The President to the Secretary of War, 16 January 1792: a statement, from authentic documents, of the circumstances of the present Indian war; the Secretary's statement follows

admission_rule: Reviewed 1792 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the President's message to both Houses of 5 March 1792: 'Knowing the friendly interest you take in whatever may promote the happiness and prosperity of the French nation, it is with pleasure that I lay before you the translation of a letter which I have received from his most Christian Majesty, announcing to the United States of America, his acceptance of the constitution presented to him by his nation'; the translation of the King's letter of 19 September 1791 follows. The President's own message, with the King's letter.
label: The President to both Houses, 5 March 1792: the King of France's letter announcing his acceptance of the constitution

admission_rule: Reviewed 1792 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the President's proclamation of September 1792: 'Whereas certain violent and unwarrantable proceedings have lately taken place, tending to obstruct the operation of the laws of the United States for raising a revenue upon spirits distilled within the same'; he exhorts all persons to desist from such proceedings. The President's own proclamation. A proclamation printed again in later issues counts again (C-08).
label: The President's proclamation, September 1792: against the violent and unwarrantable proceedings that obstruct the laws on spirits distilled within the United States

admission_rule: Reviewed 1792 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the President's message to the House of Representatives of 5 April 1792: 'I have maturely considered the act passed by the two Houses, entitled an act for an apportionment of representatives among the several states, according to the first enumeration—and I return it to your House, wherein it originated, with the following objections'; two objections follow, the first that no proportion or divisor applied to the states' numbers will yield the bill's allotment. The President's own message.
label: The President to the House, 5 April 1792: he returns the act for an apportionment of representatives with his objections

admission_rule: Reviewed 1792 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the President's speech to both Houses at the opening of the session, 6 November 1792: 'It is some abatement of the satisfaction, with which I meet you on the present occasion, that, in felicitating you on a continuance of the national prosperity generally, I am not able to add to it information that the Indian hostilities, which have for some time past distressed our North-Western frontier, have terminated'. The President's own speech.
label: The President's speech to both Houses of Congress, 6 November 1792

admission_rule: Reviewed 1791 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Three public papers of the opening of the first session of the second Congress, as the papers printed them from October to December 1791: the President's speech to both Houses of 25 October, the answer of the House of Representatives, which the Speaker delivered to the President at his house on 28 October, and the address of the Senate, which the Vice-President and the Senate presented on 31 October. Contains those three groups.
label: The opening of the session of Congress, October 1791: the President's speech and the answers of the two Houses

admission_rule: Reviewed 1780 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Commodore Paul Jones's letter of 3 October 1779 and Captain Pearson's report of 6 October to the Admiralty, on the action off Flamborough Head in which the Serapis was taken, as the papers printed them in 1780. Each letter is counted by its own words. Contains those two groups.
label: The action of the Serapis and Paul Jones's squadron, September 1779: the letters of Commodore Jones and Captain Pearson

admission_rule: Reviewed 1781 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: General Washington's letter to the President of Congress of 19 October 1781 on the surrender of the British army under Lord Cornwallis, with the correspondence and the articles of capitulation, and Lord Cornwallis's own letter to Sir Henry Clinton of 20 October, as the papers printed them.
label: The surrender of the British army at York, Virginia, as the papers printed it from October to December 1781

admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: The two public papers on the troops that surrendered at Saratoga in October 1777, whose embarkation Congress had suspended in January 1778: the British commissioners' requisition of 26 August 1778 that the troops be allowed to sail, and Congress's resolution of 4 September 1778. Contains those two groups.
label: The troops of the convention of Saratoga, August and September 1778: the commissioners' requisition and Congress's resolution

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the thirtieth bulletin of the French Grand Army, dated Austerlitz, 12 Frimaire, year 14 (3 December 1805): 'The 6th Frimaire, the emperor, upon receiving the communication of the full powers of Messrs. de Stadion and de Giulay, offered previously an armistice'. The French army's official account of the battle.
label: The thirtieth bulletin of the Grand Army

admission_rule: Reviewed 1779 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from Thomson Mason to the President of Congress, dated Leesburg, Virginia, 17 May 1779: 'My son, who is immediately from Hampton, informs me, that about forty sail of the enemy appeared in Hampton Road on Sunday the 9th instant. On Monday they attacked our fort at Portsmouth, where Major Matthews commanded with 150 men...' It goes on with the fort given up, ships burned on the stocks, and a party intercepted at the Great Bridge. The New-Hampshire Gazette of 8 June prints another letter of Mr. Mason's of the same day, in other words, sent on by General Gates; it is not counted with this one. A Virginian's letter, giving his son's account.
label: Thomson Mason to the President of Congress, Leesburg, 17 May 1779: 'about forty sail of the enemy appeared in Hampton Road'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Philadelphia report of May 1775: 'On Wednesday evening last arrived here, John Brown, Esq; from Ticonderoga, express to the General Congress, from whom we learn, that on the beginning of this instant, a company of about fifty men, from Connecticut, and the western part of Massachusetts' 'and joined by upwards of one hundred from Bennington', took the fort of Ticonderoga; it adds news of the Indians in Canada. A Philadelphia report of what the express said.
label: Philadelphia, May 1775: John Brown, express from Ticonderoga to the Congress, reports that the fort was taken by men from Connecticut and Massachusetts

admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan (round two, 6-paper threshold for 1793).
definition: Printings of a bulletin from the London Gazette, dated Tournai, 3 May 1793: on the 1st the French attacked the advanced posts of the left wing and of the centre of the combined army and were repulsed, with the loss of men and cannon. The British government's own account. Four papers print it after another Tournai paragraph on the preparations against Condé.
label: The London Gazette from Tournai, 3 May: the French attacks repulsed

admission_rule: Reviewed 1794 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an account dated 'Sunday Evening, 18th May': 'From the following detail, there is great reason to believe that the French permitted the column under the command of the Duke of York to advance yesterday further than force could have carried them'. An account from the British side, printed after the Duke of York's letter or the Tournay letter of 17 May.
label: Tournay, Sunday evening, 18 May 1794: an account of the British column's retreat

admission_rule: Reviewed 1783 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a London paragraph of 23 November 1782 and the letter it introduces: 'This day the governors and directors of the bank of England, received the following letter from the honourable T. Townshend, secretary for the home department. Whitehall, Nov. 22, 1782. Gentlemen, His majesty's ministers, anxious to prevent as early as possible, the mischiefs too commonly resulting from speculations in the funds, during the uncertain state of negotiations of peace'; it says that 'the negotiations now carrying on at Paris, are thought so near a crisis, as to promise a decisive conclusion, either for peace or war, before the meeting of parliament'. The secretary of state's own letter, with a London paper's introduction.
label: London, 23 November 1782: Mr. Townshend's letter to the governors and directors of the Bank of England on the negotiations at Paris

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: The President's message to the Senate of 10 January 1806 with the French government's complaints against American trade with St. Domingo, and the act of 28 February 1806 that prohibited trade with the parts of the island 'not in possession, and under the acknowledged government of France'. Contains those two groups.
label: Trade with St. Domingo: the French complaints and the act of 28 February 1806

admission_rule: Reviewed 1810 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of Albert Gallatin's circular letter of 2 November 1810 to the collectors of the customs: 'You will herewith receive a copy of the Proclamation of the President of the United States, announcing the revocation of the edicts of France which violated the neutral commerce of the United States'; it explains that French armed vessels may now enter American waters, and that unless the collectors are notified before 2 February 1811 that Great Britain has revoked or modified her edicts, they are from that day to enforce the restrictions against British vessels and goods. The Secretary of the Treasury's own instructions.
label: The Secretary of the Treasury's circular to the collectors of the customs, 2 November 1810

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the Treasury Department's circular to the collectors of the customs, dated 3 March 1809, signed by Albert Gallatin: 'I herewith transmit a printed copy of an act to interdict the commercial intercourse between the United States and Great Britain and France', with directions section by section on how the collectors are to carry it out.
label: The Treasury's circular of 3 March 1809 on the non-intercourse act

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the Treasury's circular to the collectors of the customs, 9 August 1809, signed by Albert Gallatin: 'You will herewith receive the copy of a Proclamation of the President'; the act of 28 June now applies to Great Britain as to France, 'any thing in my circular of 29th June last, to the contrary, notwithstanding', with rules for vessels that sailed on the faith of the April proclamation.
label: The Treasury's circular to the collectors, 9 August 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan (round two, 6-paper threshold for 1793).
definition: Printings of the circular of the Secretary of the Treasury to the collectors of the customs (Philadelphia, 4 August 1793): as repeated contraventions of neutrality had taken place in American ports, the collectors were to watch for vessels arming or equipping for the powers at war, with the schedule of 'Rules adopted by the President' on arming, equipping and prizes. The circular and its rules are one publication. An official document.
label: Hamilton's circular to the collectors, with the President's rules on neutrality

admission_rule: Reviewed 1803 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the report that the Secretary of the Treasury, Albert Gallatin, laid before the House of Representatives on 25 October 1803: 'In obedience to the directions of the act supplementary to the act entitled An act to establish the Treasury Department, the Secretary of the Treasury respectfully submits the following Reports and Estimates. The annual nett proceeds of the duties on merchandise and tonnage had, in former reports, been estimated at nine millions five hundred thousand dollars'; it estimates the revenue and the expenses of 1804 and considers whether new revenue is wanted for the debt that the treaty with France would create. The Secretary of the Treasury's own report.
label: The Secretary of the Treasury's reports and estimates laid before the House of Representatives, 25 October 1803

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the Secretary of the Treasury's report to Congress, sent 7 December 1809: Albert Gallatin's letter of transmittal and the report 'prepared in obedience to the act … to establish the Treasury Department', on the revenue of 1807 to 1809 and the expenses, with the statement that 'a loan will be necessary' unless the military and naval expenses are reduced.
label: The Secretary of the Treasury's annual report, December 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1810 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the report that the Secretary of the Treasury, Albert Gallatin, sent to the House of Representatives in December 1810: 'In obedience to the directions of the act supplementary to the act entitled "An act to establish the Treasury Department," the Secretary of the Treasury respectfully submits the following Report and Estimates'; it gives the revenue of 1808 and 1809, the receipts of the year and the estimates for 1811, and considers the provisions needed if the non-intercourse is revived against Great Britain. The Secretary of the Treasury's own report.
label: The Secretary of the Treasury's report and estimates, December 1810

admission_rule: Reviewed 1790 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the Secretary of the Treasury's report to the House of Representatives, 'Treasury Department, March 4, 1790. In obedience to the Order of the House of Representatives, of the second inst. The Secretary of the Treasury respectfully reports, THAT in his opinion, the funds in the first instance requisite towards the payment of interest on the debts of the individual States, according to the modifications proposed by him in his report of the ninth of January past, may be obtained from the following objects: An increase of the general product of the duties on goods imported ...'. The New-Hampshire papers print it inside their reports of the House's proceedings; the Kentucky Gazette prints it in three parts (17, 24 and 31 May), each under the report's heading, counted once, where its opening stands.
label: Treasury Department, 4 March 1790: the Secretary of the Treasury reports 'that in his opinion, the funds in the first instance requisite towards the payment of interest on the debts of the individual States ... may be obtained from the following objects'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1803 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: The three instruments signed at Paris on 30 April 1803 for the cession of Louisiana, as the papers printed them from 21 October 1803, after the Senate's vote of 20 October advising their ratification: the treaty of cession, the convention for the payment of sixty million francs, and the convention for the payment of debts due by France to citizens of the United States. Most papers print the three together. Contains those three groups.
label: The treaty and two conventions of 30 April 1803 between the United States and the French Republic, printed after the Senate's vote

admission_rule: Reviewed 1802 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a treaty 'Signed at Madrid, 21st March, 1801, by the Prince of Peace and Lucien Bonaparte' (the dates vary from paper to paper), from the Paris Journal des Débats of January 1802: 'The First Consul of the French republic and his Catholic Majesty, desirous of permanently determining the states which the son of the Infant of Parma shall receive, as an equivalent for the Duchy of Parma, have agreed to the following articles'; the Grand Duchy of Tuscany is given to the Prince of Parma, who will be acknowledged King of Tuscany. The National Intelligencer's headnote, which most papers repeat, says that the document 'establishes the fact, that Spain has ceded Louisiana to the French'. The two governments' treaty, as a Paris paper gave it, with the American paper's headnote.
label: The treaty signed at Madrid on 21 March 1801 by Lucien Bonaparte and the Prince of Peace, printed in 1802 as proof that 'Spain has ceded Louisiana to the French'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the treaty of peace between Austria and France signed at Pressburg on 26 December 1805: 'His majesty the emperor of Germany and Austria, and his majesty the emperor of the French, king of Italy, equally animated with a desire to put an end to the calamities of war'. Some papers printed it with the Emperor Napoleon's act of ratification before it. A treaty.
label: The treaty of Pressburg between Austria and France

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the treaty of peace between France and Austria signed at Vienna on 14 October 1809, with Napoleon's ratification before it ('Having seen and considered the treaty concluded, determined and signed at Vienna, on the 14th of this month'): the lands Austria gives up, a 'full and complete pardon for the inhabitants of the Tyrol', and the times for the French troops to leave.
label: The treaty of peace between France and Austria, Vienna, 14 October 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1801 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Two paragraphs of Tennessee papers on the meeting of the federal commissioners with the Cherokees at South West Point in 1801, as the papers printed them in September and October: a Nashville paragraph of 12 August on what the commissioners were to seek, and a Knoxville paragraph dated 19 September (9 September in three papers) that the treaty was broken up, the Cherokees refusing to sell lands or to permit roads. Both are the Tennessee papers' accounts; neither is the Cherokees' own. Contains those two groups.
label: The treaty with the Cherokees at South West Point, 1801: a Nashville paragraph on the commissioners' aims, and a Knoxville paragraph that the treaty is broken up

admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Two letters on the American squadron's attacks on Tripoli in August and September 1804, as the 1805 papers printed them after the President sent them to Congress: Richard O'Brien's letter from Malta of 5 September 1804 (sent on 31 December 1804) and Commodore Preble's letter of 18 September 1804 (sent on 20 February 1805). Contains those two groups. Each is an American official's own account.
label: Letters on the squadron before Tripoli, sent to Congress

admission_rule: Reviewed 1797 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a letter to the French Executive Directory dated 6 November 1796 and signed Truguet: 'I hasten to communicate to the Executive Directory the reception of letters from Brest, of the 3d instant (November) brought by an extraordinary courier, which announce that a general revolution has just taken place in Ireland.' It gives the report of the captains of two ships brought in from Liverpool by French privateers, that the Irish had taken 30,000 stand of arms in Dublin and defeated 10,000 English troops. Printed from the Paris papers, in the same column of French news as General Bournonville's letter (a group of its own). A report at second hand: the writer passes on what letters from Brest and two ship captains said.
label: Truguet to the Directory, 6 November 1796: letters from Brest 'announce that a general revolution has just taken place in Ireland'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1810 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a letter from Malta of 24 August 1810, headed 'Bad news from Tunis' in several papers: 'A very unpleasant business has taken place between the Bey of Tunis and our Consul. It seems an American ship was captured by a French privateer, and carried into Tunis, where she was purchased by a minister of the Bey'; it tells that the ship's former supercargo appealed at Malta to have her stopped, and that the Bey, hearing of it, confiscated the American property in Tunis. A report at second hand.
label: Malta, 24 August 1810: 'A very unpleasant business has taken place between the Bey of Tunis and our Consul'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of President Jefferson's message to Congress on the dispute with Tunis, read in the House on 14 April 1806: 'During the blockade of Tripoli by the squadron of the U. S. a small cruiser, under the flag of Tunis, with two prizes' tried to enter the port. The executive's own account.
label: The President's message on Tunis, April 1806

admission_rule: Reviewed 1797 passages describing the Two Sisters wreck off Bantry Bay, checked against the scan.
definition: Printed accounts of the Rhode Island ship Two Sisters found wrecked off Bantry Bay in August 1797: a reprinted hand-bill and a summary attributed to the Irish papers. Different wording; the wreck itself is not independently verified.
label: Two Sisters wreck

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a letter to the editor of the Moniteur (the Louisiana Monitor) of New Orleans, dated 12 September 1804: 'The following memorial was addressed by the Ursuline Nuns of this city to the President of the United States', with the memorial ('Emboldened by the favourable mention you have been pleased to make of their Order, the Nuns of Ursula ...') and the President's answer ('I have received, holy Sisters, the letter you have written me, wherein you express anxiety for the property vested in your institution, by the former governments of Louisiana'). Jenks' Portland Gazette prints the memorial and the answer without the letter to the editor. The nuns' and the President's own words.
label: The Ursuline nuns of New Orleans to the President, and his answer, 1804

admission_rule: Reviewed 1782 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph first printed by the New-Hampshire Gazette: 'We learn from good authority, that the inhabitants of the territories of the State of Vermont did, on the 21st of Feb. last, relinquish all claims to the unions which they had formed on the eastern side of Connecticut river; as also the western union, which contained part of the State of New-York; the Representatives who composed said union, have returned to...' A report from good authority, as the papers say.
label: March 1782: 'the inhabitants of the territories of the State of Vermont did, on the 21st of Feb. last, relinquish all claims to the unions which they had formed'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1783 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph from Versailles of 28 March 1783: 'On the 25th of this month, the king received some official dispatches from M. de Suffrein, which after giving a detail of the late proceedings in the East Indies between the French and English fleets, as has been already mentioned, conclude as follow', with what the dispatches report of the fighting near Madras. The French court's account of the dispatches, in the European news.
label: Versailles, 28 March 1783: the King receives official dispatches from M. de Suffren on the proceedings in the East Indies

admission_rule: Reviewed 1789 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a report from Croatia in a Vienna paragraph dated 13 May 1789: 'They write from Croatia, that on the 12th of April, 1000 Turkish cavalry attacked a post of the Bannat—five villages belonging to the Bosnians, which were under the imperial protection, experienced the fury of the enemy ...'. Three papers print it after a report that the Emperor is ill ('Our august Sovereign is again ill ...'); the Kentucky Gazette prints it alone under the dateline. Counted by its own opening sentence.
label: Vienna, 13 May 1789: 'They write from Croatia, that on the 12th of April, 1000 Turkish cavalry attacked a post of the Bannat'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph dated Strasburgh, 17 November 1805, from French papers that reached New York in January 1806: 'The city of Vienna has just opened its gates for the first time to a victorious army. This glory was reserved for Frenchmen.' A report from the French side.
label: Strasburgh, 17 November 1805: Vienna opens its gates

admission_rule: Reviewed 1797 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a report from Vienna dated 26 July 1797, printed from the London papers in two forms. Three papers print a short form: 'The Marquis DE GALLO, has this moment arrived here from Udina. The negotiations for peace in Italy, meet with great difficulties. The French require that Mantua shall be united with the Cisalpine Republic' (the Mirror's words). The Gazette of the United States and the Kentucky Gazette print a longer form that opens with the Marquis de Gallo's conferences with the Emperor and Baron Thugut, and adds that 'neither the marquis nor the persons about the court had very pleasant countenances'. Both forms then give the same account of the French demand for Mantua, the Emperor's indemnification in Istria and Dalmatia, and 'our fears that hostilities may again commence'. A correspondent's report, at second hand through the London papers.
label: Vienna, 26 July 1797: the peace talks in Italy 'meet with great difficulties'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1773 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Vienna paragraph of May 1773 (dated 25 May in the New England papers, 15 May in the Virginia papers): 'The freshest advices from Constantinople say, that they intend to push on the war with the utmost vigour against the Russians; that several couriers had been dispatched with orders ...'. A report from Vienna, as the London papers gave it and the papers reprinted it.
label: Vienna, May 1773: 'The freshest advices from Constantinople say, that they intend to push on the war with the utmost vigour against the Russians'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1794 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Vienna paragraph: 'Letters, and particularly the official accounts from Warsaw, of the 9th inst.—give the most ample details of the circumstances attending the retreat of the Prussians on the night between the 5th and 6th'. A report from Vienna, as the papers printed it.
label: Vienna, 26 September 1794: the retreat of the Prussians from Warsaw

admission_rule: Reviewed 1783 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Richmond paragraph of 7 June 1783: 'The honorable general assembly have voted an immediate payment of 50,000l. to Congress; and the funds out of which this money is directed to be paid, being fully equal to that demand, it affords sensible pleasure that Virginia, by the wisdom of the legislature, will retrieve her character of good faith and exertion among the United States'. A Richmond paper's report and comment.
label: Richmond, 7 June 1783: 'The honorable general assembly have voted an immediate payment of 50,000l. to Congress'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1774 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the resolution of the Virginia House of Burgesses of 24 May 1774, 'which was directed to be forthwith printed and published': 'This House being deeply impressed with apprehension of the great dangers to be derived to British America, from the hostile invasion of the city of Boston, in our sister colony of Massachusetts Bay, whose commerce and harbour are on the 1st day of June next to be stopped by an armed force, deem it highly necessary that the said first day of June be set apart by the members of this House as a day of fasting, humiliation and prayer'. The House of Burgesses' own resolution.
label: Williamsburg, 24 May 1774: the House of Burgesses sets apart 1 June, the day the port of Boston is to be shut, as a day of fasting, humiliation and prayer

admission_rule: Reviewed 1773 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the resolutions of the Virginia House of Burgesses of 12 March 1773 appointing a standing committee of correspondence and enquiry: 'Whereas the minds of his Majesty's faithful subjects in this colony have been much disturbed by various rumours and reports of proceedings tending to deprive them of their ancient, legal, and constitutional rights ...'. A published document, as the papers printed it; other houses' resolutions answering it are other texts.
label: Williamsburg, 12 March 1773: the House of Burgesses' resolutions: 'Whereas the minds of his Majesty's faithful subjects in this colony have been much disturbed by various rumours and reports of proceedings tending to deprive them of their ancient, legal, and constitutional rights'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1788 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the Virginia convention's ratification: 'We the delegates of the people of Virginia, duly elected, in pursuance of a recommendation of the General Assembly, and now met in Convention, having fully and fairly investigated and discussed the proceedings of the Federal Convention'. The convention's own act.
label: The Virginia convention's act ratifying the Constitution, June 1788

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the Virginia Convention's resolutions of 15 May 1776, which instructed the colony's delegates to propose that Congress declare the colonies free and independent states.
label: Virginia Convention, 15 May 1776

admission_rule: Reviewed 1810 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a letter from a gentleman on board the United States brig Vixen, Lieutenant Trippe, which the National Intelligencer published with its own account of the affair: 'On the 24th inst. [June] an occurrence took place, which was equally unpleasant and unexpected. The character of the affair however, corresponds with the treatment which we have so often received from the British naval commanders on former occasions. The Moselle, a 20 gun brig'; it tells how the Moselle fired at the Vixen near the Bahama bank, how her commander, Captain Boyce, answered that he 'was extremely sorry for having fired at us', and how the Vixen made sail. Eight papers print it after the Intelligencer's paragraph ('We are informed that on the 24th June, 1810, the United States brig Vixen ... was, in a wanton and unprovoked manner, fired into'); the Rhode-Island Republican prints the letter with remarks of its own. Counted by the letter, which every paper prints (X-1803-02). A report at second hand by a writer on board.
label: The brig Vixen fired on by the British brig Moselle near the Bahamas, 24 June 1810: a letter from a gentleman on board

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a publication from the Philadelphia Political Register, dated 20 September 1804 in two papers: 'In the discharge of an important, and to myself an indispensable duty, the subjoined statement was communicated, in the first instance, to the government.—In a respectful solicitude for the rights and interest of our country the deposition and letters are now made public. W. Jackson.' The statement, deposition and letters that follow concern the Marquis de Casa Yrujo, the Spanish minister. One side's own account.
label: W. Jackson's statement in the Political Register, September 1804, with a deposition and letters concerning the Spanish minister

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the War Department's circular to the state governors, 29 April 1809: 'I am directed by the President of the United States to inform your Excellency that the detachment of ... Militia, made in pursuance of a communication to your Excellency from this Department' may be discharged. The papers print the copies sent to different governors (10,198 men for Virginia). The Portland Gazette calls it a circular 'for disbanding the Militia'.
label: The War Department's circular to the governors on the militia, 29 April 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan (round three: stories once held back for framing, at the 6-paper threshold for 1793).
definition: Printings of a Philadelphia paragraph of early September 1793: by an express to the War Office from the commissioners for treating with the Indian nations north of the Ohio, they 'were not able even to effect a meeting' with the nations assembled at the rapids of the Miami river; the nations' deputation 'insisted upon the Ohio as the boundary between them and the United States', and, 'as so extensive a concession was inadmissible', the commissioners left on 17 August. It names the Wyandots, Delawares, Shawanese and Miamis as 'determined for war', says that a considerable part of them were for peace, and that the Six Nations, with Captain Brandt (Brant) and his Mohawks, urged peace. The United States government's account, as the papers printed it.
label: The War Office on the treaty commissioners, September 1793

admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the address of 'His Excellency George Washington, Esq; Commander in Chief of the Army of the United Colonies of North-America. To the Inhabitants of Canada. Friends and Brethren', which the papers say was to be published in Canada on the arrival there of Colonel Arnold with the troops under his command: it asks the Canadians to join the cause of liberty and says the army comes not to plunder but to protect them. General Washington's own address.
label: General Washington's address to the inhabitants of Canada, to be published on Colonel Arnold's arrival there (September 1775)

admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the address 'To the Inhabitants of New-Jersey, Pennsylvania, Maryland and Virginia. Friends, Countrymen and Fellow Citizens! After three campaigns, during which the brave subjects of these States have contended, not unsuccessfully, with one of the most powerful kingdoms on earth, we now find ourselves at least upon a level with our opponents'; it recommends that the inhabitants put up and feed as many of their stock-cattle as they can spare, so that they may be driven to the army in May, June and July, and promises a bounty. General Washington's own address, from headquarters at Valley Forge, as the papers printed it from the New-Jersey Gazette of 25 February.
label: General Washington's address to the inhabitants of New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Maryland and Virginia, February 1778: cattle to be fattened for the army

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: The letters on the exchange of prisoners that the papers printed in April 1777 (Lord Cornwallis's letter of 3 April with Lieutenant Colonel Walcott's demand, General Washington's letter to General Howe of 9 April) and in June and July 1777, by order of Congress of 16 June (General Howe's letter of 21 April, General Washington's answer of 10 June). Each letter is counted by its own words (X-1810-01). Contains those four groups.
label: Letters between General Washington and the British commanders on the exchange of prisoners, published in April and June 1777

admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of General Washington's answer to the address of the Massachusetts Provincial Congress: 'Gentlemen, Your kind congratulations on my appointment and arrival, demand my warmest acknowledgments, and will ever be retained in grateful remembrance. In exchanging the enjoyments of domestic life for the duties of my present honourable, but arduous station, I only emulate the virtue and public spirit of the whole province of the Massachusetts-Bay'. The general's own answer.
label: General Washington's answer to the Massachusetts Provincial Congress, July 1775: 'Your kind congratulations on my appointment and arrival demand my warmest acknowledgments'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1780 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of General Washington's general orders of 20 July 1780: 'The Commander in Chief has the pleasure to congratulate the army on the arrival of a large land and naval armament at Rhode Island, sent by his Most Christian Majesty ...'; black and white cockades recommended, 'emblematic of the expected union of the two armies'. Printed with two introductions (C-02). The commander's own orders.
label: General Washington's general orders, 20 July 1780, congratulating the army on the arrival of the French fleet and army

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of General Washington's letter to Congress from Chadds Ford, 11 September 1777, 5 p.m.: 'When I had the honor of addressing you this morning, I mentioned that the enemy were advancing, and had began a cannonade; I would now beg leave to inform you, that they have kept up a brisk fire from their artillery ever since'; their advanced party was attacked by General Maxwell's light troops. The commander's own report.
label: General Washington to Congress, Chadds Ford, 11 September 1777, five in the afternoon: the enemy have kept up a brisk fire from their artillery

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of General Washington's letter to Congress from Chester, 11 September 1777, at midnight: 'I am sorry to inform you that in this day's engagement we have been obliged to leave the enemy masters of the field. Unfortunately, the intelligence received of the enemy's advancing up the Brandywine, and crossing at a ford about six miles above us, was uncertain and contradictory'. Published by order of Congress. The commander's own report.
label: General Washington to Congress, Chester, 11 September 1777, midnight: 'in this day's engagement we have been obliged to leave the enemy masters of the field'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1782 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of General Washington's letter to Congress, Head-Quarters, 10 May 1782: 'Just as I am closing these dispatches, a letter from Sir Guy Carleton is handed me, covering sundry printed papers, a copy of which, with the papers, I have now the honour to enclose to your Excellency, together with a copy of my answer to him...', with the letter of Sir Guy Carleton, the British commander at New York, that it encloses ('...upon this one point we must perfectly concur, being alike interested to preserve the name of Englishmen from reproach, and individuals from experiencing such unnecessary evils, as can have no effect upon a general decision...'). Printed by all six newspapers that survive for its weeks, the New-York Gazette and the Royal Gazette of Charleston among them; admitted by the rule's first part. The commanders' own letters.
label: General Washington to Congress, 10 May 1782: 'Just as I am closing these dispatches, a letter from Sir Guy Carleton is handed me', with Sir Guy Carleton's letter

admission_rule: Reviewed 1779 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of General Washington's letter to the President of Congress, Head-Quarters, New-Windsor, 16 July 1779, 'Half after nine o'clock, A. M.', published by order of Congress: 'I have the pleasure to transmit your Excellency the inclosed copy of a letter from Brigadier General Wayne, which this moment came to hand. I congratulate Congress upon our success...', with General Wayne's note to him from Stony Point at two in the morning: 'The fort and garrison with Col. Johnston are ours. Our officers and men behaved like men who are determined to be free.' The commanders' own letters.
label: General Washington to Congress, New Windsor, 16 July 1779, 'half after nine o'clock, A. M.', with General Wayne's note from Stony Point: 'The fort and garrison ... are ours'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1779 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of General Washington's letter to the President of Congress, Head-Quarters, New-Windsor, 21 July 1779: 'On the 16th instant I had the honor to inform Congress of a successful attack upon the enemy's post at Stony-Point, on the preceding night, by Brigadier General Wayne, and the corps of light infantry under his command...', with General Wayne's report from Stony Point of 17 July ('a full and particular relation of the reduction of this point, by the light infantry under my command') and the return of the killed and wounded, published by order of Congress. The commanders' own letters.
label: General Washington to Congress, New Windsor, 21 July 1779, with General Wayne's report of 17 July on the reduction of Stony Point

admission_rule: Reviewed 1780 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of General Washington's letter to the President of Congress, Morristown, 18 January 1780: 'The severity of the weather having rendered a descent upon Staten-Island practicable by the ice ...', with Lord Stirling's report of the expedition enclosed (one item, X-1810-01). The commander's own letter.
label: General Washington to Congress, Morristown, 18 January 1780, on the descent upon Staten Island over the ice, with Lord Stirling's report

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of General Washington's letter to Congress of 25 June 1777: 'When I had the honour to address you last, it was on the subject of the enemy's retreat from Brunswick to Amboy, and of the measures pursued to annoy them'; he writes that their loss fell chiefly on the grenadiers and light infantry who covered the retreat. The commander's own report.
label: General Washington to Congress, Quibbletown, 25 June 1777: on the enemy's retreat from Brunswick to Amboy and their loss

admission_rule: Reviewed 1780 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of General Washington's letter to Congress, Head Quarters, Bergen County, 26 July 1780: 'Having received information that there were considerable numbers of cattle and horses in Bergen Neck, within reach of the enemy ... I detached Brigadier General Wayne, on the 20th, with the first and second Pennsylvania brigades ...'. The commander's own letter.
label: General Washington to Congress, Bergen County, 26 July 1780: General Wayne sent to Bergen Neck for the cattle; the blockhouse

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of General Washington's letter to Congress of 28 June 1777: 'On Thursday morning General Howe advanced with his whole army, in several columns, from Amboy as far as Westfield'; he judges the design was to bring on a general engagement on disadvantageous terms or to cut off the light parties and Lord Stirling's division. The commander's own report.
label: General Washington to Congress, Middlebrook, 28 June 1777: General Howe advanced with his whole army from Amboy as far as Westfield

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of General Washington's letter to General Howe of 10 June 1777: 'Your several letters of the 21st of April, 22d of May, and 5th instant, have been received. Having stated my sentiments in an explicit manner, in my letter of the ninth of April, upon the subject of your demand'; as General Howe has called upon him for his final determination, he gives it. The commander's own letter.
label: General Washington to General Howe, Middlebrook, 10 June 1777: his final determination on the exchange of prisoners

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of General Washington's letter to General Howe of 16 July 1777: 'The fortune of war having thrown Major General Prescott into our hands, I beg leave to propose his exchange for that of Major General Lee'; most papers print it after his letter to Congress of 25 July, 'I do myself the honour to transmit you a copy of my letter to General Howe, of the 16th instant, proposing an exchange between Generals Lee and Prescott', and the New-York Gazette prints it alone, from the Pennsylvania Packet. A letter and the copy it sends are one item, counted by the first that stands on the page (X-1810-01). Of the same affair, General Washington's letter to Congress of 16 July on the capture (4 papers) and the Providence account of it (4) are not chosen (X-1800-01); Congress's resolutions of 25 July thank Lieutenant Colonel Barton. The commander's own letters.
label: General Washington to General Howe, 16 July 1777, proposing General Prescott, taken at Rhode Island, in exchange for General Lee, with his letter of 25 July sending it to Congress

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of General Washington's letter to General Howe of 9 April 1777: 'I take the liberty of transmitting you a copy of a paper addressed to me by Lieut. Col. Walcott of your army, which came inclosed in a letter from Lieut. Gen. Lord Cornwallis'; he answers the demand, says the prisoners returned to him had been so treated that they could not be deemed fit for exchange, and holds that the discrimination made in the case of General Lee is an obstacle to compliance. Purdie's Virginia Gazette prints a summary of it in its own words (not counted, C-07). The commander's own letter.
label: General Washington to General Howe, 9 April 1777, on Lieutenant Colonel Walcott's demand and the exchange of prisoners

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: General Washington's two letters to Congress of 11 September 1777, from Chadds Ford at five in the afternoon and from Chester at midnight, printed together in most papers. Contains those two groups.
label: General Washington's letters to Congress of 11 September 1777 on the battle on the Brandywine

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Extracts of General Washington's letters to Congress of 25 and 28 June 1777, on the British army's retreat from Brunswick to Amboy and on General Howe's advance from Amboy towards Westfield, as the papers printed them in July and August. Each letter is counted by its own words; his letter of 20 June (4 papers) is not chosen (X-1800-01). Contains those two groups.
label: General Washington's letters to Congress of 25 and 28 June 1777 on the British army's retreat to Amboy and its advance to Westfield

admission_rule: Reviewed 1783 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the orders of 18 April 1783: 'The commander in chief orders the cessation of hostilities between the united states of America and the king of Great-Britain, to be publicly proclaimed to morrow at twelve o'clock, at the new building; and that the proclamation, which will be communicated herewith, be read to morrow evening at the head of every regiment and corps of the army; after which the chaplains, with the several brigades, will render thanks to Almighty God'. The commander in chief's own orders.
label: Head-quarters, 18 April 1783: General Washington's orders that the cessation of hostilities be publicly proclaimed to the army

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the account of the interview of 20 July 1776 between General Washington and Colonel Patterson, General Howe's adjutant general.
label: Washington meets Colonel Patterson

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of General Washington's proclamation given at headquarters, Morristown, 25 January 1777: 'Whereas several persons, inhabitants of the United States of America, influenced by inimical motives, intimidated by the threats of the enemy, or deluded by a proclamation issued the 30th of November last, by Lord and General Howe, styled the King's commissioners for granting pardons, &c. ... have been so lost to the interest and welfare of this country, as to repair to the enemy, sign a declaration of fidelity'; it commands everyone who has taken such protections to repair to headquarters or the nearest general officer, deliver them up and take the oath of allegiance to the United States, or withdraw within the enemy's lines. The New-York Gazette prints it with its own heading. The commander's own proclamation.
label: General Washington's proclamation of 25 January 1777 on inhabitants who signed the British commissioners' declaration of fidelity

admission_rule: Reviewed 1777 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of General Washington's proclamation of 24 October 1777 (printed in November and December): 'Whereas sundry soldiers belonging to the armies of the said states have deserted from the same, these are to make known to all those who have so offended, and who shall return to their respective corps ... before the first day of January next, that they shall obtain a full and free pardon'; those who do not may expect the punishment of the law. The commander's own proclamation.
label: General Washington's proclamation of 24 October 1777: a full and free pardon to deserters who return to their corps before 1 January

admission_rule: Reviewed 1779 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a proclamation 'By His Excellency George Washington, Esq. General and Commander in Chief of the Forces of the United States of America': 'Whereas it hath been represented, that many of those soldiers who have been induced from divers motives to desert their corps, and are now dispersed in different parts of these States, having seen their error, would be glad to return to their duty, but are restrained by the fear of punishment... I do hereby proclaim full pardon to all those who shall rejoin their respective corps by the first of May next', with a warning to those who do not. Given at Head-Quarters, Middlebrook, 10 March 1779. The Pennsylvania Packet printed it in four issues. The commander in chief's own proclamation.
label: General Washington's proclamation of 10 March 1779: 'full pardon to all those who shall rejoin their respective corps by the first of May next'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1802 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph from Washington of 13 October 1802: 'We understand that letters have been received in this country from Algiers, as late as the 7th of July, which furnish the following information: The Dey of Algiers has demanded of the American Consul to direct the United States frigate the George Washington, to be brought to Algiers, for the purpose of being sent by the Dey to Constantinople'; the Dey later turned to the consuls of nearer nations; a Tripolitan corsair brought the American brig Franklin into Algiers as a prize; Spain bought off a threatened war. A report at second hand, from letters the paragraph does not name.
label: Washington, 13 October 1802: 'letters have been received in this country from Algiers, as late as the 7th of July'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of General Washington's letter to the President of Congress dated Englishtown, 1 July 1778: 'I embrace this first moment of leisure to give Congress a more full and particular account of the movements of the army under my command, since its passing the Delaware, than the situation of our affairs would heretofore permit'. The commander's own account to Congress.
label: General Washington to Congress, Englishtown, 1 July 1778: a full account of the movements of the army and the action of 28 June

admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of General Washington's letter to Congress dated Valley Forge, 24 May 1778: 'On the night of the 19th the enemy moved out in force against the detachment under the Marquis la Fayette, mentioned in my letter of the 18th, which made a timely and handsome retreat'. The commander's own report to Congress, as the York-Town paper published the extract on 30 May.
label: General Washington to Congress, Valley Forge, 24 May 1778: the enemy's move against the Marquis de la Fayette's detachment

admission_rule: Reviewed 1781 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of General Washington's letter of 19 October 1781: 'Head quarters, near York, 19th October, 1781. Sir, I have the honour to inform Congress, that a reduction of the British army under the command of lord Cornwallis is most happily effected', printed with Lord Cornwallis's and General Washington's letters of 17 and 18 October and the articles of capitulation. General Washington's own account; one publication, counted by its opening (X-1810-01).
label: General Washington to the President of Congress, near York, 19 October 1781, with the correspondence and the articles of capitulation

admission_rule: Reviewed 1794 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the general's letter: 'Head Quarters Grand Glaize, 28 Aug. 1794. Sir, It is with infinite pleasure that I now announce to you the brilliant success of the Federal army under my command, in a general action with the combined force of the hostile Indians, and a considerable number of the volunteers and militia of Detroit on the 20th instant on the banks of the Miamis'. The American commander's own words.
label: General Wayne's letter of 28 August 1794 to the Secretary of War on the action of 20 August on the banks of the Miamis

admission_rule: Reviewed 1810 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the Marquis Wellesley's letter to Mr. Pinkney, dated Foreign Office, 14 March 1810: 'The letter which I had the honor to receive from you under date of the 2d of January, together with the additional paragraph received on the 24th January, has been laid before the king'; it says that Mr. Jackson 'does not appear, on the present occasion, to have committed any intentional offence against the government of the United States', and that 'Mr. Jackson is ordered to deliver over the charge of his Majesty's affairs in America, to a person properly qualified to carry on the ordinary intercourse between the two governments'. The Delaware Gazette prints it with remarks of its own. The British Secretary of State's own letter.
label: Lord Wellesley's answer to Mr. Pinkney, Foreign Office, 14 March 1810: Mr. Jackson to deliver over the charge of his Majesty's affairs

admission_rule: Reviewed 1810 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the declaration that the representatives of the people of West Florida, in convention at Baton Rouge, signed on 26 September 1810: 'It is known to the world with how much fidelity the good people of this territory have professed and maintained allegiance to their legitimate sovereign while any hope remained of receiving from him protection for their property and lives'; it declares West Florida a free and independent state, and the representatives pledge themselves to support it with their lives and fortunes. Several papers print it again in December with other papers of the convention. A sub-story in 6 papers under a parent in 9 (C-01). The convention's own declaration.
label: The declaration of the convention of West Florida, Baton Rouge, 26 September 1810

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Two reports from Natchez, in the Mississippi Territory, of an armed party that marched from near the line with Spanish West Florida against the fort of Baton Rouge in August 1804 and posted a paper declaring West Florida free. Contains those two groups.
label: An armed party marches against the Spanish fort of Baton Rouge in West Florida, August 1804: two reports from Natchez

admission_rule: Reviewed 1810 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Four texts on the Spanish province of West Florida, between the Mississippi and the Perdido, as the papers printed them from October to December 1810: a Natchez report of the taking of the Spanish fort of Baton Rouge, the declaration of the convention of West Florida of 26 September, a letter from Washington, Mississippi Territory, of 30 October, and the President's proclamation of 27 October directing that possession be taken of the territory as far as the Perdido. Contains those four groups.
label: West Florida, September to December 1810: the fort of Baton Rouge taken, the convention's declaration, a letter from the Mississippi Territory and the President's proclamation

admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a report of late July 1775: 'Captain Lowndes, from Dominica, and Captain Hodge, from St. Kitts, confirm the above accounts' (of the Parliament House pulled down and Lord North fled to France), adding that a ship had arrived at St. Eustatia from Amsterdam with the same news. A report at second and third hand of a rumour from the West Indies; the papers print it as news.
label: New York, July 1775: captains from Dominica and St. Kitts are said to confirm the report that the Parliament House was pulled down and Lord North fled to France

admission_rule: Reviewed 1800 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph of London news: 'It was on the 29th ult. that Lord Whitworth signed the Convention with Count Bernstorff, the Danish Minister. The following is a note written by his Lordship to one of our Ministers abroad on the subject', followed by the note ('I have the satisfaction to acquaint you that I yesterday signed a convention with the Danish Minister, on terms satisfactory to his Majesty') and, in most papers, what the London paper gives as its principal articles: 'The Danish frigate and convoy, carried into Deal, shall be repaired at the expense of Great-Britain, and then released', and the question of the right to visit convoys adjourned to a negotiation in London. A London paper's report with the British envoy's own note.
label: London, September 1800: Lord Whitworth's convention with Denmark, and his note

admission_rule: Reviewed 1773 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a letter of John Wilkes to Sir Fletcher Norton, Speaker of the House of Commons, dated Prince's Court, 20 April 1773: 'In pursuance of your orders to the Sheriff of Middlesex, on the 7th of this month, to summon the Representatives of this County, I have received a letter from Richard Oliver, Esq; and Sir Watkin Lewes ...'. A letter in its writer's words, as the papers reprinted it (an 'attested copy' in two papers).
label: Prince's Court, 20 April 1773: Mr. Wilkes's letter to Sir Fletcher Norton, Speaker of the House of Commons: 'In pursuance of your orders to the Sheriff of Middlesex, on the 7th of this month, to summon the Representatives of this County, I have received a letter from Richard Oliver, Esq; and Sir Watkin Lewes'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1771 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a letter of John Wilkes to Sir Fletcher Norton, the Speaker of the House of Commons, dated London, 20 March 1771: 'I this morning received an order commanding my attendance this day in the House of Commons. I observe that no notice was taken of me in your order as a member of the House, and that I am not required to attend in my place ... In the name of the freeholders of Middlesex, I again demand my seat in Parliament ...'. Both Virginia Gazettes print it after a London paragraph of 22 March ('Mr. Wilkes, on Tuesday, having been served with an order to attend the House of Commons on Wednesday, wrote the following letter to Sir Fletcher Norton'); the Massachusetts Spy and the New-Hampshire Gazette print it under a heading of their own. A letter in its writer's words, as the papers reprinted it.
label: London, 20 March 1771: Mr. Wilkes's letter to Sir Fletcher Norton: 'I this morning received an order commanding my attendance this day in the House of Commons ... In the name of the freeholders of Middlesex, I again demand my seat in Parliament'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the speech of John Wilkes, Lord Mayor of London, in the House of Commons on the motion for an address to the King at the opening of the session in October 1775, against the war in America.
label: Wilkes's speech in the Commons

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Documents and reports of the charges that General James Wilkinson had taken money from the Spanish government, as the 1808 papers printed them: his challenge to John Randolph and Randolph's answer (December 1807), Daniel Clark's statement to the House, the President's message of 20 January, and the opinion of the military court of inquiry (printed from 4 July). Contains those four groups. The statement and the letters are allegations and each writer's own account; the court found no evidence.
label: Charges against General Wilkinson, 1808

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the opinion of the military court of inquiry at Washington on General Wilkinson (signed by its president, Colonel Burbeck, and approved by the President), printed from 4 July 1808: it found no evidence that Wilkinson had received a pension or money from the Spanish government for corrupt purposes.
label: The court of inquiry's opinion on Wilkinson

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan (round two: stories once held back for framing, at the year's 7-paper rule).
definition: Printings of notes exchanged at Baltimore on 26 and 27 October 1808, as published there: General James Wilkinson's note to Captain Robert Goodloe Harper, commanding a company of volunteer artillery, charging that Harper had 'secretly assailed the General's honour' and demanding 'the only admissible atonement'; Harper's refusal, which says that his advice to Mr. Clark to lay before Congress documents on Wilkinson's 'connection with the Spanish government' gave no ground for a challenge; and Wilkinson's reply. Each man's own words. The papers print them under their own introductions or headings, such as 'MODERN CHIVALRY' and '"HECTOR" AGAIN.'
label: General Wilkinson's challenge to Robert Goodloe Harper, October 1808

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
