definition: Printings of an extract of a letter of General Wilkinson, dated Rapids of Red River, 19 September 1806: 'My orders, and the conduct of the Mexicans, are so much at variance'; 'I fear you will be informed blood has been spilt'. The American commander's own account, with his forecast.
label: General Wilkinson's letter from the Rapids of Red River, 19 September

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract from the orders of General Wilkinson 'given at the camp of the American troops, on the left bank of the Mississippi, near the city of New Orleans, Dec. 17, 1803', with the parole 'Columbia': 'The operation before us, however simple or safe, will require much self denial and restraint'; the orders tell the troops how they are to conduct themselves on entering the city. A commander's orders, as printed.
label: General Wilkinson's orders at the camp near New Orleans, 17 December 1803: 'The operation before us, however simple or safe, will require much self denial and restraint'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of two letters of 24 and 25 December 1807, from a pamphlet: General James Wilkinson asks John Randolph, a member of the House, for satisfaction for words injurious to his reputation, and Randolph refuses. Each letter is its writer's own account.
label: Wilkinson's challenge and Randolph's answer

admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan (round two: stories once held back for framing, at the year's 7-paper rule).
definition: Printings of General Wilkinson's address to the court at New Orleans, as a letter from that city of 18 December 1806 reports it (Washington, 21 January 1807): appearing on a writ of habeas corpus for a man he had arrested, he said he was 'called to account for an act in which I glory', warned that 'the artifices of the confederates' must no longer 'cheat the public judgment' and that 'treason stalks abroad', and spoke of 'the friends of Burr and rebellion'. The report adds that he then charged two lawyers with being parties to the conspiracy. The general's own words, as the letter gives them.
label: General Wilkinson's speech in the court at New Orleans

admission_rule: Reviewed 1770 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Williamsburg paragraph of 18 October 1770: 'On Monday the 15th instant, about one o'clock in the morning, departed this life, universally lamented throughout this colony, his Excellency the Right Honourable Norborne Baron de Botetourt, his Majesty's Lieutenant and Governor General of the colony and dominion of Virginia ...'. A report of the governor's death, in the Virginia papers' words. Proclamations and notices that only name the governor are not counted.
label: Williamsburg, 18 October 1770: 'On Monday the 15th instant, about one o'clock in the morning, departed this life, universally lamented throughout this colony, his Excellency the Right Honourable Norborne Baron de Botetourt'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1797 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a report from Wilmington, North Carolina, of 12 October 1797: 'A gentleman who arrived in town on Sunday last from New-Providence, via the Havannah, has favored the Printer with the following information—on the authenticity of which he places the greatest confidence': on 20 August, the day he left Pensacola, he saw an official letter from the Baron de Carondelet saying that orders had come from his court 'to put into full execution, the treaty between Spain and the United States of America', and that the commandants of the forts on the Mississippi were to deliver up the posts; Governor Gayoso had been appointed governor-general of the Floridas and Louisiana. A traveller's report at second hand.
label: Wilmington, 12 October 1797: a traveller from Pensacola reports orders to deliver up the Spanish posts

admission_rule: Reviewed 1787 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph from the Wilmington Gazette, late September 1787: 'his Excellency General Washington passed through Wilmington, on his return from Philadelphia to his seat in Mount Vernon, and on the same day, in crossing the bridge near the Head of Elk, the bridge gave way and his horse fell into the river. His Excellency had alighted in order to walk over the bridge, which fortunate circumstance probably saved a life so dear to his country'. A report from a paper, at second hand.
label: Wilmington, September 1787: General Washington, returning to Mount Vernon, alights to walk over the bridge near the Head of Elk, which gives way

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from a gentleman at Wythe Court-House, Virginia, to his friend in Frederick-Town, Maryland, dated 30 July 1804: 'We have for 12 days been clouded with a dark smoke, and this day I was informed by a gentleman from Kentucky that the Clinch Mountain had sunk for many miles to the depth of 50 feet'; the writer supposes it 'occasioned by the burning of the stone coal which is in the mountain'. Two papers print a shorter form headed 'Singular Phenomenon', without the date and with 'for ten days'; the Rhode-Island Republican also prints 'ten days', and the Norfolk Gazette 'twelve days' in words. A report at second hand: the writer passes on what a traveller told him.
label: A letter from Wythe Court-House, Virginia, 30 July 1804: 'the Clinch Mountain had sunk'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: The Marquis de Casa Yrujo, Spain's minister to the United States, and the American government in January 1806: his circular to the other foreign ministers against the President's message, and the letter in which the Secretary of State told him that the President expected his departure, with his answers. Contains those two groups.
label: The Spanish minister Yrujo and the government, 1806

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the circular of the Marquis de Casa Yrujo to the foreign ministers in the United States, dated Philadelphia, 21 January 1806, in a translation from the French: 'The want of correctness which appears to prevail throughout the article, relative to Spain, of the message' of the President. With his note to the Secretary of State. The Spanish minister's own account.
label: Yrujo's circular to the foreign ministers

admission_rule: Reviewed 1803 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the Spanish minister's letter to the Secretary of State of 19 April 1803, which the National Intelligencer published as an important letter 'sent by Express to New-Orleans': 'I have the pleasure to impart to you, without a moment's delay, that by dispatches which I have just received from my government, brought by a Brig of war of the King my master, dispatched for this purpose alone, I see confirmed all the assurances which I gave you'; his Catholic Majesty 'has provided that the deposit should continue at New-Orleans until the two governments shall come to an agreement about another equivalent place', and the orders to the Intendant and the Captain-General of Louisiana are enclosed for forwarding. The Spanish minister's own letter.
label: The Marquis de Casa Yrujo's letter to the Secretary of State, 19 April 1803: the deposit to continue at New Orleans

admission_rule: Reviewed 1803 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the translation, published by the National Intelligencer as official, of the Spanish minister's letter to the Secretary of State of 10 March 1803: 'When you represented to me towards the end of November last, that the port of New Orleans had been shut against the citizens of the United States, without the assignment of any equivalent place of deposit for their merchandise on the Banks of the Mississippi'; 'I have now the satisfaction of informing you that my first opinion has been verified, and of declaring in the most positive terms, that the proclamation of the Intendant is an act purely personal, without the sanction and even without the knowledge of his Catholic Majesty'. The National Intelligencer printed it again on 30 March ('We, therefore, re-insert it'). The Spanish minister's own letter.
label: The Marquis de Casa Yrujo's letter to the Secretary of State, 10 March 1803: the Intendant's proclamation 'an act purely personal'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a letter from the Spanish minister to the Secretary of State, published in the National Intelligencer of 5 October 1804 'at the request of the Marquis de Casa Yrujo': 'Having been absent from Philadelphia for these 18 days past and travelled far into a part of Virginia where I had no opportunity to see the late newspapers from the Northward', he answers the publication in the Political Register (the other group). The minister's own account; the New Hampshire Gazette and the Kentucky Gazette misprint his name 'Trujo' (their transcriptions read 'Trujillo'), and the Oracle Post prints the letter over two issues.
label: The Marquis de Casa Yrujo's letter to the Secretary of State, published at his request, October 1804
